items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a GS-12 Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency’s Small Business/Self- Employed Division, Specialty Collection– Insolvency Office in Houston, Texas. On September 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment on the bases of disability (Major Depression, Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety, TIA, Myofascial Pain, Acute Stress Disorder) and reprisal (prior protected EEO activity) when: 1. 1.Beginning February 2021 to the present, she has been denied paid leave under the Family Medical and Leave Act (FMLA); 2. On June 19, 2021, a manager reassigned all of a retired co-worker’s complex cases to her; 3. On August 3, 2021, she was denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave; 4. On August 24, 2021, her final appeal of a requested reasonable accommodation was denied; and 5. On October 26, 2021, her supervisor denied her official time request to work on her EEO complaint. Claims 1 & 3 – Leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) Complainant challenged leave issues, including her receipt of Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and placement in Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status in a prior EEO complaint before an EEOC Administrative Judge. On May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge in that case found that the Agency had proven that it had placed Complainant in AWOL and LWOP status on various dates in February and March 2021, because Complainant had depleted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work. In the instant complaint, Complainant again raised leave issues previously adjudicated, including her February and March 2021 receipt of AWOL charges and placement in LWOP status. Complainant also alleges that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave. Complainant’s first-line supervisor (Supervisor1) explained that management’s calculations showed that Complainant had exhausted her paid, available sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, the Agency’s February 26, 2021, letter to Complainant regarding her request for FMLA provided that Complainant had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA to use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. As such, on March 1, 2021, and on other dates, Supervisor notified Complainant that she had no paid leave available to use under FMLA. On various dates, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor granted Complainant FMLA-LWOP, rather than paid leave. Complainant did not request an audit of her leave until August 5, 2021. The audit of Complainant’s leave, conducted by a payroll representative, showed that Complainant had some paid leave available to use under FMLA. Accordingly, management retroactively granted Complainant paid leave, including for August 3, 2021. Complainant conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave that she requested and was entitled to receive. Complainant did not identify any similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding leave. Claim 2 – Reassignment of Casework In June 2021, one of Complainant’s GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired. Complainant claimed that Supervisor emailed Complainant (a GS- 12) and two other GS-12 employees in the group to inform them that the now- retired employee’s cases would be reassigned among the three GS-12s. Complainant asserted that she should not have been reassigned this casework because she had previously submitted a request for reasonable accommodation and believed she should have been on indefinite weather and safety leave. 2 The Administrative Judge found that Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave, and that the Agency had met all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal is currently pending and docketed as EEOC [number removed]. Supervisor explained that she reassigned the cases because it was her job to assign inventory to employees in her group. Supervisor also explained that all reassigned work was appropriate for Complainant’s grade level. Supervisor further explained that the work was split among Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists in the group, based upon the alphabetical order of case names. The documentary record also contains a spreadsheet, provided by Supervisor1, showing the case assignments to Complainant and the two other Bankruptcy Specialists in the group. The record is devoid of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding this claim. Claim 4 –Reasonable Accommodations On May 6, 2021, Complainant requested the following accommodations: (1) that her manager and/or secretary assistant print and mail her letters; and (2) a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her reasonable accommodation request to include reassignment. Complainant concedes that her medical impairment does not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. The Agency’s Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator met with Complainant on May 21, 2021, to hold an interactive meeting. Regarding her request for reduced workload and/or reassignment, the Agency issued a denial, noting that there was no medical explanation supporting Complainant’s need for such accommodations. The Agency’s denial also noted that lowering Complainant’s caseload would lower performance or production standards and would compromise the Agency’s ability to achieve its mission. Moreover, with an inventory of then only 25 cases, the undisputed record showed that Complainant already maintained a caseload well below other Bankruptcy Specialists and below the number of cases she typically held. 3 Regarding her request for reassignment, the Agency’s denial noted that Complainant was not eligible for reassignment because it is the accommodation of last resort (i.e., granted only when an employee is unable to meet the essential functions of her position). For example, to support a previous 2018 request for reduced inventory, Complainant’s psychologist had noted that Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38-40 cases. When Complainant requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency explained that Complainant failed to submit medical documentation supporting that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence showed that Complainant wished to be reassigned because she had an unpleasant working relationship with her supervisors, and not because of any medical impairment’s effect on her ability to perform the essential functions of her job. To accommodate Complainant’s physical limitations, in response to Complainant’s May 6, 2021 reasonable accommodation request, the Agency approved Complainant to receive a small portable printer so that she could print and mail letters to taxpayers. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. Before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket cancelling the printer because she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Complainant later averred that she would not be able to lift either the smaller printer or its paper. The Agency denied Complainant’s request for reconsideration of her reasonable accommodation denial. On July 12, 2021, Complainant appealed the Agency’s denial of her reconsideration request. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations (Director) denied Complainant’s appeal. The denial noted that Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency’s offer to provide her with a smaller portable printer that she could lift. Further, the denial noted that Complainant had an already-reduced workload and was not eligible for reassignment because she was capable of performing the essential functions of her job. Claim 5 – Official Time On October 20, 2021, Complainant requested to use official time from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20 through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021, to respond to an EEO Investigator’s request that Complainant complete an affidavit for the instant complaint. Complainant availed herself of six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four hours on October 21, 2021. Despite being provided these hours, Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional time on October 25, 2021. On October 25, 2021, Supervisor approved Complainant’s request to use additional official time that day. On October 26, 2021, Complainant emailed the Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline to complete her affidavit. In response, OCRD noted that Complainant could request an extension from the investigator if she needed more time to complete the affidavit. After receiving OCRD’s response, Complainant asked Supervisor for official time to complete the affidavit that day. When Supervisor asked Complainant if she had completed the affidavit, Complainant told Supervisor that she had two questions remaining. Because Complainant had already received approximately 18 hours of official time and because OCRD had instructed Complainant to contact the investigator if she needed an extension of her deadline, Supervisor denied Complainant’s request to continue working on her affidavit on official time on October 26, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC AJ. Complainant timely requested a hearing. The AJ issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency. In the decision, the AJ determined that the alleged incidents were insufficiently severe or pervasive to establish a hostile work environment. Further, the AJ found that there was no evidence demonstrating that the conduct at issue was based on discriminatory or retaliatory animus. For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.
items.record:
# INVESTIGATION RECORD AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION

## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT STATUS

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Grade 12 (GS-12) Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency's Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office, located in Houston, Texas. On September 17, 2021, the Complainant filed a formal complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Commission, alleging that the Agency had discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment. The Complainant based her allegations on two protected grounds: disability and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity.

The Complainant identified multiple physical and mental health conditions as the basis for her disability claim, specifically: Major Depression with Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA), Myofascial Pain Syndrome, and Acute Stress Disorder.

## SUMMARY OF ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY ACTS

The Complainant's complaint enumerated five separate incidents that she contended constituted discrimination and/or retaliation. These allegations span a period from February 2021 through October 2021 and include the following: (1) denial of paid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) from February 2021 onward; (2) reassignment of complex cases from a retired co-worker on June 19, 2021; (3) denial of eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave on August 3, 2021; (4) denial of her final appeal regarding a requested reasonable accommodation on August 24, 2021; and (5) denial of an official time request to work on her EEO complaint on October 26, 2021.

## ANALYSIS OF LEAVE ISSUES (CLAIMS 1 AND 3)

The Complainant raised leave-related grievances that had been previously addressed in prior EEO proceedings before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In that prior proceeding, dated May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had properly established its case regarding the Complainant's Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status during February and March 2021. The Administrative Judge determined that these placements were justified because the Complainant had exhausted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work on the relevant dates.

In the present complaint, the Complainant again raised substantially similar leave issues, including the February and March 2021 AWOL charges and LWOP status. Additionally, the Complainant alleged that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied her request for eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave.

The Complainant's first-line supervisor (referred to herein as Supervisor1) provided documentation showing that management's calculations had determined that the Complainant had exhausted her available paid sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, a letter dated February 26, 2021, addressed to the Complainant regarding her FMLA request indicated that she had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA available for use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. Accordingly, beginning March 1, 2021, and on subsequent dates, Supervisor1 notified the Complainant that no paid leave remained available for use under FMLA provisions. On the various dates in question, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor1 granted the Complainant FMLA Leave Without Pay status rather than paid leave, as no paid leave was available according to the Agency's calculations.

However, the Complainant did not request a formal audit of her leave balance until August 5, 2021. Upon conducting this audit, a payroll representative discovered that the Complainant actually had some paid leave available for use under FMLA. Following this discovery, the Agency retroactively granted the Complainant paid leave status for the disputed dates, including August 3, 2021. Significantly, the Complainant acknowledged and conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave to which she was entitled.

In evaluating this claim, the record was examined for evidence of similarly situated employees who had been treated more favorably with respect to leave entitlements and FMLA administration. No such evidence was identified.

## ANALYSIS OF CASE REASSIGNMENT (CLAIM 2)

In June 2021, one of the Complainant's GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired from the Agency. Following this retirement, the Complainant's supervisor emailed the Complainant and two other GS-12 employees in their work group to inform them that the retiring employee's cases would be reassigned among the three remaining GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists.

The Complainant objected to receiving any of the reassigned cases, asserting that she should not have been included in the distribution because she believed she was entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave status and that a prior reasonable accommodation request should have been honored. An Administrative Judge in a separate proceeding found that the Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency had satisfied all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal of this determination remains pending.

Supervisor1 explained that the reassignment of cases was performed as part of her regular managerial duties to distribute work inventory among employees in her group. Supervisor1 further explained that all reassigned work was appropriate and suitable for the Complainant's grade level. The supervisor noted that work was distributed among the Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based upon an objective, neutral method: the alphabetical order of case names. Supervisor1 provided a spreadsheet documenting the case assignments to the Complainant and her two co-workers, which supported her testimony regarding the allocation method.

The investigative record contained no evidence of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding case assignments and workload distribution.

## ANALYSIS OF REASONABLE ACCOMMODATIONS (CLAIM 4)

On May 6, 2021, the Complainant submitted a formal request for reasonable accommodations under the Rehabilitation Act. This initial request sought two specific accommodations: (1) that her manager or secretary assistant print and mail her letters to taxpayers, and (2) a reduction in her workload. On May 18, 2021, the Complainant amended her request to include job reassignment as an additional accommodation.

Notably, the Complainant conceded during the investigative process that her medical impairments did not limit her ability to perform any essential functions of her position as a Bankruptcy Specialist.

The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator conducted an interactive meeting with the Complainant on May 21, 2021, as required by law. Following this meeting, the Agency issued a denial of the requested reduced workload and reassignment accommodations. The denial letter explained that no medical documentation had been submitted that supported the necessity for such accommodations. The Agency further noted that reducing the Complainant's caseload would lower performance and production standards, thereby compromising the Agency's ability to achieve its mission and serve the public effectively.

The record demonstrated, without dispute, that the Complainant maintained a caseload of only 25 cases at the time of her request. This caseload was substantially lower than those carried by other Bankruptcy Specialists in the office and below the typical number of cases the Complainant herself had historically managed.

With respect to the reassignment request, the Agency denied this accommodation, explaining that reassignment is considered the accommodation of last resort and is granted only when an employee is unable to perform the essential functions of their position. The Agency cited evidence from a 2018 request in which the Complainant's psychologist had noted that the Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38 to 40 cases. When the Complainant had previously requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency noted that she had failed to submit medical documentation establishing that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence suggested that the Complainant sought reassignment due to interpersonal difficulties with her supervisors, not because of any limitation imposed by her medical conditions on job performance.

With respect to the letter printing and mailing request, the Agency approved the Complainant's request and offered to provide her with a small, lightweight, portable printer that she could operate independently. While awaiting delivery of this printer, the Agency agreed to temporarily have the Complainant's correspondence printed and mailed by her manager. However, before the printer was delivered, the Complainant submitted a cancellation ticket, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its materials. The Complainant subsequently asserted that she would be unable to lift either the printer or its paper supplies. Despite this change in position, the Agency's management continued to print and mail the Complainant's correspondence for her.

On July 12, 2021, the Complainant appealed the Agency's denial of reconsideration regarding her reasonable accommodation requests. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations issued a decision denying the Complainant's appeal. The Director's decision noted that the Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency's offer to provide an accommodating device that was specifically designed to address her stated needs. The decision further emphasized that the Complainant maintained an already-reduced workload relative to peers and was not eligible for reassignment, as the record demonstrated she was capable of performing all essential functions of her position.

## ANALYSIS OF OFFICIAL TIME REQUEST (CLAIM 5)

On October 20, 2021, the Complainant requested official time to respond to an EEO Investigator's request that she complete and submit an affidavit in connection with her discrimination complaint. The Complainant's request specified a time period extending from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20, 2021, through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021.

Supervisor1 approved the Complainant's request. The Complainant utilized six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four additional hours on October 21, 2021, for a total of ten hours. Despite the provision of these hours, the Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional official time on October 25, 2021. Supervisor1 approved this subsequent request as well.

On October 26, 2021, the Complainant emailed the Agency's Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline for completing the affidavit. OCRD responded by informing the Complainant that she could directly request an extension from the EEO Investigator if she required additional time.

Following receipt of OCRD's response, the Complainant requested additional official time from Supervisor1 on October 26, 2021. When Supervisor1 inquired regarding the Complainant's progress on the affidavit, the Complainant indicated that she had only two remaining questions. Given that the Complainant had already been granted approximately eighteen hours of official time for this task and given that OCRD had explicitly directed the Complainant to contact the investigator directly for extension requests, Supervisor1 denied the Complainant's request for continued official time on October 26, 2021.

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. The Complainant timely requested such a hearing.

The Administrative Judge issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency on all claims. The Administrative Judge determined that the alleged incidents were neither sufficiently severe nor sufficiently pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment under applicable law. Furthermore, the Administrative Judge found that no evidence in the record demonstrated that the conduct at issue was motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

Specifically with respect to the leave claims, the Administrative Judge noted that the Complainant had failed to demonstrate that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes had been treated more favorably regarding FMLA and other leave entitlements.

Regarding the case reassignment, the Administrative Judge found that the record evidence clearly established that cases from the retired co-worker were split equally among the Complainant and two other Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers based on unrebutted, legitimate reasons related to grade level, skill level, and appropriateness of assignment given the Complainant's comparatively low existing workload.

With respect to the reasonable accommodations claim, the Administrative Judge noted that the Complainant's May 6, 2021 request specifically sought assistance with printing and mailing letters and requested a reduced workload. The amended request on May 18, 2021 included a request for reassignment. The Administrative Judge emphasized that the Complainant had admitted during investigation that her impairments did not limit her ability to perform essential job duties. Furthermore, the Complainant had produced no probative evidence that the accommodations previously offered by the Agency—including a post of duty with telework options away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable her to perform her essential functions.

The Administrative Judge found that the Agency properly denied the request for reduced inventory, noting that agencies are not required to lower production standards or employee quotas. The Complainant provided no evidence establishing that she could not adequately perform her assigned cases given her unusually low inventory of 25 cases.

Regarding the printer accommodation, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had, following the interactive meeting, approved the Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery, the Agency had agreed to print and mail the Complainant's correspondence. However, before delivery, the Complainant cancelled the order, stating she did not wish accountability for the equipment and supplies. The Agency continued to provide printing and mailing services. Accordingly, the Administrative Judge concluded that the Agency did not deny reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.

Finally, the Administrative Judge found that eighteen hours of official time was objectively reasonable for completing an affidavit, particularly given that the Complainant was largely restating information and documentation from previous complaints.

## FINAL AGENCY ACTION

The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the Administrative Judge's findings and conclusions. The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to establish by preponderant evidence that the Agency had subjected her to discrimination, reprisal, or hostile work environment as alleged in her complaint.

For example, Complainant failed to show that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes were treated more favorably by being granted FMLA or other leave entitlements. Additionally, the record evidence showed that the reassigned cases from the retired, former coworker were split equally amongst Complainant and two of her Bankruptcy Specialists coworkers for unrebutted reasons relative to grade, skill level and appropriateness given Complainant’s low workload. With respect to her denial of reasonable accommodation claim, the AJ determined that in her May 6, 2021 request, Complainant requested that her manager and/or secretary assist her to print and mail her letters and also requested a reduced workload. On May 18, 2021, Complainant amended her request to include reassignment. During the investigation of the instant complaint, Complainant admitted that her impairment did not limit her ability to perform any essential job duties. Moreover, she did not adduce any probative evidence that previously offered accommodations—a post of duty (with telework) away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable the Complainant to perform the essential functions of her position. Further, the AJ found that the record supported the Agency’s denial of Complainant’s request for a reduced inventory. An agency is not required to change production standards, e.g., to lower an employee’s quota for cases. Complainant provided no evidence that she could not adequately perform her assignments given she had an unusually low inventory of only 25 cases. Finally, the AJ concluded that the undisputed record showed, after an interactive meeting, the Agency approved Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery of the smaller printer, Complainant’s management agreed to send Complainant’s correspondence for her. However, before the printer was delivered, Complainant submitted a ticket requesting cancellation of the printer delivery, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its paper. Management continued to print and mail her letters. As a result, the AJ found that the Agency did not deny Complainant reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Finally, the AJ found that the Agency’s grant of 18 hours of official time was objectively reasonable for Complainant to complete her affidavit despite the investigators’ numerous questions. The record showed that Complainant’s time was spent including information and documentation she previously provided in previous complaints. The Agency was entitled to limit the Complainant’s use of official time to 18 hours to complete her affidavit for this complaint and to have her seek additional time from the investigator. Accordingly, the AJ concluded that Complainant was not subjected to discrimination, reprisal, or a hostile work environment as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION

## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT STATUS

At the time of the events giving rise to this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Grade 12 (GS-12) Senior Bankruptcy Specialist with the Agency's Small Business/Self-Employed Division, Specialty Collection–Insolvency Office, located in Houston, Texas. On September 18, 2021, the Complainant filed a formal complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Commission, alleging that the Agency had discriminated against her and subjected her to a hostile work environment. The Complainant based her allegations on two protected grounds: disability and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity.

The Complainant identified multiple physical and mental health conditions as the basis for her disability claim, specifically: Major Depression with Recurrence, Somatic Symptoms Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder, Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA), Myofascial Pain Syndrome, and Acute Stress Disorder.

## SUMMARY OF ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY ACTS

The Complainant's complaint enumerated five separate incidents that she contended constituted discrimination and/or retaliation. These allegations span a period from February 2021 through October 2021 and include the following: (1) denial of paid leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) from February 2021 onward; (2) reassignment of complex cases from a retired co-worker on June 19, 2021; (3) denial of eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave on August 3, 2021; (4) denial of her final appeal regarding a requested reasonable accommodation on August 24, 2021; and (5) denial of an official time request to work on her EEO complaint on October 26, 2021.

## ANALYSIS OF LEAVE ISSUES (CLAIMS 1 AND 3)

The Complainant raised leave-related grievances that had been previously addressed in prior EEO proceedings before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In that prior proceeding, dated May 25, 2022, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had properly established its case regarding the Complainant's Absent Without Leave (AWOL) charges and Leave Without Pay (LWOP) status during February and March 2021. The Administrative Judge determined that these placements were justified because the Complainant had exhausted her available paid leave balances and failed to report to work on the relevant dates.

In the present complaint, the Complainant again raised substantially similar leave issues, including the February and March 2021 AWOL charges and LWOP status. Additionally, the Complainant alleged that on August 3, 2021, her manager denied her request for eight hours of paid FMLA sick leave.

The Complainant's first-line supervisor (referred to herein as Supervisor1) provided documentation showing that management's calculations had determined that the Complainant had exhausted her available paid sick leave by March 2021. Specifically, a letter dated February 26, 2021, addressed to the Complainant regarding her FMLA request indicated that she had only 32 hours of unpaid FMLA available for use between March 1, 2021, and December 3, 2021. Accordingly, beginning March 1, 2021, and on subsequent dates, Supervisor1 notified the Complainant that no paid leave remained available for use under FMLA provisions. On the various dates in question, including August 3, 2021, Supervisor1 granted the Complainant FMLA Leave Without Pay status rather than paid leave, as no paid leave was available according to the Agency's calculations.

However, the Complainant did not request a formal audit of her leave balance until August 5, 2021. Upon conducting this audit, a payroll representative discovered that the Complainant actually had some paid leave available for use under FMLA. Following this discovery, the Agency retroactively granted the Complainant paid leave status for the disputed dates, including August 3, 2021. Significantly, the Complainant acknowledged and conceded that she ultimately received all paid leave to which she was entitled.

In evaluating this claim, the record was examined for evidence of similarly situated employees who had been treated more favorably with respect to leave entitlements and FMLA administration. No such evidence was identified.

## ANALYSIS OF CASE REASSIGNMENT (CLAIM 2)

In June 2021, one of the Complainant's GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers retired from the Agency. Following this retirement, the Complainant's supervisor emailed the Complainant and two other GS-12 employees in their work group to inform them that the retiring employee's cases would be reassigned among the three remaining GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists.

The Complainant objected to receiving any of the reassigned cases, asserting that she should not have been included in the distribution because she believed she was entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave status and that a prior reasonable accommodation request should have been honored. An Administrative Judge in a separate proceeding found that the Complainant was not entitled to indefinite weather and safety leave and that the Agency had satisfied all its obligations under the Rehabilitation Act. The appeal of this determination remains pending.

Supervisor1 explained that the reassignment of cases was performed as part of her regular managerial duties to distribute work inventory among employees in her group. Supervisor1 further explained that all reassigned work was appropriate and suitable for the Complainant's grade level. The supervisor noted that work was distributed among the Complainant and the two other GS-12 Bankruptcy Specialists based upon an objective, neutral method: the alphabetical order of case names. Supervisor1 provided a spreadsheet documenting the case assignments to the Complainant and her two co-workers, which supported her testimony regarding the allocation method.

The investigative record contained no evidence of similarly situated employees who were treated more favorably regarding case assignments and workload distribution.

## ANALYSIS OF REASONABLE ACCOMMODATIONS (CLAIM 4)

On May 6, 2021, the Complainant submitted a formal request for reasonable accommodations under the Rehabilitation Act. This initial request sought two specific accommodations: (1) that her manager or secretary assistant print and mail her letters to taxpayers, and (2) a reduction in her workload. On May 18, 2021, the Complainant amended her request to include job reassignment as an additional accommodation.

Notably, the Complainant conceded during the investigative process that her medical impairments did not limit her ability to perform any essential functions of her position as a Bankruptcy Specialist.

The Agency's Reasonable Accommodations Coordinator conducted an interactive meeting with the Complainant on May 21, 2021, as required by law. Following this meeting, the Agency issued a denial of the requested reduced workload and reassignment accommodations. The denial letter explained that no medical documentation had been submitted that supported the necessity for such accommodations. The Agency further noted that reducing the Complainant's caseload would lower performance and production standards, thereby compromising the Agency's ability to achieve its mission and serve the public effectively.

The record demonstrated, without dispute, that the Complainant maintained a caseload of only 25 cases at the time of her request. This caseload was substantially lower than those carried by other Bankruptcy Specialists in the office and below the typical number of cases the Complainant herself had historically managed.

With respect to the reassignment request, the Agency denied this accommodation, explaining that reassignment is considered the accommodation of last resort and is granted only when an employee is unable to perform the essential functions of their position. The Agency cited evidence from a 2018 request in which the Complainant's psychologist had noted that the Complainant desired a reduced inventory of approximately 38 to 40 cases. When the Complainant had previously requested reassignment as a reasonable accommodation in March 2020, the Agency noted that she had failed to submit medical documentation establishing that she was unable to meet the essential functions of her position. Rather, the evidence suggested that the Complainant sought reassignment due to interpersonal difficulties with her supervisors, not because of any limitation imposed by her medical conditions on job performance.

With respect to the letter printing and mailing request, the Agency approved the Complainant's request and offered to provide her with a small, lightweight, portable printer that she could operate independently. While awaiting delivery of this printer, the Agency agreed to temporarily have the Complainant's correspondence printed and mailed by her manager. However, before the printer was delivered, the Complainant submitted a cancellation ticket, stating that she did not wish to be held accountable for the printer and its materials. The Complainant subsequently asserted that she would be unable to lift either the printer or its paper supplies. Despite this change in position, the Agency's management continued to print and mail the Complainant's correspondence for her.

On July 12, 2021, the Complainant appealed the Agency's denial of reconsideration regarding her reasonable accommodation requests. On August 24, 2021, the Director of Collection Operations issued a decision denying the Complainant's appeal. The Director's decision noted that the Complainant had summarily rejected the Agency's offer to provide an accommodating device that was specifically designed to address her stated needs. The decision further emphasized that the Complainant maintained an already-reduced workload relative to peers and was not eligible for reassignment, as the record demonstrated she was capable of performing all essential functions of her position.

## ANALYSIS OF OFFICIAL TIME REQUEST (CLAIM 5)

On October 20, 2021, the Complainant requested official time to respond to an EEO Investigator's request that she complete and submit an affidavit in connection with her discrimination complaint. The Complainant's request specified a time period extending from approximately 10:30 a.m. on October 20, 2021, through 11:30 a.m. on October 21, 2021.

Supervisor1 approved the Complainant's request. The Complainant utilized six hours of official time on October 20, 2021, and four additional hours on October 21, 2021, for a total of ten hours. Despite the provision of these hours, the Complainant did not complete her affidavit and requested additional official time on October 25, 2021. Supervisor1 approved this subsequent request as well.

On October 26, 2021, the Complainant emailed the Agency's Department of Treasury, Office of Civil Rights and Diversity (OCRD) to request an extension of her deadline for completing the affidavit. OCRD responded by informing the Complainant that she could directly request an extension from the EEO Investigator if she required additional time.

Following receipt of OCRD's response, the Complainant requested additional official time from Supervisor1 on October 26, 2021. When Supervisor1 inquired regarding the Complainant's progress on the affidavit, the Complainant indicated that she had only two remaining questions. Given that the Complainant had already been granted approximately eighteen hours of official time for this task and given that OCRD had explicitly directed the Complainant to contact the investigator directly for extension requests, Supervisor1 denied the Complainant's request for continued official time on October 26, 2021.

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

Upon conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. The Complainant timely requested such a hearing.

The Administrative Judge issued a summary judgment decision in favor of the Agency on all claims. The Administrative Judge determined that the alleged incidents were neither sufficiently severe nor sufficiently pervasive to constitute a hostile work environment under applicable law. Furthermore, the Administrative Judge found that no evidence in the record demonstrated that the conduct at issue was motivated by discriminatory or retaliatory animus.

Specifically with respect to the leave claims, the Administrative Judge noted that the Complainant had failed to demonstrate that similarly situated employees outside of her protected classes had been treated more favorably regarding FMLA and other leave entitlements.

Regarding the case reassignment, the Administrative Judge found that the record evidence clearly established that cases from the retired co-worker were split equally among the Complainant and two other Bankruptcy Specialist co-workers based on unrebutted, legitimate reasons related to grade level, skill level, and appropriateness of assignment given the Complainant's comparatively low existing workload.

With respect to the reasonable accommodations claim, the Administrative Judge noted that the Complainant's May 6, 2021 request specifically sought assistance with printing and mailing letters and requested a reduced workload. The amended request on May 18, 2021 included a request for reassignment. The Administrative Judge emphasized that the Complainant had admitted during investigation that her impairments did not limit her ability to perform essential job duties. Furthermore, the Complainant had produced no probative evidence that the accommodations previously offered by the Agency—including a post of duty with telework options away from her manager and communication primarily by email—did not enable her to perform her essential functions.

The Administrative Judge found that the Agency properly denied the request for reduced inventory, noting that agencies are not required to lower production standards or employee quotas. The Complainant provided no evidence establishing that she could not adequately perform her assigned cases given her unusually low inventory of 25 cases.

Regarding the printer accommodation, the Administrative Judge found that the Agency had, following the interactive meeting, approved the Complainant for a lightweight, portable printer. While awaiting delivery, the Agency had agreed to print and mail the Complainant's correspondence. However, before delivery, the Complainant cancelled the order, stating she did not wish accountability for the equipment and supplies. The Agency continued to provide printing and mailing services. Accordingly, the Administrative Judge concluded that the Agency did not deny reasonable accommodation in violation of the Rehabilitation Act.

Finally, the Administrative Judge found that eighteen hours of official time was objectively reasonable for completing an affidavit, particularly given that the Complainant was largely restating information and documentation from previous complaints.

## FINAL AGENCY ACTION

The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the Administrative Judge's findings and conclusions. The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to establish by preponderant evidence that the Agency had subjected her to discrimination, reprisal, or hostile work environment as alleged in her complaint.

# CASE FILE DOCUMENT

## Investigation Summary and Disposition

**Complainant Position:** Carrier Technician, Garland-South Station, Garland, Texas

**Complaint Filing Date:** April 17, 2021

**Basis of Complaint:** Disability Discrimination (Physical – Neck and Shoulder Injury) under the Rehabilitation Act

---

## Allegations and Timeline

The complainant alleged that her supervisor, the Manager of Customer Service, subjected her to discriminatory treatment based on her disability throughout a period spanning November 2020 through April 2021. The specific allegations include:

Beginning in November 2020, the complainant was continuously questioned regarding her work restrictions and denied work assistance. Despite documented medical restrictions, she was required to complete the walking portion of her mail route beginning November 9, 2020, and continuing thereafter.

On December 23, 2020, the complainant was reprimanded in a manner she characterized as yelling and public embarrassment in the presence of coworkers. On the same date, she was directed to submit a new CA-17 form (employee injury documentation) without compensation for time spent obtaining completion of this document. Additionally, on this date, she was reassigned from Route 74 to Route 23, requiring her to perform casing and carrying duties.

On February 1, 2021, the complainant was summoned to supervisory desk to discuss her medical documentation. On March 23, 2021, she reported harassment and was subsequently referred to the District Reasonable Accommodation Committee (DRAC). Following denial of a leave request on April 2, 2021, the complainant was charged with Absent Without Leave (AWOL), despite her assertion that the leave request had been previously approved by the Supervisor of Customer Service. Finally, on or about April 15, 2021, management assigned her modified duties with a 10:00 a.m. start time but failed to provide a mail cart to assist with her work duties.

---

## Collateral Attack Dismissal

The complainant filed an additional claim alleging that she was attacked by a dog while performing her duties and was not properly compensated for missed work time. The Agency dismissed this claim under 29 C.F.R. §1614.107(a)(1) as a collateral attack on the Office of Workers' Compensation Programs (OWCP), which maintains exclusive jurisdiction over work-related injury compensation matters. This dismissal was affirmed consistent with established Commission precedent prohibiting use of the EEO complaint process to challenge OWCP adjudicatory proceedings.

---

## Central Allegations

The core allegations constitute claims of Rehabilitation Act violations, specifically that the Manager subjected the complainant to harassment based on disability and compelled her to work outside medically prescribed restrictions. The complainant further contended that the denial of a mail cart—despite prior leave approval—constituted discriminatory treatment.

---

## Adjudication and Final Disposition

Following investigation completion, the complainant was provided a copy of the investigation report and notice of her right to request an Administrative Judge hearing. Although the complainant requested a hearing, the Administrative Judge denied the request as a sanction for failure to submit required Preliminary Case Information and failure to respond to the Order to Show Cause. The matter was remanded to the Agency, which issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), concluding that the complainant failed to establish discriminatory conduct by the Agency.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full-time Mail Handler Equipment Operator at the Agency’s Morgan Processing and Distribution Center facility in New York, New York. On November 18, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), disability (physical), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII and the Rehabilitation Act when: 1. On June 25, 2021, and ongoing, she was denied overtime work within her limitations; 2. On July 19, 2021, she was verbally abused by a coworker and no action was taken; 2 3. Beginning on August 1, 2021, and ongoing, she was micromanaged and assigned to either the rewrap section or city manual section and/or confronted about her job duties; and 4. On August 31, 2021, her request for a temporary change of schedule was denied. After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency indicated that, on April 5, 2022, it transmitted to Complainant and her non-attorney representative a copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing (Notice) before an EEOC AJ. On April 5, 2022, the Agency emailed Complainant and her representative, stating that a copy of the final ROI was available for download for a period of 30 days and requesting that the parties send an email confirming receipt. CF at 98-103. The record contains an April 5, 2022, message reflecting that the message was relayed to Complainant and her representative but that the destination server did not send a delivery notification. CF at 97. The Agency initially accepted the following for investigation: “On July 20, 2021, you were verbally abused by a supervisor and no action was taken.” CF at 60. Complainant clarified during the investigation that this incident occurred on July 19, 2021, that it was a coworker who verbally abused her, and that, when she reported it to supervisors, nothing was done about it. CF at 205-08. Also on April 5, 2022, the Agency provided Complainant and her representative 3 with a copy of documents that were submitted after the completion of the investigative file, asking that they be added to Complainant’s copy of the recently submitted file. CF at 85-96. The documents consist of an Acting Supervisor’s investigative affidavit, completed on March 28, 2022, and the Acting Supervisor’s Litigation Hold Notice, which was signed on March 31, 2022. CF at 86-95. In the affidavit, the Acting Supervisor stated that he had no organizational relationship to Complainant during the relevant time and that he was not at the facility on July 20, 2021. CF at 86-93. On May 17, 2022, the Agency again emailed Complainant and her non- attorney representative, notifying them that an electronic copy of the ROI would be available for download for a period of 30 days. CF at 82-83. The record contains a May 17, 2022, message reflecting that the message was relayed to Complainant and her representative but that the destination server did not send a delivery notification. CF at 84. On May 31, 2022, Complainant mailed a hearing request to the Agency and to the Commission’s New York District Office. CF at 40-42. The Agency stamped the mailing envelope and the hearing request form as received on June 6, 2022. CF at 40, 42. Complainant included a May 28, 2022, letter with her hearing request, in which she stated that, after receiving the Acting Supervisor’s affidavit in April 2022, she wanted to refute his response that he was not present on the date of the incident and requested a copy of his Employee Everything Report from the Agency. CF at 41. According to Complainant, on May 18, 2022, she called an EEO Services Analyst to refute the Acting Supervisor’s statement, and the EEO Services Analyst told her that her case was closed on May 1, 2022. CF at 41. Complainant averred that she asked how her case could be closed if she and her representative had not been notified or received a copy of the ROI. CF at 41. Complainant stated that the EEO Services Analyst told her that she could request a hearing but should attach a letter stating that she found out her case was closed on May 18, 2022. CF at 41. It appears that these documents were provided to Complainant and her representative via first class mail. CF at 85. On June 2, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision. The Agency stated that it was issuing the decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) because Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged. On June 10, 2022, the EEOC’s New York District Office received Complainant’s hearing request, which was docketed as Hearing No. 520- 2022-00326X. On June 15, 2022, Complainant filed the instant appeal. On July 6, 2022, the Agency provided Complainant and her representative with documents that were submitted after the completion of the investigative file, asking that they be added to Complainant’s copy of the recently submitted file. CF at 1-10. The document is an updated June 7, 2022, affidavit from the Acting Supervisor. CF at 2-10. The Acting Supervisor stated that, during the timeframe of the complaint, his organizational relationship with Complainant was Acting Supervisor. CF at 2. The Acting Supervisor stated that he was not present when the coworker verbally abused Complainant on July 19, 2021, and that he did not know if Complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported any harassment. CF at 4-9. On November 29, 2022, an EEOC AJ issued an order dismissing Complainant’s hearing request, noting that the Agency had already issued a final decision, which Complainant had appealed.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD AND CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## COMPLAINANT INFORMATION AND EMPLOYMENT STATUS

The complainant in this matter was employed as a Full-time Mail Handler Equipment Operator at the Agency's Morgan Processing and Distribution Center facility located in New York, New York at the time of the events giving rise to this complaint. The complainant's employment status and job classification remained consistent throughout the relevant period under investigation.

## COMPLAINT FILING AND ALLEGATIONS

On November 18, 2021, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency. The complaint alleged that the Agency discriminated against the complainant on multiple protected bases, specifically citing sex (female), disability (physical), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. The legal framework for these allegations encompasses protections under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Rehabilitation Act.

The complaint encompassed four distinct categories of alleged discriminatory conduct occurring over a five-month period. First, beginning on June 25, 2021, and continuing thereafter, the complainant alleged that she was denied overtime work within her stated limitations. Second, on July 19, 2021, the complainant asserted that she was subjected to verbal abuse by a coworker, and that no remedial action was taken by management when the incident was reported. Third, beginning on August 1, 2021, and ongoing, the complainant alleged that she was subjected to micromanagement, was assigned to either the rewrap section or city manual section in a manner suggesting discriminatory intent, and was confronted regarding her job duties. Fourth, on August 31, 2021, the complainant alleged that her request for a temporary change of schedule was denied in a manner consistent with discriminatory treatment.

## AGENCY INVESTIGATION AND REPORT OF INVESTIGATION

Following completion of its investigation into the complaint, the Agency transmitted a Report of Investigation (ROI) and Notice of Right to Request a Hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) to the complainant and her non-attorney representative on April 5, 2022. Concurrent with this transmission, the Agency emailed both parties, indicating that an electronic copy of the final ROI would be available for download for a period of thirty days and requesting confirmation of receipt via email. Documentary evidence in the case file reflects that the message was relayed to the complainant and her representative; however, the destination server did not provide a delivery notification, creating ambiguity regarding actual receipt.

It is noteworthy that the Agency initially accepted a formulation of the coworker verbal abuse allegation that differed from the complainant's original statement. The Agency's initial framing dated the incident as July 20, 2021, and characterized the alleged abuser as a supervisor rather than a coworker. During the investigation, the complainant clarified that the incident occurred on July 19, 2021, that it was indeed a coworker (not a supervisor) who engaged in the verbal abuse, and that supervisory personnel failed to take corrective action after she reported the incident.

## ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTS AND AFFIDAVITS

On April 5, 2022, coinciding with transmission of the ROI, the Agency provided the complainant and her representative with additional documents that had been submitted after the completion of the investigative file, requesting that these materials be added to the complainant's copy of the file. These supplementary documents included an investigative affidavit from an Acting Supervisor, completed on March 28, 2022, and the Acting Supervisor's Litigation Hold Notice, signed on March 31, 2022. In this initial affidavit, the Acting Supervisor stated that he maintained no organizational relationship to the complainant during the relevant time period and that he was not present at the facility on July 20, 2021.

On May 17, 2022, the Agency again emailed the complainant and her representative, advising that an electronic copy of the ROI would be available for download for thirty days. Similar to the prior transmission, the Agency's system indicated that the message was relayed but that the destination server did not provide a delivery notification. The documentary evidence suggests that materials were ultimately provided via first-class mail.

## COMPLAINANT'S RESPONSE AND HEARING REQUEST

On May 31, 2022, the complainant mailed a formal hearing request to both the Agency and the Commission's New York District Office. The Agency's stamped records indicate receipt on June 6, 2022. Accompanying the hearing request was a letter dated May 28, 2022, in which the complainant expressed her intent to refute statements made by the Acting Supervisor in his affidavit, particularly his claim that he was not present on the date of the verbal abuse incident. The complainant requested that the Agency provide her with the Acting Supervisor's Employee Everything Report to corroborate his presence or absence on that date.

According to the complainant's account, on May 18, 2022, she contacted an EEO Services Analyst to discuss the Acting Supervisor's contradictory statements. The complainant alleged that the EEO Services Analyst informed her that her case had been closed on May 1, 2022. When the complainant questioned how her case could be closed without notification or provision of a copy of the ROI, she was reportedly instructed that she could file a hearing request but should attach a letter explaining that she discovered the case closure date of May 18, 2022.

## SUBSEQUENT AGENCY DECISION AND APPEAL

On June 2, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision, citing 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) as the basis for the decision and asserting that the complainant failed to submit a hearing request within the timeframe specified in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The Agency concluded in its decision that the complainant failed to establish that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged in her complaint.

The EEOC's New York District Office received the complainant's hearing request on June 10, 2022, which was subsequently docketed as Hearing No. 520-2022-00326X. On June 15, 2022, the complainant filed an appeal of the Agency's final decision.

## UPDATED AGENCY AFFIDAVIT AND ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION

On July 6, 2022, the Agency submitted an updated affidavit from the Acting Supervisor, requesting that this document also be added to the complainant's file. In this revised affidavit dated June 7, 2022, the Acting Supervisor provided substantially different testimony. He stated that, during the timeframe of the complaint, his organizational relationship with the complainant was that of Acting Supervisor. The Acting Supervisor reiterated that he was not present when the coworker verbally abused the complainant on July 19, 2021, and stated that he did not know whether the complainant or anyone acting on her behalf reported the harassment incident.

On November 29, 2022, an EEOC Administrative Judge issued an order dismissing the complainant's hearing request, noting that the Agency had already issued a final decision on the matter, which the complainant had appealed.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Level 1 City Carrier at the Agency’s Meadow Mesa Station facility in North Las Vegas, Nevada. On February 25, 2023, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him and subjected him to harassment on the basis of age (born 1973) when: 1. On August 30, 2022, Complainant was put on Emergency Placement. 2. On September 14, 2022, Complainant was suspended. 3. On September 20, 2022, one of Complainant’s supervisors followed him to the bathroom, yelled at him to get back to work, and threatened him with discipline. 4. On September 24, 2022, one of Complainant’s supervisors accused him of not fastening his seatbelt before starting the engine. 5. On November 1, 2022, Complainant was escorted out of the facility. The Agency accepted these claims and conducted an investigation which produced the following evidence. Claim 1 In his investigative affidavit, Complainant stated that on August 30, 2022, he asked one of his supervisors, S1, to sign or initial his copy of a request for Union time. Complainant stated that S1 said she would do so later, and he then asked her why she could not just sign or initial the request at that time. Complainant stated that S1 repeated she would do so later and that he needed to get back to work. At this point, Complainant stated that Postmaster (PM) asked him what was going on, and after explaining the situation, PM asked him whether S1 gave him instructions to get back to work. Complainant stated that he said yes, and then PM asked him whether he was refusing to do so. Complainant stated that he said he was not refusing to get back to work but wanted to understand why he was being held to policy and not S1. After leaving the office area, and while he was in the locker room, Complainant stated that PM walked in and asked him why he had not left yet. PM further questioned what Complainant was doing for the last hour, and when Complainant tried to explain, Complainant stated that PM interrupted him, yelled at him, and leaned over him in an attempt to intimidate him. After this exchange, and while Complainant was still in the locker room, Complainant stated that PM walked in again and told him he needed to deliver to the apartments that day. Complainant stated that he asked PM whether he needed to finish the apartments that day because it would put him over eight hours. Complainant stated PM then accused him of failing to follow instructions, refused his request for a union steward, demanded his badge, yelled at him to clean out his locker, and threatened to call the authorities to have him removed from the premises. In his affidavit, PM stated that he observed Complainant engaging in several time-wasting practices and was given instructions which he failed to follow. PM further stated that in alignment with Agency policy, Complainant was placed on Emergency Placement (EP) in an off- duty status without pay for failure to follow instructions. With respect to Complainant’s intimidation claim, PM stated that the claim was ridiculous, and since having COVID, he does not get close to any employee. PM also stated that a union steward was not available, and Complainant was told he could speak with his union steward, but he had to leave the facility immediately. In her affidavit, S1 confirmed that she asked Complainant around three times to deliver his route, but he did not listen to her. S1 stated that Complainant then became argumentative with PM. With respect to Complainant’s intimidation claim, S1 stated that she did not have any knowledge of what might have occurred in the men’s locker room. S1 further stated that no employee placed on EP was allowed to have a conversation with the union before leaving the premises. Complainant stated that his age was a factor when he was placed on EP because he was tasked with trying to complete an overburdened route within eight hours and was compared constantly to younger carriers. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 2 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 14, 2022, after completing vehicle inspection and as he was loading his mail truck, S1 and his other supervisor, herein identified as S2, approached him and S2 demanded his badge. Complainant stated that S2 explained he was being walked out because he did not fasten his seatbelt before starting the vehicle and that he got out of the driver’s seat while the engine was running. Complainant stated that he then asked for a union steward but S2 denied his request. Complainant further stated that it was his understanding that Section 812. of Handbook M-41 specified that seatbelts were to be worn at all times the vehicle was in motion. The record reflects that Complainant was again placed on EP in an off-duty status without pay. While Complainant received a Notice of 14-Day Suspension Letter on September 22, 2022, the letter cites to incident(s) of failing to follow instructions on August 30, 2022, as the reason for Complainant’s suspension. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 00192-00193. In his affidavit, S2 stated that Complainant was observed exiting the mail truck and walking in front of it while the engine was running. S2 stated that this was a safety violation, and it was Agency policy for seatbelts to be worn at all times while operating a vehicle. S2 further stated that since Complainant was immediately placed on EP, he had to contact the union off postal property. In her affidavit, S1 stated that she had no knowledge of this incident since she was not present when it occurred. Complainant stated that he did not think his age factored into this incident and did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 3 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 20, 2022, S2 followed him into the bathroom two separate times and yelled at him. Complainant further stated that S2 threatened to discipline him. S2 denied raising his voice to Complainant, and stated that if he followed him, it was because of Complainant’s performance. S2 further stated that rather than washing up in the bathroom, Complainant was spending a long time in the locker room and doing something in his locker. Complainant stated that he believed his age was a factor when he was purportedly yelled at and threatened with discipline because now that he is older, he has to use the bathroom more often than he did when he was younger. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 4 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on September 24, 2022, he started the engine of his mail truck and was fastening his seatbelt when S2 walked up to the passenger-side window and yelled at him for not fastening his seatbelt before he started the engine. Citing to Section 812. of Handbook M-41, Complainant stated that S2 improperly demanded that seatbelts are to be fastened before the engine is started as opposed to before the vehicle is shifted into gear and put into motion. Complainant further stated that S1 walked over to them and S2 asked her whether she saw anything wrong. Complainant stated that S1 said no and while S1 and S2 were talking to each other and making calls, he called the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office. Complainant stated that someone from NALC confirmed his understanding of the Agency’s seatbelt policy, and when he asked the NALC officer to repeat what he said to S1 and S2, S1 told him it was not necessary, and he could go and deliver his route. Complainant stated that S1 also told him he had to follow all supervisor instructions and starting right then, he needed to fasten his seatbelt before he started the engine. S2 stated that he thought seatbelts needed to be fastened before starting a vehicle. S2 stated that he called safety and was told that it was not a written Agency policy. S2 further stated that he informed Complainant of this conversation and Complainant was then allowed to continue to his route. S1 confirmed that S2 called her over and asked whether she observed Complainant doing anything wrong. S1 stated that she did not, and ultimately told Complainant to follow the instructions of his supervisor. When asked if the requirement to fasten seatbelts before starting a vehicle applied to all employees going forward, S1 stated that she was not sure whether the request was sent to all carriers or if other carriers already fastened their seatbelts before starting their vehicles. S1 further stated that the relevant conversation was between S2 and Complainant. Complainant stated that he did not think his age factored into this incident and did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. Claim 5 In his affidavit, Complainant stated that on November 1, 2022, he gave S1 a doctor’s note for 30 days of no overtime due to repetitive motion pain in his right shoulder. Complainant stated that S1 told him she did not need to honor his doctor’s note. Later that evening, Complainant returned with undelivered mail and clocked out. Complainant stated that S1 told him he needed to continue delivering the mail until he finished his route. Complainant stated that he reminded S1 of his doctor’s note and that he was unable to work overtime. Complainant stated that S1 asked him whether he was refusing to follow instructions. Complainant further stated that he told S1 he did not have to follow unsafe supervisor instructions, and ignoring his doctor’s note and demanding he work overtime did not seem safe to him. 2 Complainant stated that S1 then demanded his badge, and he was escorted off the premises. The record reflects that Complainant was again placed on EP in an off-duty status without pay, effective November 2, 2022. S1 stated that Complainant told her, based on union advice, that he could bring his mail back and he did not have to listen to management. S1 stated that she asked Complainant three times to finish his route, but Complainant kept reiterating what the union told him. S1 stated that, while the union could provide guidance, she told Complainant that he had to follow supervisor instruction. S1 further explained that she sent Complainant’s medical documentation to Occupational Health Management (OHM) for guidance, and OHM advised her that Complainant could finish his route that day. S1 stated that OHM advised her that they were looking into the matter and to wait for an update as to whether the doctor’s note needed to be honored as a limited duty job offer, or if it needed to be a light duty request that required submission to the PM for approval. Complainant stated that he believed his age was a factor when he was escorted off the premises because he was expected to finish an overburdened route, and now that he is older, he has noticed that he does not recover from pain and injuries as quickly as he did when he was younger. Complainant did not have any specific examples of similarly situated employees outside his protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Disability was not a basis raised in Complainant’s complaint. Complainant timely requested a hearing. When Complainant did not object, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s December 14, 2023, motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision without a hearing on January 4, 2024. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment as alleged. The AJ found that the Agency's unrebutted facts served to establish nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The AJ noted, for example, that Complainant argued with his supervisors, wasted time on his phone in the locker room, neglected to fasten his seatbelt, and failed to turn his vehicle off when exiting. The AJ found that these predicates, which Complainant did not dispute, provided sufficient nondiscriminatory justification for the discipline and other actions management meted out. The AJ found that Complainant did not offer evidence that management made biased comments about his age or that they treated younger workers more favorably. As a result, the AJ found that no reasonable factfinder, even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to Complainant, could conclude the Agency's actions were tainted by considerations of Complainant's age. The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s decision. The instant appeal from Complainant followed.
