# INVESTIGATIVE CASE FILE RECORD

## COMPLAINANT EMPLOYMENT STATUS AND INCIDENT TIMELINE

At the time of the events that precipitated this employment discrimination complaint, the Complainant was employed by the United States Postal Service (Agency) as a Level 1 City Carrier assigned to the Meadow Mesa Station facility located in North Las Vegas, Nevada. On February 25, 2023, the Complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint with the Agency, alleging unlawful discrimination and harassment based on his age. According to records, the Complainant was born in 1973, which would have made him approximately 49-50 years old at the time the alleged discriminatory incidents occurred. The complaint encompasses five distinct incidents occurring between August 30, 2022, and November 2, 2022, each of which the Complainant contends was motivated by discriminatory considerations related to his age.

## CLAIM 1: EMERGENCY PLACEMENT ON AUGUST 30, 2022

### Complainant's Account

In his investigative affidavit, the Complainant provided a detailed narrative of the events leading to his initial Emergency Placement (EP) on August 30, 2022. According to his account, he approached Supervisor S1 and requested that she sign or initial his request form for Union time. The Complainant stated that when S1 declined to execute the request immediately, informing him that she would attend to the matter later, he inquired why the signature could not be provided at that moment. S1 allegedly reiterated that the task would be completed at a later time and instructed him to return to work activities.

The Complainant further stated that Postmaster (PM) then intervened in the conversation, asking what situation was developing. After the Complainant explained the circumstances, PM inquired whether S1 had issued instructions to return to work. The Complainant confirmed that she had, and PM then questioned whether the Complainant was refusing to comply with those instructions. The Complainant denied refusing to work but expressed his desire to understand why he was being held to established policy while S1 apparently was not.

Subsequently, while the Complainant was in the employee locker room, PM allegedly entered and asked why he had not yet left the facility. PM further questioned what the Complainant had been doing for the preceding hour. When the Complainant attempted to provide an explanation, he stated that PM interrupted him, raised his voice, and leaned toward him in what the Complainant characterized as an intimidation tactic. PM then re-entered the locker room and directed the Complainant to deliver mail to apartments that day. When the Complainant asked whether he needed to complete the apartment delivery, noting that doing so would exceed his eight-hour work limit, PM allegedly accused him of failing to follow instructions, refused his request for union representation, demanded his work badge, yelled at him to remove his personal items from his locker, and threatened to contact law enforcement to have him forcibly removed from the facility.

### Agency Respondents' Accounts

In his affidavit, the Postmaster acknowledged observing the Complainant engaging in what he characterized as time-wasting activities and stated that he issued instructions that the Complainant failed to follow. The PM asserted that, in accordance with established Agency policy, he placed the Complainant on Emergency Placement in off-duty, non-compensated status due to the failure to follow management instructions. Regarding the Complainant's allegation of intimidation, the PM characterized the claim as without merit. He further explained that owing to health considerations following his recovery from COVID-19, he maintains distance from all employees and therefore would not have leaned toward or attempted to intimidate the Complainant.

The PM also addressed the union representation issue, indicating that a union steward was unavailable at the time but that the Complainant was informed he could subsequently speak with his union representative after departing the facility immediately.

Supervisor S1 corroborated elements of the PM's account. She stated in her affidavit that she had instructed the Complainant approximately three times to proceed with mail delivery, but he did not comply with those directives. S1 indicated that the Complainant subsequently became argumentative with the Postmaster. Regarding the intimidation allegation, S1 stated she possessed no knowledge of events that may have transpired in the men's locker room, as she was not present in that location. She further clarified that Agency policy prohibited employees placed on Emergency Placement from engaging in conversations with union representatives before departing the premises.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant advanced the theory that his age was a contributing factor in his placement on EP, arguing that he was assigned an overburdened mail route that management expected him to complete within an eight-hour timeframe. He further alleged that he was subjected to constant unfavorable comparisons with younger carriers. However, the Complainant could not identify specific examples of younger employees who were similarly situated in all material respects yet received more favorable treatment.

## CLAIM 2: SUSPENSION AND SEATBELT VIOLATION ON SEPTEMBER 14, 2022

### Complainant's Allegations

According to his affidavit, on September 14, 2022, following completion of his vehicle inspection and while loading mail into his assigned truck, Supervisor S2 approached the Complainant and demanded his work badge. S2 allegedly explained that the Complainant was being removed from the premises because he had not fastened his seatbelt before starting the vehicle and had exited the driver's seat while the engine remained running. The Complainant stated that he requested union representation, but S2 denied this request.

The Complainant further noted that, according to his understanding, Section 812 of Postal Service Handbook M-41 specified that seatbelts must be worn at all times when a vehicle is in motion, not before the engine is started. The Complainant was placed on EP in off-duty, unpaid status. On September 22, 2022, he received a formal Notice of 14-Day Suspension Letter; however, this letter cited the August 30, 2022 failure-to-follow-instructions incident as the rationale for the suspension.

### Supervisor S2's Account

In his affidavit, S2 stated that he observed the Complainant exiting the mail truck and walking in front of the vehicle while its engine was still running. S2 characterized this conduct as a safety violation and asserted that Agency policy required seatbelts to be worn at all times while operating a vehicle. S2 explained that because the Complainant was immediately placed on EP, union contact was required to occur off postal property.

### Supervisor S1's Statement

S1 stated she possessed no knowledge of the September 14 incident because she was not present when it occurred.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant stated that he did not believe his age was a factor in this particular incident. He also could not provide specific examples of younger employees similarly situated who received more favorable treatment.

## CLAIM 3: BATHROOM INCIDENT AND ALLEGED YELLING ON SEPTEMBER 20, 2022

### Complainant's Allegations

The Complainant alleged that on September 20, 2022, Supervisor S2 followed him into the facility bathroom on two separate occasions and yelled at him. The Complainant further asserted that S2 threatened him with disciplinary action.

### Supervisor S2's Response

S2 denied raising his voice toward the Complainant. He stated that if he did follow the Complainant to the bathroom area, such action was warranted based on concerns regarding the Complainant's job performance. S2 further explained that rather than performing standard hygiene activities, the Complainant appeared to be spending an extended amount of time in the locker room and engaging in unspecified activities at his locker.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant advanced the theory that his age was a factor in this incident, reasoning that as he has aged, he requires more frequent bathroom breaks than he did during his younger years. He could not, however, provide specific examples of younger employees treated more favorably under similar circumstances.

## CLAIM 4: SEATBELT POLICY DISPUTE ON SEPTEMBER 24, 2022

### Complainant's Account

On September 24, 2022, the Complainant started his vehicle's engine while fastening his seatbelt when S2 approached the passenger-side window and yelled at him for not having the seatbelt fastened before starting the engine. The Complainant cited Section 812 of Handbook M-41, arguing that the correct policy required seatbelts to be fastened before the vehicle was shifted into gear and put into motion, not before the engine is merely started.

The Complainant stated that S1 then approached, and S2 asked her whether she observed anything improper. S1 replied in the negative. While S1 and S2 engaged in conversation and made telephone calls, the Complainant called the National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC) office. According to the Complainant, an NALC representative confirmed his interpretation of the Agency's seatbelt policy. When the Complainant asked to have the NALC officer repeat this confirmation to S1 and S2, S1 stated this was unnecessary. S1 told the Complainant he could proceed with his mail delivery route. S1 also instructed him that he must comply with all supervisor instructions and, going forward, must fasten his seatbelt before starting the engine.

### Supervisor S2's Account

S2 stated he believed that seatbelts needed to be fastened before a vehicle is started. He indicated that he subsequently called the Agency's safety office and was informed that no written Agency policy exists establishing when seatbelts must be fastened. S2 stated he informed the Complainant of this conversation, after which the Complainant was permitted to proceed to his delivery route.

### Supervisor S1's Account

S1 confirmed that S2 called her over and asked whether she had observed any improper conduct by the Complainant. S1 stated she did not observe anything wrong. S1 stated she ultimately directed the Complainant to comply with supervisor instructions. When asked whether the requirement to fasten seatbelts before starting an engine was applied to all employees going forward, S1 expressed uncertainty, stating she was not sure whether this directive was communicated to all carriers or whether other carriers were already fastening seatbelts before starting their vehicles. S1 further stated the relevant conversation was between S2 and the Complainant.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant stated he did not believe his age factored into this incident and could not provide examples of younger employees treated more favorably in similar circumstances.

## CLAIM 5: MEDICAL ACCOMMODATION DENIAL AND REMOVAL ON NOVEMBER 1-2, 2022

### Complainant's Account

On November 1, 2022, the Complainant provided S1 with a physician's note recommending thirty days of no overtime work due to repetitive motion pain affecting his right shoulder. The Complainant stated that S1 told him she was not obligated to honor the medical documentation. Later that evening, when the Complainant returned to the facility with undelivered mail and clocked out, S1 allegedly told him he needed to continue delivering mail until completing his assigned route. When the Complainant reminded S1 of his medical restriction and explained his inability to work overtime, S1 allegedly asked whether he was refusing to follow instructions.

The Complainant stated he responded that he was not obligated to follow instructions he considered unsafe, and that ignoring physician guidance while demanding overtime work did not constitute a safe work practice. S1 allegedly then demanded his work badge, and he was escorted from the facility. The Complainant was placed on EP in off-duty, unpaid status, effective November 2, 2022.

### Supervisor S1's Account

S1 provided a different characterization of events. She stated that the Complainant told her, based on union advice, that he could return his undelivered mail and was not required to listen to management directives. S1 stated she requested that the Complainant complete his route three times, but he repeatedly reiterated what union counsel had allegedly told him. S1 explained that while the union could provide guidance, the Complainant remained obligated to follow supervisor instructions.

S1 further explained that she forwarded the Complainant's medical documentation to the Agency's Occupational Health Management (OHM) department for guidance. According to S1, OHM advised her that the Complainant could complete his delivery route that day. S1 stated that OHM indicated they were investigating the matter and would provide updated guidance regarding whether the physician's note constituted a limited duty job offer or required submission to the Postmaster as a formal light duty request requiring PM approval.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant argued that age was a factor in his removal from the facility, asserting that he was expected to complete an overburdened mail route and that, having grown older, he has noticed that his body does not recover from pain and injuries as quickly as it did during his youth. He could not, however, provide specific examples of younger employees treated more favorably in similar circumstances.

## ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION

At the conclusion of the Agency's investigation, the Complainant received a copy of the Report of Investigation and written notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. The Complainant timely requested a hearing. However, when he failed to lodge objections to the Agency's motion, the assigned Administrative Judge granted the Agency's December 14, 2023 motion for a decision rendered without an evidentiary hearing and issued a written decision on January 4, 2024.

The Administrative Judge found that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment as alleged. The judge determined that the Agency's unrebutted factual findings established legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its personnel actions. The Administrative Judge specifically noted that the Complainant had argued with supervisors, engaged in time-wasting activities while using his cellular telephone in the locker room, neglected to properly fasten his seatbelt, and failed to turn off his vehicle when exiting it. The judge found that these established facts, which the Complainant did not dispute, provided substantial nondiscriminatory justification for the disciplinary measures and other management actions imposed.

The Administrative Judge concluded that the Complainant failed to present evidence demonstrating that management made age-based biased comments or treated younger workers more favorably. Based on this analysis, the judge determined that no reasonable factfinder, even when viewing evidence in the light most favorable to the Complainant, could rationally conclude that the Agency's actions were motivated by age-related considerations.

The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting and implementing the Administrative Judge's decision. This action prompted the Complainant to file the instant appeal.

S1 allegedly then demanded his work badge, and he was escorted from the facility. The Complainant was placed on EP in off-duty, unpaid status, effective November 2, 2022.

### Supervisor S1's Account

S1 provided a different characterization of events. She stated that the Complainant told her, based on union advice, that he could return his undelivered mail and was not required to listen to management directives. S1 stated she requested that the Complainant complete his route three times, but he repeatedly reiterated what union counsel had allegedly told him. S1 explained that while the union could provide guidance, the Complainant remained obligated to follow supervisor instructions.

S1 further explained that she forwarded the Complainant's medical documentation to the Agency's Occupational Health Management (OHM) department for guidance. According to S1, OHM advised her that the Complainant could complete his delivery route that day. S1 stated that OHM indicated they were investigating the matter and would provide updated guidance regarding whether the physician's note constituted a limited duty job offer or required submission to the Postmaster as a formal light duty request requiring PM approval.

### Complainant's Age-Based Theory

The Complainant argued that age was a factor in his removal from the facility, asserting that he was expected to complete an overburdened mail route and that, having grown older, he has noticed that his body does not recover from pain and injuries as quickly as it did during his youth. He could not, however, provide specific examples of younger employees treated more favorably in similar circumstances.

## ADMINISTRATIVE ADJUDICATION

At the conclusion of the Agency's investigation, the Complainant received a copy of the Report of Investigation and written notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge. The Complainant timely requested a hearing. However, when he failed to lodge objections to the Agency's motion, the assigned Administrative Judge granted the Agency's December 14, 2023 motion for a decision rendered without an evidentiary hearing and issued a written decision on January 4, 2024.

The Administrative Judge found that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency subjected him to discrimination and harassment as alleged. The judge determined that the Agency's unrebutted factual findings established legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its personnel actions. The Administrative Judge specifically noted that the Complainant had argued with supervisors, engaged in time-wasting activities while using his cellular telephone in the locker room, neglected to properly fasten his seatbelt, and failed to turn off his vehicle when exiting it. The judge found that these established facts, which the Complainant did not dispute, provided substantial nondiscriminatory justification for the disciplinary measures and other management actions imposed.

The Administrative Judge concluded that the Complainant failed to present evidence demonstrating that management made age-based biased comments or treated younger workers more favorably. Based on this analysis, the judge determined that no reasonable factfinder, even when viewing evidence in the light most favorable to the Complainant, could rationally conclude that the Agency's actions were motivated by age-related considerations.

The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully adopting and implementing the Administrative Judge's decision. This action prompted the Complainant to file the instant appeal.

# CASE FILE RECORD - EEO COMPLAINT INVESTIGATION

**COMPLAINANT POSITION AND EMPLOYMENT:**
The complainant was employed as a PSE Sales and Services Distribution Associate, Grade Level 06 P, at the Agency's Cape Central Post Office in Cape Coral, Florida, during the relevant period of this investigation.

**FORMAL COMPLAINT FILING AND ALLEGATIONS:**
On April 4, 2022, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging racial harassment based on her race as a White employee. She claimed that during February 2022, her first-line supervisor, an African American male, subjected her to racial slurs, made threatening statements regarding physical assault, and created a hostile work environment. The complainant further alleged that when she reported these incidents to management officials, no corrective action was taken.

**DETAILED ALLEGATIONS:**
During the investigation, the complainant provided specific accounts of alleged incidents. In late January or early February 2022, she reported that the supervisor told her not to clock out for lunch due to overtime. When she requested that he input her hours into the computer system, she claimed he responded with the threat, "I'll slap the shit out of you." She further alleged that when she asked permission to take her break, the supervisor made a racially charged remark: "people shouldn't be allowed breaks, Black people used to be slaves."

On February 3, 2022, the complainant stated that after asking for clarification of work instructions, the supervisor again threatened her with the statement, "I'll slap the shit out of you if you don't catch on." On February 5, 2022, regarding a package she deemed too heavy to lift, she reported the supervisor said she was "full of shit. You can't lift that?" 

The complainant alleged that on February 8, 2022, when instructed to move wagons, the supervisor stated, "You need to do it because you're White." On February 24, 2022, after she said "huh?" upon not hearing the supervisor clearly, he allegedly responded, "What do you mean huh? I'll slap the shit out of you." Finally, on March 3, 2022, while retrieving disposable gloves from the housekeeping closet, she reported the supervisor yelled, "White people don't steal, they buy their own shit."

**WITNESS STATEMENTS AND DENIALS:**
The supervisor categorically denied making any of the alleged statements, asserting that he and the complainant had maintained a positive working relationship until the complaint was filed. The Manager of Customer Service stated unequivocally that the complainant never reported any of the alleged comments to her office. A second supervisor recounted that the complainant mentioned the supervisor had threatened to "slap her upside the head" and advised her to report the matter to management. However, this supervisor denied receiving any reports of racial comments and stated the complainant declined to formally report the incident to the manager.

**COMPLAINT WITHDRAWAL AND REASSIGNMENT:**
The complainant originally alleged unlawful retaliation but withdrew this claim during the investigation, proceeding only with the racial harassment allegations. Subsequently, the Agency reassigned the complainant to a different supervisor, a change she did not contest or raise as a separate claim.

**ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING AND FINAL DETERMINATION:**
Following the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with the investigative report and notice of her right to request an EEOC Administrative Judge hearing. The complainant exercised this right; however, she failed to respond to the Administrative Judge's October 24, 2022 order requesting preliminary case information and did not appear at the scheduled initial conference on November 24, 2022. Consequently, on January 19, 2023, the Administrative Judge dismissed the hearing request and remanded the complaint to the Agency for final disposition. The Agency subsequently issued a final decision determining that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation was established based on the allegations presented. This appeal followed.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENT

## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT'S EMPLOYMENT STATUS

At the time of the events forming the basis of this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency's Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center located in Atlanta, Georgia. Prior to filing the current complaint, the Complainant had submitted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint in September 2018, which remained pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) at the time the Complainant provided her affidavit for the instant complaint. The Complainant's prior complaint involved allegations of sexual harassment by a co-worker, a matter that would subsequently prove relevant to her current claims.

## COMPLAINANT'S MEDICAL CONDITION AND DOCUMENTED RESTRICTIONS

The Complainant reported suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression resulting from an incident of sexual harassment and assault by a co-worker. Beyond her mental health conditions, the Complainant also documented physical limitations affecting her ability to perform standard work duties. Specifically, she suffers from back, foot, and knee issues that prevent her from standing or walking for extended periods. Additionally, the Complainant has documented restrictions on climbing and descending stairs, as well as limitations on bending, stooping, and lifting activities.

Most significantly, the Complainant's physician provided written documentation stating that due to her PTSD resulting from the co-worker's sexual assault, she could no longer work in the same facility as the individual who assaulted her. This medical restriction established a clear occupational need for relocation to accommodate her documented disability.

## TIMELINE OF EVENTS AND ALLEGED FAILURES TO ACCOMMODATE

The sexual harassment and assault incident occurred in September 2019. Following this incident, the Complainant took Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave. In April 2020, after her medical leave concluded, the Complainant was cleared to return to work at a facility different from her harasser. However, upon her return, the Complainant discovered that her harasser remained at the original facility, apparently without any transfer or reassignment action having been taken.

In June 2020, the Complainant sustained a workplace knee injury. She submitted documentation regarding this injury to the Agency in July 2020 but received no response. When the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Committee eventually requested additional documentation, the Committee ignored the Complainant's PTSD-related limitation requiring separation from her harasser and instead focused exclusively on her physical restrictions stemming from the knee injury.

The record reflects significant delays in addressing the Complainant's accommodation needs. Not until July 2021—nearly two years after the initial sexual assault and approximately one year after her return-to-work clearance—was the Complainant finally provided a modified assignment at a different location that accommodated her physical restrictions. Notably, the record contains no explanation or documentation concerning the nature of this new position or why the Agency required a full year to relocate the Complainant away from her harasser.

The Complainant went on COVID-related leave on August 16, 2021, and was subsequently hospitalized for sepsis. She was not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021. However, from that date forward, the Complainant was not returned to work. According to her account, management informed her only that no work was available based on her documented restrictions. Critically, the record contains no statement from any Agency official documenting that any effort was undertaken to accommodate the Complainant's restrictions from September 2021 onward, nor any evidence that such accommodation efforts were attempted and failed.

## LEAVE AND BID POSITION DENIAL

The Complainant alleged that she should not have been placed on leave without pay (LWOP) beginning November 21, 2021, given that her inability to work resulted from the Agency's failure to accommodate her documented medical restrictions. In January 2022, the Complainant submitted a bid for a position. However, her bid was denied, and the position was awarded to another employee with less seniority. The Complainant was marked "ineligible" with no explanation provided at the time of the denial.

When questioned about the bid denial, the Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that the Complainant's bid was rejected because the Complainant had not provided updated medical documentation demonstrating that she could fully perform her duties within six months. However, the record contains no evidence that the Complainant was ever formally requested to provide such documentation or informed that such documentation was required. The Complainant consistently stated she received no explanation for the denial.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement governing this matter specifically provides that management may request medical certification at the time of bid submission or thereafter, but no evidence exists that the Complainant was informed of this procedural requirement.

## THE FORMAL EEO COMPLAINT

On May 13, 2022, the Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging discrimination by the Agency on the bases of race (African-American, Native American, and Cuban), sex (female), color (Brown), disability (both physical and mental), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. These allegations were made under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. The complaint specifically addressed three primary claims: failure to accommodate her medical restrictions since November 10, 2021; charging her LWOP since November 10, 2021; and denying her a bid position on January 24, 2022.

The Complainant also asserted three additional claims: denial of accommodation between April 2020 and November 9, 2021; improper coding of leave as workers' compensation (OWCP) leave on unspecified dates; and denial of insurance benefits on unspecified dates.

## AGENCY DISMISSALS AND PROCEDURAL DETERMINATIONS

The Agency issued a final decision on December 6, 2022, pursuant to applicable federal regulations. The Agency found that the Complainant had not submitted required medical documentation to support reasonable accommodation requests or to demonstrate her ability to perform the bid position within six months. The Agency also determined that the Complainant had not established pretext for discrimination.

Regarding the additional claims, the Agency dismissed the denial of reasonable accommodation claim for dates prior to November 10, 2021, citing untimely EEO counselor contact. The Agency further dismissed the leave coding and insurance benefits claims as collateral attacks on the workers' compensation adjudicatory process. The Complainant subsequently appealed this decision.

On January 24, 2022, she was denied a bid position. 5 The Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that Complainant’s bid was denied because she did not receive any updated medical documentation stating Complainant could fully perform her duties within 6 months. See ROI at 152. There is no evidence in the record indicating that Complainant was actually requested to provide such documentation or told she needed to do so as Complainant stated she was given no explanation for the denial. In addition, we note that the Collective Bargaining Agreement specifically states that in such a situation “management may, at the time of the submission of the bid or at any time thereafter, request that the employee provide medical certification indicating that the employee will be able to fully perform the duties of the bid for position within six months of the bid.” See ROI at 337. Complainant’s complaint also included three additional claims, specifically that between April 2020 and November 9, 2021, she was not accommodated per her medical restrictions; that on unspecified dates, her leave was not properly coded as workers’ compensation (OWCP) leave; and on unspecified dates, she was denied insurance benefits. See ROI at 63-65. We find that the Agency’s affirmance of the claims regarding Complainant’s leave not being properly coded as OWCP leave and the denial of insurance benefits were On December 6, 2022, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). # INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENT

## CASE BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANT'S EMPLOYMENT STATUS

At the time of the events forming the basis of this complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Mail Processing Clerk at the Agency's Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center located in Atlanta, Georgia. Prior to filing the current complaint, the Complainant had submitted an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint in September 2018, which remained pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) at the time the Complainant provided her affidavit for the instant complaint. The Complainant's prior complaint involved allegations of sexual harassment by a co-worker, a matter that would subsequently prove relevant to her current claims.

## COMPLAINANT'S MEDICAL CONDITION AND DOCUMENTED RESTRICTIONS

The Complainant reported suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression resulting from an incident of sexual harassment and assault by a co-worker. Beyond her mental health conditions, the Complainant also documented physical limitations affecting her ability to perform standard work duties. Specifically, she suffers from back, foot, and knee issues that prevent her from standing or walking for extended periods. Additionally, the Complainant has documented restrictions on climbing and descending stairs, as well as limitations on bending, stooping, and lifting activities.

Most significantly, the Complainant's physician provided written documentation stating that due to her PTSD resulting from the co-worker's sexual assault, she could no longer work in the same facility as the individual who assaulted her. This medical restriction established a clear occupational need for relocation to accommodate her documented disability.

## TIMELINE OF EVENTS AND ALLEGED FAILURES TO ACCOMMODATE

The sexual harassment and assault incident occurred in September 2019. Following this incident, the Complainant took Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) leave. In April 2020, after her medical leave concluded, the Complainant was cleared to return to work at a facility different from her harasser. However, upon her return, the Complainant discovered that her harasser remained at the original facility, apparently without any transfer or reassignment action having been taken.

In June 2020, the Complainant sustained a workplace knee injury. She submitted documentation regarding this injury to the Agency in July 2020 but received no response. When the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Committee eventually requested additional documentation, the Committee ignored the Complainant's PTSD-related limitation requiring separation from her harasser and instead focused exclusively on her physical restrictions stemming from the knee injury.

The record reflects significant delays in addressing the Complainant's accommodation needs. Not until July 2021—nearly two years after the initial sexual assault and approximately one year after her return-to-work clearance—was the Complainant finally provided a modified assignment at a different location that accommodated her physical restrictions. Notably, the record contains no explanation or documentation concerning the nature of this new position or why the Agency required a full year to relocate the Complainant away from her harasser.

The Complainant went on COVID-related leave on August 17, 2021, and was subsequently hospitalized for sepsis. She was not cleared to return to work until September 21, 2021. However, from that date forward, the Complainant was not returned to work. According to her account, management informed her only that no work was available based on her documented restrictions. Critically, the record contains no statement from any Agency official documenting that any effort was undertaken to accommodate the Complainant's restrictions from September 2021 onward, nor any evidence that such accommodation efforts were attempted and failed.

## LEAVE AND BID POSITION DENIAL

The Complainant alleged that she should not have been placed on leave without pay (LWOP) beginning November 21, 2021, given that her inability to work resulted from the Agency's failure to accommodate her documented medical restrictions. In January 2022, the Complainant submitted a bid for a position. However, her bid was denied, and the position was awarded to another employee with less seniority. The Complainant was marked "ineligible" with no explanation provided at the time of the denial.

When questioned about the bid denial, the Supervisor of Distribution Operations stated in her affidavit that the Complainant's bid was rejected because the Complainant had not provided updated medical documentation demonstrating that she could fully perform her duties within six months. However, the record contains no evidence that the Complainant was ever formally requested to provide such documentation or informed that such documentation was required. The Complainant consistently stated she received no explanation for the denial.

The Collective Bargaining Agreement governing this matter specifically provides that management may request medical certification at the time of bid submission or thereafter, but no evidence exists that the Complainant was informed of this procedural requirement.

## THE FORMAL EEO COMPLAINT

On May 13, 2022, the Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging discrimination by the Agency on the bases of race (African-American, Native American, and Cuban), sex (female), color (Brown), disability (both physical and mental), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity. These allegations were made under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. The complaint specifically addressed three primary claims: failure to accommodate her medical restrictions since November 10, 2021; charging her LWOP since November 10, 2021; and denying her a bid position on January 24, 2022.

The Complainant also asserted three additional claims: denial of accommodation between April 2020 and November 9, 2021; improper coding of leave as workers' compensation (OWCP) leave on unspecified dates; and denial of insurance benefits on unspecified dates.

## AGENCY DISMISSALS AND PROCEDURAL DETERMINATIONS

The Agency issued a final decision on December 6, 2022, pursuant to applicable federal regulations. The Agency found that the Complainant had not submitted required medical documentation to support reasonable accommodation requests or to demonstrate her ability to perform the bid position within six months. The Agency also determined that the Complainant had not established pretext for discrimination.

Regarding the additional claims, the Agency dismissed the denial of reasonable accommodation claim for dates prior to November 10, 2021, citing untimely EEO counselor contact. The Agency further dismissed the leave coding and insurance benefits claims as collateral attacks on the workers' compensation adjudicatory process. The Complainant subsequently appealed this decision.

On November 4, 2021, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican). By letter dated November 16, 2021, the Agency accepted the formal complaint for investigation and framed the claims in the following fashion: Whether a co-worker who was an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI), as well as a Lead, subjected Complainant to harassment based on her race/national origin (Hispanic/Mexican) on multiple occasions beginning in June 2020 and continuing through July 2021 when, among other matters, the OJI/Lead: 1. Made fun of Complainant’s accent and said she disliked speaking to Complainant. 2. Tried to sabotage Complainant’s work by creating a list of inventory late actions and expired casework, and purposely gave Complainant misinformation regarding how to process cases. 3. Filled Complainant’s calendar with unrealistic appointments that not even experienced employees could complete. 4. Advised Complainant’s manager to have Complainant process a fraudulent tax return. After an investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. When Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination. Specifically, the Agency determined that “assuming [Complainant’s initial supervisor, S1] made these and other similar comments [as set forth in incident (1)], the statements would be unwelcome verbal conduct based on Complainant’s protected categories of race/national origin/ethnicity.” Final Agency Decision (FAD) at 12. However, the Agency, in its final decision, further set forth that: Complainant has produced no persuasive evidence that management’s actions described in [alleged incidents] 2, 3, and 4 were harassment based on her statutorily protected classes. Complainant’s uncorroborated statements that management was motivated by race/ethnicity and/or national origin to take the actions complained of are not sufficient to sustain her burden of showing harassment…Finally, we note that Complainant’s allegations of harassment were addressed through an internal anti-harassment inquiry, which did not substantiate Complainant’s claims.” FAD at 13. The instant appeal followed. Complainant asserts that the Agency’s final decision did not properly set forth that the alleged harasser was initially her former manager (prior to serving as her Lead and OJI). Complainant reiterates that S1 made derogatory comments regarding her accent since her first day of employment. Complainant asserts that she provided notice to S2 regarding S1’s behavior and requested a change of supervisor, but that S2 ignored the harassment and allowed the behavior to continue. In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision finding no discrimination. The Agency reiterates that Complainant failed to establish that she was subjected to harassment. Regarding the alleged comments made by S1 to Complainant regarding her accent, the Agency sets forth that “[a]ssuming the truth of Complainant’s allegations, nothing in S1’s comments indicate she mocked Complainant’s accent or that the comments were based on her being of Mexican descent. At best, [S1] indicated she expressed difficulty in communicating with Complainant. At worst, S1’s comments were the type of insensitive, hurtful comments that the Commission has declined to find as discriminatory.” Agency Response Brief at 11. The Agency asserts that Complainant’s claims fall short of the severity and pervasiveness required for a hostile work environment. Furthermore, the Agency states that management promptly separated Complainant and S1. Specifically, the Agency states that after Complainant raised the issue of harassment by S1 in late July 2021, S4 separated Complainant and S1 and that Complainant set forth that she had no further contact with S1 after this separation. The Agency further sets forth regarding Complainant raising the matter of alleged harassment by S1 with S2, it “appears” that Complainant only expressed a “lack of support.” Agency Response Brief at 17- 18.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD – CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## COMPLAINANT BACKGROUND AND INITIAL COMPLAINT

The complainant was employed by the Agency as a Taxpayer Advocate at the Laguna Niguel, California office during the period under review. On November 4, 2021, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint asserting that the Agency had discriminated against her on the basis of race (Hispanic) and national origin (Mexican). The Agency formally accepted this complaint for investigation by letter dated November 16, 2021.

## ALLEGATIONS AND FRAMING OF CLAIMS

The Agency framed the formal complaint as an investigation into whether a co-worker serving as an On-the-Job Instructor (OJI) and Lead subjected the complainant to harassment based on her race and national origin. The alleged harassment reportedly occurred on multiple occasions beginning in June 2020 and continuing through July 2021. The specific allegations included four categories of conduct:

First, the OJI/Lead made derogatory comments about the complainant's accent and stated a dislike for communicating with her. Second, the OJI/Lead allegedly attempted to sabotage the complainant's work by creating lists of inventory issues and expired casework, while providing intentionally false guidance regarding case processing procedures. Third, the OJI/Lead filled the complainant's calendar with unrealistic appointment schedules that would have been difficult for even experienced employees to complete. Fourth, the OJI/Lead advised the complainant's manager to have her process a fraudulent tax return.

## INVESTIGATION PROCESS AND AGENCY DECISION

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with a copy of the investigative report and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge, as provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f). The complainant did not timely request such a hearing. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), concluding that no discrimination had occurred.

The Agency's final decision acknowledged that if the initial supervisor (S1) had indeed made the comments described in the first allegation regarding the complainant's accent, such statements would constitute unwelcome verbal conduct based on the complainant's protected categories. However, regarding the remaining allegations, the Agency determined that the complainant had failed to produce persuasive evidence that management's actions were harassment based on statutorily protected classes. The Agency noted that the complainant's uncorroborated assertions that race, ethnicity, and national origin motivated management's conduct were insufficient to meet her burden of proof. The Agency also referenced an internal anti-harassment inquiry that did not substantiate the complainant's claims.

## COMPLAINANT'S APPEAL ARGUMENTS

On appeal, the complainant asserted that the Agency's final decision failed to adequately recognize that the alleged harasser was initially her former manager before later serving as her Lead and OJI. The complainant reiterated that S1 made derogatory comments regarding her accent beginning on her first day of employment. She further asserted that she had notified another supervisor (S2) of S1's harassing behavior and requested a supervisory change, but that S2 failed to address the harassment and permitted the conduct to continue.

## AGENCY'S RESPONSE

The Agency requested affirmation of its final decision. Regarding the accent-related comments, the Agency argued that even accepting the complainant's allegations as true, S1's comments did not indicate mockery based on Mexican descent but rather reflected difficulty in communication. The Agency characterized such comments as insensitive remarks that the Commission has traditionally declined to find discriminatory. The Agency asserted that the complainant failed to establish the severity and pervasiveness required for a hostile work environment finding. Additionally, the Agency noted that management promptly separated the complainant and S1 after the harassment was raised in late July 2021, with no subsequent contact occurring between them.

Her decisions were overruled making it impossible for her to execute the duties of her position; she felt forced to prove negatives regarding false portrayals and claims made by supervisors and other employees. Agency officials used their influence to disparage and isolate her; and did not reward her for her work. # OFFICIAL CASE FILE DOCUMENT
## Investigation Record and Administrative Decision Summary

---

## I. BACKGROUND AND EMPLOYMENT CONTEXT

This case involves a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by a Counseling Psychologist and Licensed Marriage and Family Therapist who was employed at the Agency's Health Clinic located in Baumholder, Germany. At the time the events giving rise to this complaint occurred, the Complainant held a professional clinical position responsible for providing mental health services, including marriage and family counseling, to the clinic's patient population.

The period covered by this investigation spans from September 2014 through January 2017, representing a significant period during which the Complainant experienced various workplace challenges and filed multiple formal complaints with different Agency offices and oversight bodies, including an Administrative Grievance filed in November 2014 and subsequent complaints to the Regional Health Command-Europe Inspector General (IG) office in October 2016.

---

## II. ALLEGATIONS AND COMPLAINTS

### A. General Workplace Environment Concerns (September 2014 - Present)

The Complainant alleged that beginning in September 2014 and continuing throughout her employment, management failed to provide her with necessary professional development and training opportunities. She asserted that she was subjected to what she characterized as demeaning treatment, including derogatory comments, unjustified interrogations, and excessive criticism of her work performance. The Complainant further claimed to experience non-verbal forms of hostility, including negative facial expressions from supervisory and managerial personnel.

Additionally, the Complainant alleged that her professional authority was systematically undermined through various mechanisms. She contended that coworkers and other employees were encouraged to bypass the established chain of command, and that her clinical decisions regarding patient care were frequently overruled without appropriate justification. According to her account, these actions made it impossible for her to effectively execute the duties and responsibilities of her position as a clinical mental health professional.

The Complainant further alleged that she was required to expend considerable energy defending herself against what she characterized as false portrayals and claims made by supervisors and other employees. She asserted that Agency officials used their positions of authority to disparage her professional reputation and to isolate her within the workplace. She claimed that despite her work efforts, her contributions were neither recognized nor appropriately rewarded. The Complainant reported these concerns through her supervisory chain on multiple occasions, yet alleged that the Agency failed to conduct thorough investigations or to address and remediate the underlying causes of her concerns.

### B. Client Assignment and Scheduling Issues

The Complainant alleged that on unspecified dates, other employees unilaterally rescheduled her clients with alternative providers without her knowledge or consent. As a result of these actions, when patients requested to continue their therapeutic relationship with the Complainant, they were informed that such arrangements were not permitted. This action effectively removed the Complainant's caseload and professional responsibilities without formal clinical review or documented clinical justification.

### C. October 5, 2016 Staff Meeting Incident

During a staff meeting held on October 5, 2016, the Complainant alleged that a Captain made clinical decisions regarding her patients without soliciting or considering her input, despite her being the primary treating clinician for these patients. The Complainant viewed this action as a failure to respect her professional clinical judgment and authority.

### D. October 12, 2016 Meeting with Command Staff

On October 12, 2016, the Complainant met with the Lieutenant Colonel (identified as Deputy Chief of Clinical Services and Chief Nursing Officer) and the Lieutenant (identified as Commander of Baumholder and Kaiserslautern Clinics) to discuss her request for reassignment from the Baumholder Team. During this meeting, the Complainant alleged that she felt personally attacked, primarily through what she perceived as disrespectful tone of voice and aggressive demeanor from both officials.

### E. November 12, 2016 Performance Evaluation

The Complainant challenged the accuracy and truthfulness of a performance evaluation issued on or about November 12, 2016. She asserted that the evaluation failed to fairly and accurately characterize her work performance based on her understanding of her actual job performance.

### F. December 21, 2016 Caseload Reduction

Upon returning to work on December 21, 2016, following a two-day sick leave absence (December 19-20, 2016), the Complainant discovered that two clients had been removed from her schedule and reassigned to other providers. The Complainant further alleged that despite an acknowledged shortage of behavioral health providers within the office due to holiday staffing shortages, staff members refused to engage her to assist in covering cases or addressing the documented provider shortage.

### G. Staff Integration Issues

The Complainant alleged that the Non-Commissioned Officer-In-Charge (NCOIC) brought a new staff member to the clinic and proceeded to introduce this individual to all providers and other staff members within the office. However, despite the fact that the NCOIC was conversing with the Complainant directly outside her office at the time, the new staff member was not introduced to the Complainant. The Complainant claimed not to know the identity of this new staff member as a result of this alleged slight.

### H. Investigation and Legal Representation Issues

In October 2016, the Complainant contacted the Regional Health Command-Europe Inspector General regarding allegations of discrimination and harassment. On December 6, 2016, the Sergeant First Class, representing the IG office, contacted the Complainant to discuss her complaint. The Complainant indicated that her legal counsel would be in Germany during the week of January 9, 2017, and she desired to coordinate a meeting with the IG office. Her counsel subsequently emailed the Sergeant First Class seeking clarification regarding the purpose and nature of the proposed meeting. However, the Sergeant First Class did not respond to this communication, and the anticipated meeting did not occur.

### I. Developmental Counseling and Reassignment

On January 27, 2017, the Complainant received developmental counseling regarding a temporary reassignment that had been implemented on January 4, 2017, to the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center (LRMC).

---

## III. PRIOR ADMINISTRATIVE ACTION

The Complainant's initial concerns regarding workplace conditions were previously addressed through the Agency's Administrative Grievance process. On November 28, 2014, the Complainant filed a formal Administrative Grievance that included many of the claims subsequently included in the present EEO complaint. In response to this grievance, on January 30, 2015, the Complainant received a notice of decision stating that she had been granted her requested remedy, which consisted of formal mediation to work through her concerns and improve the work environment. The Administrative Grievance was closed following this resolution.

---

## IV. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS AND AGENCY RESPONSES

### A. Training and Professional Development

Regarding the Complainant's allegations concerning denial of training opportunities, the Commander of the Baumholder, Landstuhl, and Kaiserslautern Clinics stated that the Complainant had expressed her desire to participate in a non-military professional development session regarding suicide and military personnel. The Commander indicated that while the Agency could not fund her participation in what he characterized as personal research, he offered to provide her the time necessary to participate, though without financial support.

In a separate request, the Lieutenant stated that while he had approved the Complainant's request to attend a Suicide Prevention training scheduled in Vicenza, Italy, no funds were available for attendance. The Lieutenant further noted that the training was ultimately cancelled, rendering the funding issue moot.

### B. Client Transfer Incidents and September 20, 2016 Email

On September 20, 2016, the Complainant sent an email to the Supervisory Psychologist and Chief of Behavioral Health alleging that a Nurse Practitioner had informed two of her patients that they were being transferred to another provider for treatment, and had informed another patient that the Complainant was no longer working at the clinic and could not see him.

During the investigation, the Social Services Assistant noted that the Complainant had previously stated that she worked exclusively with marriage and family counseling patients, which limitation had led to some patient transfers and restricted the patient population she could serve. The Nurse Practitioner similarly confirmed this restriction in her professional scope of practice.

The Lieutenant Colonel reported that he had investigated the client transfer situation and resolved the matter. In one instance, he determined that a transfer had been unintentional, and the client was reassigned back to the Complainant's care.

### C. October 5, 2016 High-Risk Meeting and ICE Complaints

On October 5 and 7, 2016, two separate Interactive Customer Evaluation (ICE) complaints were submitted by two different patients of the Complainant's regarding her standard of care to the Inspector General office.

On October 5, 2016, during a standard High-Risk meeting, a Captain discussed clinical concerns regarding two of the Complainant's patients. Immediately following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Captain. The Captain asserted that the Complainant had been aggressive during their conversation, had recorded the discussion without her consent, and had spoken loudly about the two patients in an open space within earshot of other patients. The Captain denied making any changes to patient care decisions as a result of the discussion.

The Captain characterized the October 5 meeting as a standard coordination of care discussion that routinely occurred with all providers. The Social Services Assistant confirmed that High-Risk meetings were conducted to enable various providers to coordinate appropriate patient care, and that all providers were expected to contribute their clinical perspectives. She further stated that no provider was being told how to conduct their clinical work.

Following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Lieutenant Colonel, expressing that she no longer wished to participate in High-Risk meetings and requesting reassignment from the Baumholder Team.

### D. October 12, 2016 Reassignment Meeting

During the October 12, 2016 meeting with the Lieutenant Colonel and Lieutenant to discuss the Complainant's request for removal from the Baumholder Team, both officials noted that while the Complainant repeatedly alleged that the work environment was hostile, she was unable to provide specific examples or detailed instances when pressed for such information.

During this meeting, the Complainant asserted that both the Lieutenant Colonel and another Colonel had been hostile toward her. Both officials denied conducting themselves in an aggressive manner, stated that they did not wish to continue the conversation if she felt uncomfortable, and offered to invite a neutral third party to be present during future discussions to ensure a more objective environment.

### E. Inspector General Investigation and Report

The IG issued its formal report on November 15, 2016, based on the complaints submitted on October 5, 7, and 13, 2016. The IG investigation concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the Complainant's allegations of harassment or discrimination by Agency personnel.

However, the IG report did identify that the Complainant had created a disruptive work environment within the Baumholder Behavioral Health Clinic. The report noted that the Complainant's interactions with other behavioral health staff members were contentious in nature. The primary recommendation issued by the IG was to reassign the Complainant out of the Baumholder Health Clinic, citing concerns that her continued assignment to the clinic would result in ongoing conflict with other team members, which demonstrably impacted patient care and significantly decreased morale throughout the clinical unit.

Notably, the IG report also found that the Complainant had violated German law by unlawfully recording a conversation without the other party's consent on November 15, 2016.

### F. Performance Evaluation of November 12, 2016

The Lieutenant Colonel issued a performance evaluation to the Complainant on or about November 12, 2016, based on fifteen standard performance metrics. The Lieutenant Colonel documented that the Complainant received eleven "Exceed" ratings and four "Met" ratings across these metrics. The areas marked as "Met" specifically related to collaboration with staff. The Lieutenant Colonel provided detailed examples to support his ratings, noting that for the period from May 2016 through October 31, 2016, there was minimal collaboration with staff.

Despite the four "Met" ratings, the Complainant ultimately received an overall "Excellent" rating on the performance evaluation. The Lieutenant, serving as the Complainant's second-line rater, concurred with the evaluation and its conclusions.

### G. December 21, 2016 Client Reassignments

Regarding the Complainant's allegation that two clients were removed from her schedule upon her return from sick leave on December 21, 2016, the Lieutenant Colonel, the Colonel, and the Chief of Behavioral Health all attested during the investigation that they were unaware of any issues or incidents occurring on that particular date. No documentation was provided establishing the factual basis for the alleged client reassignments.

### H. New Staff Member Introduction Incident

Concerning the allegation that the NCOIC failed to introduce a new staff member to the Complainant despite speaking with her outside her office, the investigation revealed that the Complainant acknowledged she did not leave her office to introduce herself to the new employee, nor did she inform the NCOIC or any other staff member of her concern regarding the lack of introduction.

### I. Developmental Counseling of January 27, 2017

The Chief of Behavioral Health stated that the developmental counseling provided to the Complainant on January 27, 2017, regarding her temporary reassignment was standard in nature and contained nothing negative. The reassignment itself had been implemented on January 4, 2017, to the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center.

---

## V. ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING AND FINAL DECISION

Following the completion of the EEO investigation, the Complainant was provided with a copy of the investigation report and was notified of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The Complainant timely requested such a hearing.

On October 18, 2021, the Agency submitted a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing, contending that the investigative record was sufficiently developed to permit resolution of the matter without further proceedings. The Complainant submitted a response to this motion.

On January 31, 2022, the Administrative Judge issued his formal decision. The AJ determined that the investigative record was adequately developed and contained sufficient evidence to permit a decision on the merits. After making all reasonable inferences in favor of the Complainant, as required by EEO regulations, the AJ concluded that there were no material facts in dispute that would preclude summary disposition.

Regarding the substantive merits of the Complainant's discrimination claim, the AJ determined that the Agency had articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for each of the employment actions challenged by the Complainant. The AJ further determined that the Complainant had failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Agency's stated reasons were pretextual or were merely a cover for unlawful discriminatory motivation.

With respect to the Complainant's hostile work environment claim, the AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to establish the severe and pervasive nature of the alleged conduct necessary to sustain a legal claim for unlawful hostile work environment harassment. The AJ characterized the Complainant's complaint as primarily reflecting her dissatisfaction with her coworkers and management, as well as her expression of personal grievances, rather than demonstrating unlawful workplace conduct.

The Administrative Judge granted the Agency's Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing. When the Agency failed to issue a final administrative action, the Administrative Judge's decision became the Agency's final administrative action by operation of law, in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110.

---

**END OF INVESTIGATION RECORD**

On November 28, 2014, the Complainant filed a formal Administrative Grievance that included many of the claims subsequently included in the present EEO complaint. In response to this grievance, on January 30, 2015, the Complainant received a notice of decision stating that she had been granted her requested remedy, which consisted of formal mediation to work through her concerns and improve the work environment. The Administrative Grievance was closed following this resolution.

---

## IV. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS AND AGENCY RESPONSES

### A. Training and Professional Development

Regarding the Complainant's allegations concerning denial of training opportunities, the Commander of the Baumholder, Landstuhl, and Kaiserslautern Clinics stated that the Complainant had expressed her desire to participate in a non-military professional development session regarding suicide and military personnel. The Commander indicated that while the Agency could not fund her participation in what he characterized as personal research, he offered to provide her the time necessary to participate, though without financial support.

In a separate request, the Lieutenant stated that while he had approved the Complainant's request to attend a Suicide Prevention training scheduled in Vicenza, Italy, no funds were available for attendance. The Lieutenant further noted that the training was ultimately cancelled, rendering the funding issue moot.

### B. Client Transfer Incidents and September 20, 2016 Email

On September 20, 2016, the Complainant sent an email to the Supervisory Psychologist and Chief of Behavioral Health alleging that a Nurse Practitioner had informed two of her patients that they were being transferred to another provider for treatment, and had informed another patient that the Complainant was no longer working at the clinic and could not see him.

During the investigation, the Social Services Assistant noted that the Complainant had previously stated that she worked exclusively with marriage and family counseling patients, which limitation had led to some patient transfers and restricted the patient population she could serve. The Nurse Practitioner similarly confirmed this restriction in her professional scope of practice.

The Lieutenant Colonel reported that he had investigated the client transfer situation and resolved the matter. In one instance, he determined that a transfer had been unintentional, and the client was reassigned back to the Complainant's care.

### C. October 5, 2016 High-Risk Meeting and ICE Complaints

On October 5 and 7, 2016, two separate Interactive Customer Evaluation (ICE) complaints were submitted by two different patients of the Complainant's regarding her standard of care to the Inspector General office.

On October 5, 2016, during a standard High-Risk meeting, a Captain discussed clinical concerns regarding two of the Complainant's patients. Immediately following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Captain. The Captain asserted that the Complainant had been aggressive during their conversation, had recorded the discussion without her consent, and had spoken loudly about the two patients in an open space within earshot of other patients. The Captain denied making any changes to patient care decisions as a result of the discussion.

The Captain characterized the October 5 meeting as a standard coordination of care discussion that routinely occurred with all providers. The Social Services Assistant confirmed that High-Risk meetings were conducted to enable various providers to coordinate appropriate patient care, and that all providers were expected to contribute their clinical perspectives. She further stated that no provider was being told how to conduct their clinical work.

Following this meeting, the Complainant spoke with the Lieutenant Colonel, expressing that she no longer wished to participate in High-Risk meetings and requesting reassignment from the Baumholder Team.

### D. October 12, 2016 Reassignment Meeting

During the October 12, 2016 meeting with the Lieutenant Colonel and Lieutenant to discuss the Complainant's request for removal from the Baumholder Team, both officials noted that while the Complainant repeatedly alleged that the work environment was hostile, she was unable to provide specific examples or detailed instances when pressed for such information.

During this meeting, the Complainant asserted that both the Lieutenant Colonel and another Colonel had been hostile toward her. Both officials denied conducting themselves in an aggressive manner, stated that they did not wish to continue the conversation if she felt uncomfortable, and offered to invite a neutral third party to be present during future discussions to ensure a more objective environment.

### E. Inspector General Investigation and Report

The IG issued its formal report on November 15, 2016, based on the complaints submitted on October 5, 7, and 13, 2016. The IG investigation concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support the Complainant's allegations of harassment or discrimination by Agency personnel.

However, the IG report did identify that the Complainant had created a disruptive work environment within the Baumholder Behavioral Health Clinic. The report noted that the Complainant's interactions with other behavioral health staff members were contentious in nature. The primary recommendation issued by the IG was to reassign the Complainant out of the Baumholder Health Clinic, citing concerns that her continued assignment to the clinic would result in ongoing conflict with other team members, which demonstrably impacted patient care and significantly decreased morale throughout the clinical unit.

Notably, the IG report also found that the Complainant had violated German law by unlawfully recording a conversation without the other party's consent on November 15, 2016.

### F. Performance Evaluation of November 12, 2016

The Lieutenant Colonel issued a performance evaluation to the Complainant on or about November 12, 2016, based on fifteen standard performance metrics. The Lieutenant Colonel documented that the Complainant received eleven "Exceed" ratings and four "Met" ratings across these metrics. The areas marked as "Met" specifically related to collaboration with staff. The Lieutenant Colonel provided detailed examples to support his ratings, noting that for the period from May 2016 through October 31, 2016, there was minimal collaboration with staff.

Despite the four "Met" ratings, the Complainant ultimately received an overall "Excellent" rating on the performance evaluation. The Lieutenant, serving as the Complainant's second-line rater, concurred with the evaluation and its conclusions.

### G. December 21, 2016 Client Reassignments

Regarding the Complainant's allegation that two clients were removed from her schedule upon her return from sick leave on December 21, 2016, the Lieutenant Colonel, the Colonel, and the Chief of Behavioral Health all attested during the investigation that they were unaware of any issues or incidents occurring on that particular date. No documentation was provided establishing the factual basis for the alleged client reassignments.

### H. New Staff Member Introduction Incident

Concerning the allegation that the NCOIC failed to introduce a new staff member to the Complainant despite speaking with her outside her office, the investigation revealed that the Complainant acknowledged she did not leave her office to introduce herself to the new employee, nor did she inform the NCOIC or any other staff member of her concern regarding the lack of introduction.

### I. Developmental Counseling of January 27, 2017

The Chief of Behavioral Health stated that the developmental counseling provided to the Complainant on January 27, 2017, regarding her temporary reassignment was standard in nature and contained nothing negative. The reassignment itself had been implemented on January 4, 2017, to the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center.

---

## V. ADMINISTRATIVE HEARING AND FINAL DECISION

Following the completion of the EEO investigation, the Complainant was provided with a copy of the investigation report and was notified of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The Complainant timely requested such a hearing.

On October 18, 2021, the Agency submitted a Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing, contending that the investigative record was sufficiently developed to permit resolution of the matter without further proceedings. The Complainant submitted a response to this motion.

On January 31, 2022, the Administrative Judge issued his formal decision. The AJ determined that the investigative record was adequately developed and contained sufficient evidence to permit a decision on the merits. After making all reasonable inferences in favor of the Complainant, as required by EEO regulations, the AJ concluded that there were no material facts in dispute that would preclude summary disposition.

Regarding the substantive merits of the Complainant's discrimination claim, the AJ determined that the Agency had articulated legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for each of the employment actions challenged by the Complainant. The AJ further determined that the Complainant had failed to present sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Agency's stated reasons were pretextual or were merely a cover for unlawful discriminatory motivation.

With respect to the Complainant's hostile work environment claim, the AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to establish the severe and pervasive nature of the alleged conduct necessary to sustain a legal claim for unlawful hostile work environment harassment. The AJ characterized the Complainant's complaint as primarily reflecting her dissatisfaction with her coworkers and management, as well as her expression of personal grievances, rather than demonstrating unlawful workplace conduct.

The Administrative Judge granted the Agency's Motion for a Decision Without a Hearing. When the Agency failed to issue a final administrative action, the Administrative Judge's decision became the Agency's final administrative action by operation of law, in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110.

---

**END OF INVESTIGATION RECORD**
