# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## CASE BACKGROUND AND PARTIES

This investigation record documents formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints filed by two individuals (hereinafter "Complainants") against a federal agency (hereinafter "Agency"). At the time of the events giving rise to the complaints, both Complainants were employed as Emergency Management Specialists in the positions of Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons at the Agency's First Responder Network Authority. Complainants performed their duties remotely from locations in California, with one working from Pauma Valley and the other from Thousand Palms. Both individuals commenced employment with the Agency in October 2015, initially hired at the Pay Band IV level.

## FORMAL COMPLAINTS AND PROTECTED GROUNDS

On June 13, 2019, each Complainant independently filed comprehensive formal EEO complaints alleging unlawful discrimination, harassment, and retaliatory actions by the Agency. The complaints identified three protected bases for discrimination: race (specifically, Native American status), national origin (Native American ancestry), and sex. Additionally, Complainants alleged that they experienced reprisal for engaging in prior protected EEO activity. It should be noted that Complainants subsequently withdrew their claims of sex discrimination during the formal hearing process, narrowing the focus of their allegations to the remaining protected bases.

## SUBSTANTIVE ALLEGATIONS - DISCRIMINATORY PAY AND COMPENSATION

The primary allegation centers on systematic discrimination in pay and compensation. Complainants assert that since their initial hiring, they have been subjected to disparate treatment regarding salary negotiations and pay band assignments. Complainant 1 specifically alleges that during pre-employment negotiations, Agency representatives informed him that the Agency would only offer him 70 percent of his previous wages and stated that he could "accept this offer or decline it entirely." Complainant 1 further contends that non-Native employees did not encounter similar constraints during their hiring negotiations. Complainant 2 claims that the Agency failed to properly account for her prior salary history and teaching wages in calculating her initial offer, instead providing compensation based solely on her current tribal salary.

Both Complainants assert that they performed substantially identical work to peers who were hired at the Pay Band V level, yet they themselves were hired at the lower Pay Band IV level and received compensation at the lowest tier available. This disparity in pay classification created a cascading barrier to career advancement, as Complainants later discovered that senior leadership positions were available exclusively to employees at the Pay Band V level.

## MANAGEMENT RESPONSE TO PAY DISPARITIES

In April 2018, the Executive Director of the Public Safety Advocacy Directorate directed Complainants' supervisor ("Supervisor 1") to conduct a comprehensive review addressing wage and pay band disparities within the organization. However, after the review was completed, both the Executive Director and a Senior Director took no corrective action and failed to acknowledge that such a review had ever been commissioned or completed.

During a telephone conversation on May 31, 2018, the Senior Director claimed to have no knowledge of the April 2018 review. Subsequently, Complainants learned from Supervisor 1 that the Senior Director was, in fact, fully aware of the review and its contents. In January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 (Complainants' subsequent supervisor) that he had received the completed review but stated that he felt no institutional obligation to act upon its findings or recommendations.

## PERSONNEL POLICIES AND PROCEDURAL FAILURES

On June 15, 2018, Complainants inquired with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer regarding hiring authorities and direct hiring procedures available within the Agency. They were informed that the Agency "does not have established personnel policies and practices." The Deputy Chief Administrative Officer and Chief Administrative Officer further failed to advise Complainants of their rights to pursue formal EEO processes to address and remediate their allegations of discriminatory compensation.

## ORGANIZATIONAL RESTRUCTURING AND HARASSMENT ALLEGATIONS

In June 2018, Complainants underwent a reorganization process that they characterize as deliberately designed to "bury" them more deeply within the organizational hierarchy. Complainants allege that this restructuring was undertaken in an effort to provoke them to voluntarily resign from their positions and, additionally, served as a mechanism to "limit any escalation of human resources issues originating from the tribal team."

## DISCRIMINATORY WORKING CONDITIONS AND RESOURCE DENIAL

Since June 2018 on an ongoing basis, Complainants have been required to develop and maintain separate strategic plans, while none of their non-Tribal team peers have been subjected to similar requirements. Additionally, Complainants were precluded from accessing resources on an equal basis with their counterparts. They were required to coordinate all activities through a separate, discriminatory process to access resources and tribal shareholders. This included being compelled to engage with contracting staff and tribal shareholders exclusively through a designated "gatekeeper" and being prohibited from participating in certain meetings. An Agency Contracting Officer's Representative was mandated to attend all daily engagements between contractors and Complainants.

## HOSTILE CONTRACTOR TREATMENT AND MANAGEMENT INACTION

Between June 2018 and February 2019, Complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly notified senior leadership that tribal team members were experiencing hostile and discriminatory treatment from officials employed by an Agency contractor. Despite these persistent complaints, senior leadership neither remedied the situation nor took disciplinary action against the contractor. Instead, senior leadership allegedly condoned the contractor's conduct and continued to place Complainants in hostile working environments with these contractor officials.

## PUBLIC RECOGNITION FAILURE

On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public social media communication thanking local, state, and federal workers for their service and dedication. Notably, this communication failed to acknowledge or reference Complainants and other tribal team members, despite their contributions to the Agency's mission.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDING AND APPEALS

Following investigation, Complainants received copies of investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges. The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges in the Commission's Washington Field Office. Both Complainants' shared legal counsel filed consolidation motions, which the Agency opposed. One Administrative Judge denied consolidation while the other did not address the motion. Both Administrative Judges issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established. The Agency subsequently implemented these decisions as final actions. Both Complainants have filed appeals from these determinations.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Registered Nurse in the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC) in West Los Angeles, California. During the relevant time, Complainant’s first level supervisor was the Nurse Manager for the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit (S1). 1. Complainant’s first line supervisor, the Nurse Manager 4 East (S1), demanded that Complainant work twelve-hour shifts, which Complainant refused. 2 2. In May 2018, S1 stated in front of coworkers that because the Agency canceled her surgery, she should go to another hospital for services, thereby disclosing her confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. 3 3. During January 2019, Complainant was required to work with coworkers who had improperly accessed her confidential medical records without authorization. 4. During January 2019, management failed to resolve Complainant’s sick leave issues in a timely manner. 5. On March 5, 2019, Complainant’s coworker referred to her as “a 50-year-old mental patient.” 6. On May 1, 2019, S1 told Complainant’s coworker, who was allegedly bullying and harassing Complainant, not to worry and that she “had her back.” 7. On May 1, 2019, Complainant was accused of being intimidating and aggressive and was accused of engaging in harassing behavior by a coworker who was bullying Complainant. 8. On May 3, 2019, Complainant was accused of sending an email from another employee’s email account. 9. On May 3, 2019, S1 requested that Complainant sign a misconduct form. 10. On May 28, 2019, S1 paced in front of Complainant’s work area. 11. On May 28, 2019, S1 accused her of misconduct. 12. On June 6, 2019, an unnamed employee interfered with Complainant’s privacy violation investigation. 13. # INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD

## COMPLAINANT EMPLOYMENT AND SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIP

At the time of the events giving rise to this formal complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Registered Nurse assigned to the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC) located in West Los Angeles, California. During the relevant period covered by this investigation, the Complainant's immediate supervisor and first-line manager was the Nurse Manager for the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit, hereinafter referred to as "S1" in this investigative record.

## SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS

The Complainant raised fourteen distinct allegations against her employer and supervisor, which are detailed below. The Agency's Office of Resolution Management (ORM) initially issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance, which dismissed a portion of Claim 7 for failure to state a claim, while accepting the remaining allegations for investigation. The Agency ultimately accepted thirteen claims for formal investigation and analysis.

### Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute and Shift Modification Demand

The Complainant alleged that S1 demanded that she work twelve-hour shifts, which the Complainant refused to do. During the investigation, it was discovered that the original claim description was inaccurate. The Complainant later clarified in a supplemental affidavit that the event did not occur in May 2018 as initially stated, but rather took place in November or December 2017. The Complainant further clarified that she had not requested to work twelve-hour shifts; rather, S1 had allegedly demanded that the Complainant change her work schedule from eight-hour shifts to twelve-hour shifts. The ORM noted that Claim 1 constituted a timely raised independently actionable claim and was also incorporated into the broader harassment allegations.

### Claim 2: Unauthorized Disclosure of Confidential Medical Information

In May 2018, the Complainant alleged that S1 disclosed the Complainant's confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Specifically, the Complainant claimed that S1, speaking loudly within earshot of coworkers, stated: "And you, you need to go somewhere else to have your surgery. If the VA is not taking care of you, you need to go to UCLA." This statement allegedly occurred as S1 was walking down the hallway between the reception station and the nurses' station, following the Complainant's presentation of leave documentation in S1's private office.

The Complainant identified two witnesses to this incident. Witness 1 allegedly heard S1 discussing the Complainant's surgery and asked if the Complainant was okay. Witness 13 reportedly observed S1 speaking loudly from the reception station and questioned why S1 was telling everyone about the Complainant's surgery. The Complainant contended that this public disclosure violated her rights under the Rehabilitation Act.

### Claim 3: Improper Access to Confidential Medical Records

During January 2019, the Complainant alleged that she was required to work with coworkers who had improperly and without authorization accessed her confidential medical records. The Complainant suspected that multiple employees had violated her privacy by reviewing her Veterans Affairs medical records without legitimate clinical justification.

In April 2019, the Complainant formally contacted the VAMC Privacy Office requesting a comprehensive printout of all individuals who had accessed her medical records over the preceding three years. Upon receiving the report, the Complainant reviewed the documentation and identified six coworkers whom she believed had accessed her medical records improperly. The report provided included four columns: employee names, dates and times of access, specific notes regarding the type of access (such as "CPRS Chart version 1, Appointment Management, Case No. Exam Edit, Register Patient, Clinical Scheduling"), and designations indicating "Yes" or "No." The Complainant marked six names with arrows and added handwritten notes indicating where each employee worked.

Subsequently, on June 18, 2019, the Complainant submitted an email to the Privacy Office identifying three specific nurses—Coworker 2, Coworker 3, and Coworker 4—as having inappropriately accessed her medical record. The Privacy Office investigation determined that Coworker 4 accessed the Complainant's medical records on June 15, 2018, and had no valid clinical reason for doing so. Coworker 4 subsequently stated that "everyone was talking about [Complainant's] surgery" and that she had witnessed another employee accessing the Complainant's medical record. The investigation further found that Coworker 3 had accessed the Complainant's medical records six times throughout 2018 and 2019. Coworker 3 stated she accessed the records because the Complainant had written her up on several occasions and she did not want to work on the same shift as the Complainant. The Privacy Investigation Report concluded that Coworker 3 accessed this information intentionally, despite it having no relevance to scheduling purposes or job-related duties.

On July 1, 2019, the Privacy Officer issued a letter to the Complainant confirming that two coworkers—identified only as Coworker 4 and one additional employee—had inappropriately accessed her medical record outside the scope of their duties and responsibilities. The letter noted that the other employees identified by the Complainant had accessed her records within their job responsibilities. Supervisory staff of the identified employees were notified, and both employees were recommended to immediately retake mandatory privacy and security training.

S1 submitted documentation confirming that, in response to the Complainant's April 9, 2019 email alleging unauthorized medical record access, S1 immediately initiated an inquiry with the Privacy Officer. The investigation confirmed that coworkers had indeed violated the Complainant's privacy rights. Documentation in the case file includes two disciplinary letters from the Acting Director: one dated September 4, 2019 (designated as "Employee 1"), upholding a proposed seven-calendar-day suspension for a Privacy Act Violation; and another dated September 5, 2019 (designated as "Employee 2"), mitigating a proposed seven-day suspension to a one-day suspension for a Privacy Act Violation. S1 provided evidence that two coworkers working with the Complainant received disciplinary action as a result of the privacy violations.

### Claim 4: Failure to Timely Resolve Sick Leave Issues

During January 2019, the Complainant alleged that management failed to resolve her sick leave issues in a timely manner. The Complainant noted that she had been scheduled to undergo surgery at the VAMC, and this surgery had been canceled on multiple occasions. Following each cancellation, the Complainant was required to redo her request for leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and obtain S1's signature on the new form. After the fourth cancellation, occurring in November or December 2017, the Complainant had to present an additional leave form to S1 for signature.

### Claim 5: Derogatory Reference to Mental Health Status

On March 5, 2019, the Complainant alleged that a coworker referred to her as "a 50-year-old mental patient." This remark constituted alleged harassment based on the Complainant's disability status.

### Claim 6: Supervisory Support for Alleged Harasser

On May 1, 2019, the Complainant alleged that S1 told a coworker who was allegedly bullying and harassing the Complainant not to worry and that she "had her back." The Complainant contended that this statement constituted supervisory endorsement and encouragement of harassment directed at the Complainant.

### Claim 7: Accusations of Intimidating, Aggressive, and Harassing Conduct

On May 1, 2019, the Complainant was accused by a coworker—who the Complainant contended was actually bullying and harassing her—of being intimidating and aggressive and of engaging in harassing behavior. The Agency's ORM partially dismissed this claim for failure to state a claim but accepted the remaining portion as part of the overall harassment allegation.

### Claim 8: Accusation of Unauthorized Email Access

On May 3, 2019, the Complainant was accused of sending an email from another employee's email account. This allegation was investigated as part of the broader disciplinary actions taken against the Complainant.

### Claim 9: Demand to Sign Misconduct Form

On May 3, 2019, S1 requested that the Complainant sign a misconduct form in connection with the allegations raised in Claim 8.

### Claim 10: Intimidating Supervisory Conduct

On May 28, 2019, the Complainant alleged that S1 paced in front of the Complainant's work area, which the Complainant characterized as intimidating conduct.

### Claim 11: Accusation of Misconduct

Also on May 28, 2019, S1 accused the Complainant of engaging in misconduct. This accusation was made contemporaneously with S1's alleged pacing behavior described in Claim 10.

### Claim 12: Interference with Privacy Violation Investigation

On June 6, 2019, the Complainant alleged that an unnamed employee interfered with the Complainant's privacy violation investigation. The Complainant did not provide specific details regarding the nature of this alleged interference.

### Claim 13: Posted Article Regarding Mental Disability

On August 20, 2019, the Complainant discovered an article posted on the report table regarding nurses with mental disabilities. The Complainant believed this article had been directed at her personally, thereby constituting harassment based on her disability status.

### Claim 14: Pattern of Supervisory Mismanagement

On unspecified dates, the Complainant alleged that S1 "split the staff against each other" and failed to properly resolve issues that occurred on the unit floor. This allegation was characterized as part of a broader pattern of hostile work environment conduct.

## INVESTIGATIVE FINDINGS

### Analysis of Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute

The Agency's investigation established through undisputed evidence that the Complainant remained on her eight-hour tour of duty at all times. The Agency therefore found that Claim 1 was not supported by the record. Furthermore, even accepting the Complainant's allegation as true, the Agency found no indication of discriminatory motive behind any alleged demand to change her work schedule.

### Analysis of Claim 2: Unauthorized Medical Information Disclosure

Regarding the alleged public disclosure of the Complainant's surgical needs, S1 asserted that she had discussed the Complainant's surgery only in private to offer emotional support. S1 further argued that there was no evidence beyond the Complainant's subjective testimony that anyone actually overheard the statement made in the hallway.

The investigative record indicates that six coworkers were interviewed as part of the privacy investigation process. All six coworkers confirmed that S1 had not disclosed any information about the Complainant's surgery or any other confidential medical information to them. Instead, these coworkers stated they learned of the Complainant's surgery because the Complainant herself shared this information directly with them. The investigative record further documents that the Complainant acknowledged telling at least one coworker that she was going to have surgery, though it had been canceled.

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to demonstrate that S1 improperly disclosed her confidential medical information. The Agency further noted that even if it were to credit the Complainant's version of the incident and assume that others overheard the statement—which the Agency found no evidence to support—the vague reference allegedly made by S1 would not constitute a disclosure of confidential medical information.

### Analysis of Claim 3: Improper Medical Record Access

The Agency noted that, pursuant to established Equal Employment Opportunity Commission precedent, allegations that the Privacy Act has been violated are not within the purview of EEOC regulations absent a further allegation that the Privacy Act violation resulted from prohibited discrimination. The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to provide evidence of discriminatory animus based on her disability.

The privacy investigation established that the two coworkers who accessed the Complainant's medical records did so to determine when the Complainant would be out for surgery and, in one instance, because the coworker did not want to work during the same shifts as the Complainant. The Agency found no indication and no evidence of discriminatory motivation or wrongdoing beyond the Privacy Act violation itself. Although the investigation confirmed that privacy violations had occurred, the Agency concluded that these violations were not motivated by prohibited discrimination related to disability status.

### Analysis of Claim 12: Alleged Interference with Investigation

Regarding the alleged interference with the privacy violation investigation, the Agency stated there was no indication of any alleged "resistance" from the Complainant's coworkers during the Privacy Investigation process. The Agency noted that even if such resistance were accepted as true, there was no evidence that any such resistance was based on discriminatory animus.

The Agency emphasized that S1 had promptly reported the Complainant's concern regarding privacy violations to the Privacy Office. A comprehensive privacy investigation was subsequently conducted, and all employees identified by the Complainant as potentially accessing her medical records were interviewed. Two employees were identified as having improperly accessed the Complainant's records, and both were subsequently disciplined and ordered to retake privacy training. The Agency found no evidence that any failure to take additional or more severe disciplinary measures was motivated by discriminatory animus.

### Analysis of Hostile Work Environment Claim

The Agency conducted a comprehensive analysis of all harassment allegations raised by the Complainant. Even accepting all of the Complainant's allegations as true, the Agency concluded that she had presented no evidence that she was singled out for treatment based on her disability status.

The Agency noted that Witness 1, who had not been employed by the VAMC since 2018, provided only a vague statement alleging that S1 had told him the Complainant was having "mental issues." This statement was directly contradicted by S1's testimony. S1 indicated that she was unaware the Complainant had a disability. S1 noted that although she was aware the Complainant had taken bereavement leave following the death of a parent, to S1's knowledge, this leave was not related to any mental or other disability.

Witness 2's statement gave no indication that S1 harbored discriminatory animus against the Complainant based on disability status. The Agency noted that both witnesses expressed personal complaints about S1, rendering their statements less credible in the investigative context.

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to establish that she had been subjected to unlawful harassment based on her disability or other protected status.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES

Following the completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the full Report of Investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The Complainant initially requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew that request. Consequently, the Agency issued a Final Decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), adopting the investigative findings and providing the Complainant with the agency's formal determination on each claim.

---

**END OF INVESTIGATION RECORD**

According to the report, Coworker 3 stated she wanted to check the schedule because Complainant had written her up on several occasions and she did not want to work on the same shift as Complainant. The report noted that Coworker 3 did not have a valid reason for accessing Complainant’s medical records and that “scheduling information is not located in CPRS therefore accessing this information is not for scheduling purposes and was intentional.” Further, it was noted that “[Coworker 4] and other employees stated that [Complainant] mentioned to them that ‘she was having surgery.’” The report stated that no evidence was found to confirm that Complainant’s supervisor disclosed any information regarding her surgery in any meeting. At the conclusion of the EEO investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). In its final decision, the Agency adopted the ORM’s decision to dismiss Complainant’s claim that on May 1, 2019, a coworker asserted that Complainant had subjected the coworker to harassment by being intimidating and aggressive. The Agency noted that the claim was accepted for consideration in Complainant’s overall harassment claim. The Agency addressed claims 1, 2, 3, and 12 under a disparate treatment theory. Regarding claim 1, the Agency noted the undisputed evidence showed Complainant remained on her eight- hour tour of duty at all times. The Agency found this claim was not supported by the record. Further, the Agency stated even accepting her claim as true, there was no indication of discriminatory motive. Regarding claim 2, Complainant claimed that S1 made a statement about her seeking surgery at another facility in an area where others could overhear S1’s statement, thereby disclosing her confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. The Agency noted that S1 stated she only discussed Complainant’s surgery with Complainant privately to offer her emotional support and argued there was no evidence beyond Complainant’s subjective testimony that anyone overheard the statement. The Agency noted the six coworkers who were interviewed as part of Complainant’s privacy investigation all confirmed that S1 did not disclose any information about Complainant’s surgery or any other confidential medical information to them. Instead, the Agency stated, they learned of Complainant’s surgery from Complainant sharing the information directly. The Agency noted Complainant admitted in her testimony that she told at least one coworker that she was going to have surgery, but it had been canceled. The Agency concluded that Complainant did not show that S1 improperly disclosed her confidential medical information. The Agency stated even if it credited Complainant’s version of the incident and assumed that others overheard the statement, of which it stated there was no evidence, the vague reference allegedly made by S1 did not disclose confidential medical information. Regarding claim 3, the Agency noted the Commission has held that allegations that the Privacy Act has been violated were not within the purview of the EEOC Regulations, without a further allegation that the Privacy Act violation resulted from prohibited discrimination. The Agency stated that Complainant did not provide evidence of discriminatory animus due to her disability, and the privacy investigation determined that the two coworkers who accessed her records did so to find out when she would be out for surgery, and because one of them did not want to work when Complainant was working. The Agency found no indication and no evidence was provided by Complainant of any discriminatory motivation or wrongdoing beyond the Privacy Act violation. Regarding claim 12, the Agency stated there was no indication of any alleged “resistance” from Complainant’s coworkers during the Privacy Investigation, or that even if accepted as true, any such resistance was based on discriminatory animus. The Agency noted S1 promptly reported Complainant’s concern that her privacy had been violated to the Privacy Office, a privacy investigation was conducted, and all the employees Complainant identified as potentially accessing her medical records were interviewed, and two employees were identified as having improperly accessed her records. The Agency noted those employees were subsequently disciplined and ordered to retake privacy training. The Agency stated there was no evidence that the failure to take other disciplinary measures was due to discriminatory animus. Regarding the hostile work environment claim, the Agency stated even accepting Complainant’s allegations as true, she has presented no evidence she was singled out for treatment based on her disability. The Agency noted Witness 1, who has not worked for the Agency since 2018, provided only a vague statement that S1 allegedly told him Complainant was having “mental issues,” which was contradicted by S1’s testimony. The Agency stated S1 was unaware Complainant had a disability, and although she noted Complainant had taken bereavement leave after the death of a parent, to S1’s knowledge, it was not related to any mental or other disability. The Agency noted Witness 2’s statement gave no indication of S1 having discriminatory animus against Complainant based on her disability. The Agency noted that both witnesses expressed personal complaints about S1, rendering their statements less credible. The Agency found Complainant failed to show that she was subjected to unlawful harassment based on her disability.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE RECORD

## COMPLAINANT EMPLOYMENT AND SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIP

At the time of the events giving rise to this formal complaint, the Complainant was employed as a Registered Nurse assigned to the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center (VAMC) located in West Los Angeles, California. During the relevant period covered by this investigation, the Complainant's immediate supervisor and first-line manager was the Nurse Manager for the 4 East Medical-Surgical Unit, hereinafter referred to as "S1" in this investigative record.

## SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS

The Complainant raised fourteen distinct allegations against her employer and supervisor, which are detailed below. The Agency's Office of Resolution Management (ORM) initially issued a Notice of Partial Acceptance, which dismissed a portion of Claim 7 for failure to state a claim, while accepting the remaining allegations for investigation. The Agency ultimately accepted thirteen claims for formal investigation and analysis.

### Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute and Shift Modification Demand

The Complainant alleged that S1 demanded that she work twelve-hour shifts, which the Complainant refused to do. During the investigation, it was discovered that the original claim description was inaccurate. The Complainant later clarified in a supplemental affidavit that the event did not occur in May 2018 as initially stated, but rather took place in November or December 2017. The Complainant further clarified that she had not requested to work twelve-hour shifts; rather, S1 had allegedly demanded that the Complainant change her work schedule from eight-hour shifts to twelve-hour shifts. The ORM noted that Claim 1 constituted a timely raised independently actionable claim and was also incorporated into the broader harassment allegations.

### Claim 2: Unauthorized Disclosure of Confidential Medical Information

In May 2018, the Complainant alleged that S1 disclosed the Complainant's confidential medical information in violation of the Rehabilitation Act. Specifically, the Complainant claimed that S1, speaking loudly within earshot of coworkers, stated: "And you, you need to go somewhere else to have your surgery. If the VA is not taking care of you, you need to go to UCLA." This statement allegedly occurred as S1 was walking down the hallway between the reception station and the nurses' station, following the Complainant's presentation of leave documentation in S1's private office.

The Complainant identified two witnesses to this incident. Witness 1 allegedly heard S1 discussing the Complainant's surgery and asked if the Complainant was okay. Witness 13 reportedly observed S1 speaking loudly from the reception station and questioned why S1 was telling everyone about the Complainant's surgery. The Complainant contended that this public disclosure violated her rights under the Rehabilitation Act.

### Claim 3: Improper Access to Confidential Medical Records

During January 2019, the Complainant alleged that she was required to work with coworkers who had improperly and without authorization accessed her confidential medical records. The Complainant suspected that multiple employees had violated her privacy by reviewing her Veterans Affairs medical records without legitimate clinical justification.

In April 2019, the Complainant formally contacted the VAMC Privacy Office requesting a comprehensive printout of all individuals who had accessed her medical records over the preceding three years. Upon receiving the report, the Complainant reviewed the documentation and identified six coworkers whom she believed had accessed her medical records improperly. The report provided included four columns: employee names, dates and times of access, specific notes regarding the type of access (such as "CPRS Chart version 1, Appointment Management, Case No. Exam Edit, Register Patient, Clinical Scheduling"), and designations indicating "Yes" or "No." The Complainant marked six names with arrows and added handwritten notes indicating where each employee worked.

Subsequently, on June 19, 2019, the Complainant submitted an email to the Privacy Office identifying three specific nurses—Coworker 2, Coworker 3, and Coworker 4—as having inappropriately accessed her medical record. The Privacy Office investigation determined that Coworker 4 accessed the Complainant's medical records on June 15, 2018, and had no valid clinical reason for doing so. Coworker 4 subsequently stated that "everyone was talking about [Complainant's] surgery" and that she had witnessed another employee accessing the Complainant's medical record. The investigation further found that Coworker 3 had accessed the Complainant's medical records six times throughout 2018 and 2019. Coworker 3 stated she accessed the records because the Complainant had written her up on several occasions and she did not want to work on the same shift as the Complainant. The Privacy Investigation Report concluded that Coworker 3 accessed this information intentionally, despite it having no relevance to scheduling purposes or job-related duties.

On July 1, 2019, the Privacy Officer issued a letter to the Complainant confirming that two coworkers—identified only as Coworker 4 and one additional employee—had inappropriately accessed her medical record outside the scope of their duties and responsibilities. The letter noted that the other employees identified by the Complainant had accessed her records within their job responsibilities. Supervisory staff of the identified employees were notified, and both employees were recommended to immediately retake mandatory privacy and security training.

S1 submitted documentation confirming that, in response to the Complainant's April 9, 2019 email alleging unauthorized medical record access, S1 immediately initiated an inquiry with the Privacy Officer. The investigation confirmed that coworkers had indeed violated the Complainant's privacy rights. Documentation in the case file includes two disciplinary letters from the Acting Director: one dated September 4, 2019 (designated as "Employee 1"), upholding a proposed seven-calendar-day suspension for a Privacy Act Violation; and another dated September 5, 2019 (designated as "Employee 2"), mitigating a proposed seven-day suspension to a one-day suspension for a Privacy Act Violation. S1 provided evidence that two coworkers working with the Complainant received disciplinary action as a result of the privacy violations.

### Claim 4: Failure to Timely Resolve Sick Leave Issues

During January 2019, the Complainant alleged that management failed to resolve her sick leave issues in a timely manner. The Complainant noted that she had been scheduled to undergo surgery at the VAMC, and this surgery had been canceled on multiple occasions. Following each cancellation, the Complainant was required to redo her request for leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and obtain S1's signature on the new form. After the fourth cancellation, occurring in November or December 2017, the Complainant had to present an additional leave form to S1 for signature.

### Claim 5: Derogatory Reference to Mental Health Status

On March 5, 2019, the Complainant alleged that a coworker referred to her as "a 50-year-old mental patient." This remark constituted alleged harassment based on the Complainant's disability status.

### Claim 6: Supervisory Support for Alleged Harasser

On May 1, 2019, the Complainant alleged that S1 told a coworker who was allegedly bullying and harassing the Complainant not to worry and that she "had her back." The Complainant contended that this statement constituted supervisory endorsement and encouragement of harassment directed at the Complainant.

### Claim 7: Accusations of Intimidating, Aggressive, and Harassing Conduct

On May 1, 2019, the Complainant was accused by a coworker—who the Complainant contended was actually bullying and harassing her—of being intimidating and aggressive and of engaging in harassing behavior. The Agency's ORM partially dismissed this claim for failure to state a claim but accepted the remaining portion as part of the overall harassment allegation.

### Claim 8: Accusation of Unauthorized Email Access

On May 3, 2019, the Complainant was accused of sending an email from another employee's email account. This allegation was investigated as part of the broader disciplinary actions taken against the Complainant.

### Claim 9: Demand to Sign Misconduct Form

On May 3, 2019, S1 requested that the Complainant sign a misconduct form in connection with the allegations raised in Claim 8.

### Claim 10: Intimidating Supervisory Conduct

On May 28, 2019, the Complainant alleged that S1 paced in front of the Complainant's work area, which the Complainant characterized as intimidating conduct.

### Claim 11: Accusation of Misconduct

Also on May 28, 2019, S1 accused the Complainant of engaging in misconduct. This accusation was made contemporaneously with S1's alleged pacing behavior described in Claim 10.

### Claim 12: Interference with Privacy Violation Investigation

On June 6, 2019, the Complainant alleged that an unnamed employee interfered with the Complainant's privacy violation investigation. The Complainant did not provide specific details regarding the nature of this alleged interference.

### Claim 13: Posted Article Regarding Mental Disability

On August 20, 2019, the Complainant discovered an article posted on the report table regarding nurses with mental disabilities. The Complainant believed this article had been directed at her personally, thereby constituting harassment based on her disability status.

### Claim 14: Pattern of Supervisory Mismanagement

On unspecified dates, the Complainant alleged that S1 "split the staff against each other" and failed to properly resolve issues that occurred on the unit floor. This allegation was characterized as part of a broader pattern of hostile work environment conduct.

## INVESTIGATIVE FINDINGS

### Analysis of Claim 1: Scheduling Dispute

The Agency's investigation established through undisputed evidence that the Complainant remained on her eight-hour tour of duty at all times. The Agency therefore found that Claim 1 was not supported by the record. Furthermore, even accepting the Complainant's allegation as true, the Agency found no indication of discriminatory motive behind any alleged demand to change her work schedule.

### Analysis of Claim 2: Unauthorized Medical Information Disclosure

Regarding the alleged public disclosure of the Complainant's surgical needs, S1 asserted that she had discussed the Complainant's surgery only in private to offer emotional support. S1 further argued that there was no evidence beyond the Complainant's subjective testimony that anyone actually overheard the statement made in the hallway.

The investigative record indicates that six coworkers were interviewed as part of the privacy investigation process. All six coworkers confirmed that S1 had not disclosed any information about the Complainant's surgery or any other confidential medical information to them. Instead, these coworkers stated they learned of the Complainant's surgery because the Complainant herself shared this information directly with them. The investigative record further documents that the Complainant acknowledged telling at least one coworker that she was going to have surgery, though it had been canceled.

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to demonstrate that S1 improperly disclosed her confidential medical information. The Agency further noted that even if it were to credit the Complainant's version of the incident and assume that others overheard the statement—which the Agency found no evidence to support—the vague reference allegedly made by S1 would not constitute a disclosure of confidential medical information.

### Analysis of Claim 3: Improper Medical Record Access

The Agency noted that, pursuant to established Equal Employment Opportunity Commission precedent, allegations that the Privacy Act has been violated are not within the purview of EEOC regulations absent a further allegation that the Privacy Act violation resulted from prohibited discrimination. The Agency determined that the Complainant failed to provide evidence of discriminatory animus based on her disability.

The privacy investigation established that the two coworkers who accessed the Complainant's medical records did so to determine when the Complainant would be out for surgery and, in one instance, because the coworker did not want to work during the same shifts as the Complainant. The Agency found no indication and no evidence of discriminatory motivation or wrongdoing beyond the Privacy Act violation itself. Although the investigation confirmed that privacy violations had occurred, the Agency concluded that these violations were not motivated by prohibited discrimination related to disability status.

### Analysis of Claim 12: Alleged Interference with Investigation

Regarding the alleged interference with the privacy violation investigation, the Agency stated there was no indication of any alleged "resistance" from the Complainant's coworkers during the Privacy Investigation process. The Agency noted that even if such resistance were accepted as true, there was no evidence that any such resistance was based on discriminatory animus.

The Agency emphasized that S1 had promptly reported the Complainant's concern regarding privacy violations to the Privacy Office. A comprehensive privacy investigation was subsequently conducted, and all employees identified by the Complainant as potentially accessing her medical records were interviewed. Two employees were identified as having improperly accessed the Complainant's records, and both were subsequently disciplined and ordered to retake privacy training. The Agency found no evidence that any failure to take additional or more severe disciplinary measures was motivated by discriminatory animus.

### Analysis of Hostile Work Environment Claim

The Agency conducted a comprehensive analysis of all harassment allegations raised by the Complainant. Even accepting all of the Complainant's allegations as true, the Agency concluded that she had presented no evidence that she was singled out for treatment based on her disability status.

The Agency noted that Witness 1, who had not been employed by the VAMC since 2018, provided only a vague statement alleging that S1 had told him the Complainant was having "mental issues." This statement was directly contradicted by S1's testimony. S1 indicated that she was unaware the Complainant had a disability. S1 noted that although she was aware the Complainant had taken bereavement leave following the death of a parent, to S1's knowledge, this leave was not related to any mental or other disability.

Witness 2's statement gave no indication that S1 harbored discriminatory animus against the Complainant based on disability status. The Agency noted that both witnesses expressed personal complaints about S1, rendering their statements less credible in the investigative context.

The Agency concluded that the Complainant failed to establish that she had been subjected to unlawful harassment based on her disability or other protected status.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES

Following the completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the Complainant with a copy of the full Report of Investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). The Complainant initially requested a hearing but subsequently withdrew that request. Consequently, the Agency issued a Final Decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), adopting the investigative findings and providing the Complainant with the agency's formal determination on each claim.

---

**END OF INVESTIGATION RECORD**

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANTS' EMPLOYMENT STATUS

The complainants in this matter were employed by the Agency as Emergency Management Specialists with responsibilities as Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons. At the time the events giving rise to these complaints occurred, both complainants were performing their duties remotely—one from Pauma Valley, California, and the other from Thousand Palms, California. The complainants initiated their employment relationship with the Agency in October 2015, beginning at the Pay Band IV compensation level. On June 13, 2019, both complainants filed formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints with the Agency, alleging discrimination and harassment based on their race (Native American), national origin (Native American), and in retaliation for prior protected EEO activity. Additionally, complainants initially alleged discrimination based on sex; however, this claim was subsequently withdrawn during the hearing process.

## ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY COMPENSATION PRACTICES

### Initial Hiring and Salary Negotiations

The complainants alleged systematic discrimination in compensation dating from their initial hire. Specifically, Complainant 1 reported that during pre-employment salary negotiations, he was informed by the Agency that it was obligated only to offer him seventy percent of his previous wage, with the explicit statement that he could "take it or leave it." Complainant 1 further contended that non-Native employees were not subjected to comparable treatment during their respective hiring processes. Complainant 2 alleged that the Agency failed to properly account for changes in her prior salary history or her teaching background, instead offering only compensation commensurate with her then-current tribal salary.

### Disparate Pay Bands and Job Classification

Both complainants asserted that they performed substantially identical work as peer employees who were hired at the Pay Band V level, yet they themselves were hired at Pay Band IV and maintained at the lowest compensation tier. This disparity in classification, the complainants argued, directly resulted from discriminatory intent based on their Native American status.

### Failure to Address Documented Pay Disparities

The complainants documented what they characterized as management's deliberate inaction regarding known compensation inequities. In approximately April 2018, the Executive Director of the Public Safety Advocacy Directorate directed Complainants' supervisor to conduct a comprehensive review addressing wage and pay band disparities within the department. However, subsequent to the completion of this review, the Executive Director and a Senior Director allegedly took no remedial action and failed to acknowledge that such a review had even been commissioned.

This pattern of non-responsiveness continued when, during a May 31, 2018 telephone conversation, the Senior Director claimed to have no knowledge of the April 2018 review. The complainants later learned from their supervisor that the Senior Director was, in fact, "very well aware" of the review's existence and findings.

When complainants inquired on June 15, 2018, with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer regarding hiring authorities and direct hiring procedures, they were informed that the Agency "does not have personnel policies and practices." This same official also failed to advise the complainants of their rights to pursue the EEO process to address their allegations of discriminatory compensation.

By July 2018, when Complainants' new supervisor inquired about the April 2018 review, the Executive Director and Senior Director denied any knowledge of having committed to such an investigation. Most significantly, in January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had indeed received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act upon its findings. The Executive Director then instructed the supervisor to "tamper any escalation of HR issues for the tribal team." In a subsequent email, the Executive Director attempted to retreat from these instructions, claiming that the supervisor had misunderstood his directive.

## CAREER ADVANCEMENT RESTRICTIONS AND ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES

The complainants alleged that the discriminatory establishment of their compensation at the Pay Band IV level effectively precluded them from applying to senior leadership positions, as the Agency made such positions available exclusively to Pay Band V employees. This created a structural barrier to advancement based on the initial discriminatory classification.

Additionally, complainants contended that in June 2018, they were "buried deeper" within the organizational structure through a reorganization process undertaken with the express intent of provoking them to resign and as a mechanism to "limit any HR escalations from the tribal team."

## DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN WORK ASSIGNMENTS AND RESOURCES

From June 2018 onward, complainants were required to create separate strategic plans on an ongoing basis, while their non-Tribal team peers were not subjected to this requirement. Furthermore, complainants alleged that they were systematically denied equal access to resources necessary to perform their duties in the same manner as their non-Tribal counterparts.

Access to resources and non-federal shareholders was forced through a separate, discriminatory process. Complainants were required to engage with contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through an intermediary "gatekeeper." The Agency further restricted the categories of meetings in which complainants were permitted to participate and required that an Agency Contracting Officer's Representative be present during all daily engagements between contractors and complainants.

## HOSTILE WORK ENVIRONMENT AND CONTRACTOR CONDUCT

Between June 2018 and February 2019, complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly informed senior leadership that Tribal team members were subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by representatives of an Agency contractor. Despite these repeated notifications, senior leadership condoned the contractors' conduct and continued to place the Tribal team in situations involving hostile interactions with contracting officials.

## PUBLIC RECOGNITION OMISSION

On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public statement via social media thanking local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service in connection with their work. However, the Agency failed to acknowledge or reference the Tribal team members, despite their substantial contributions to the same initiatives.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS

Following the completion of investigations, the complainants received copies of their investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges. The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges within the Commission's Washington Field Office. Complainants' legal representative filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each judge. The Agency opposed these consolidation motions. One Administrative Judge denied the consolidation motion while the other judge did not issue a ruling on the motion. Both judges subsequently issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established. The Agency implemented the Administrative Judges' decisions as its final action. Both complainants subsequently filed appeals challenging these determinations.

As such, we find that subparts 1(c) though 1(g) fall under that allegation. 4 [number removed], [number removed] b. The Agency limited the types of meetings Complainants were allowed to participate in. d. An Agency Contracting Officer’s Representative was required to participate in daily engagements between contractors and Complainants. 7. On May 5, 2019, the Agency failed to acknowledge Complainants and other Tribal team members’ accomplishments when issuing a tweet which thanked local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service, but did not reference the Tribal team. # INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## BACKGROUND AND COMPLAINANTS' EMPLOYMENT STATUS

The complainants in this matter were employed by the Agency as Emergency Management Specialists with responsibilities as Regional and National Tribal Government Liaisons. At the time the events giving rise to these complaints occurred, both complainants were performing their duties remotely—one from Pauma Valley, California, and the other from Thousand Palms, California. The complainants initiated their employment relationship with the Agency in October 2015, beginning at the Pay Band IV compensation level. On June 13, 2019, both complainants filed formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaints with the Agency, alleging discrimination and harassment based on their race (Native American), national origin (Native American), and in retaliation for prior protected EEO activity. Additionally, complainants initially alleged discrimination based on sex; however, this claim was not subsequently withdrawn during the hearing process.

## ALLEGED DISCRIMINATORY COMPENSATION PRACTICES

### Initial Hiring and Salary Negotiations

The complainants alleged systematic discrimination in compensation dating from their initial hire. Specifically, Complainant 1 reported that during pre-employment salary negotiations, he was informed by the Agency that it was obligated only to offer him seventy percent of his previous wage, with the explicit statement that he could "take it or leave it." Complainant 1 further contended that non-Native employees were not subjected to comparable treatment during their respective hiring processes. Complainant 2 alleged that the Agency failed to properly account for changes in her prior salary history or her teaching background, instead offering only compensation commensurate with her then-current tribal salary.

### Disparate Pay Bands and Job Classification

Both complainants asserted that they performed substantially identical work as peer employees who were hired at the Pay Band V level, yet they themselves were hired at Pay Band IV and maintained at the lowest compensation tier. This disparity in classification, the complainants argued, directly resulted from discriminatory intent based on their Native American status.

### Failure to Address Documented Pay Disparities

The complainants documented what they characterized as management's deliberate inaction regarding known compensation inequities. In approximately April 2018, the Executive Director of the Public Safety Advocacy Directorate directed Complainants' supervisor to conduct a comprehensive review addressing wage and pay band disparities within the department. However, subsequent to the completion of this review, the Executive Director and a Senior Director allegedly took no remedial action and failed to acknowledge that such a review had even been commissioned.

This pattern of non-responsiveness continued when, during a May 31, 2018 telephone conversation, the Senior Director claimed to have no knowledge of the April 2018 review. The complainants later learned from their supervisor that the Senior Director was, in fact, "very well aware" of the review's existence and findings.

When complainants inquired on June 15, 2018, with the Deputy Chief Administrative Officer regarding hiring authorities and direct hiring procedures, they were informed that the Agency "does not have personnel policies and practices." This same official also failed to advise the complainants of their rights to pursue the EEO process to address their allegations of discriminatory compensation.

By July 2018, when Complainants' new supervisor inquired about the April 2018 review, the Executive Director and Senior Director denied any knowledge of having committed to such an investigation. Most significantly, in January 2019, the Executive Director acknowledged to Supervisor 2 that he had indeed received the review but asserted that he felt no obligation to act upon its findings. The Executive Director then instructed the supervisor to "tamper any escalation of HR issues for the tribal team." In a subsequent email, the Executive Director attempted to retreat from these instructions, claiming that the supervisor had misunderstood his directive.

## CAREER ADVANCEMENT RESTRICTIONS AND ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES

The complainants alleged that the discriminatory establishment of their compensation at the Pay Band IV level effectively precluded them from applying to senior leadership positions, as the Agency made such positions available exclusively to Pay Band V employees. This created a structural barrier to advancement based on the initial discriminatory classification.

Additionally, complainants contended that in June 2018, they were "buried deeper" within the organizational structure through a reorganization process undertaken with the express intent of provoking them to resign and as a mechanism to "limit any HR escalations from the tribal team."

## DIFFERENTIAL TREATMENT IN WORK ASSIGNMENTS AND RESOURCES

From June 2018 onward, complainants were required to create separate strategic plans on an ongoing basis, while their non-Tribal team peers were not subjected to this requirement. Furthermore, complainants alleged that they were systematically denied equal access to resources necessary to perform their duties in the same manner as their non-Tribal counterparts.

Access to resources and non-federal shareholders was forced through a separate, discriminatory process. Complainants were required to engage with contracting staff and Tribal shareholders through an intermediary "gatekeeper." The Agency further restricted the categories of meetings in which complainants were permitted to participate and required that an Agency Contracting Officer's Representative be present during all daily engagements between contractors and complainants.

## HOSTILE WORK ENVIRONMENT AND CONTRACTOR CONDUCT

Between June 2018 and February 2019, complainants and other Agency officials repeatedly informed senior leadership that Tribal team members were subjected to hostile and discriminatory treatment by representatives of an Agency contractor. Despite these repeated notifications, senior leadership condoned the contractors' conduct and continued to place the Tribal team in situations involving hostile interactions with contracting officials.

## PUBLIC RECOGNITION OMISSION

On May 5, 2019, the Agency issued a public statement via social media thanking local, state, and federal workers for their dedication and service in connection with their work. However, the Agency failed to acknowledge or reference the Tribal team members, despite their substantial contributions to the same initiatives.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEEDINGS

Following the completion of investigations, the complainants received copies of their investigative files and requested hearings before EEOC Administrative Judges. The complaints were assigned to different Administrative Judges within the Commission's Washington Field Office. Complainants' legal representative filed motions to consolidate the complaints for joint processing before each judge. The Agency opposed these consolidation motions. One Administrative Judge denied the consolidation motion while the other judge did not issue a ruling on the motion. Both judges subsequently issued separate summary judgment decisions concluding that no discrimination or unlawful retaliation had been established. The Agency implemented the Administrative Judges' decisions as its final action. Both complainants subsequently filed appeals challenging these determinations.

Complainant stated without providing supporting evidence that Supervisor has a history of hatred towards him and of mistreatment of other African-Americans at work. Complainant asserted for the first time that Supervisor made comments about President Obama and displayed images of the confederate flag in the hangar. Finally, Complainant claims that the Agency has withheld “vital information” about Supervisor and summary judgment denied him the opportunity to obtain this information which, Complainant asserts, “will prove a history of racial discrimination [of Supervisor] towards African Americans.” In response, the Agency argues that the AJ’s summary judgment was proper and should stand.

# CASE FILE RECORD: EEO DISCRIMINATION COMPLAINT

## CASE OVERVIEW

This case involves an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by an Aircraft Mechanic employed at the Agency's Aircraft Maintenance Squadron facility located at Robins Air Force Base, Georgia. The complainant alleged that he was subjected to a hostile work environment based on his protected status characteristics including race (African-American), color (Black), and age (52 years old).

## PARTIES AND POSITIONS OF AUTHORITY

At the time of the alleged incident, the complainant worked under the direct supervision of an Aircraft Overhaul Supervisor, who served as his first-level supervisor. The complainant's second-level supervisor was the Production Team Lead. The hierarchical structure is documented in the original Report of Investigation.

## FACTUAL BACKGROUND OF THE INCIDENT

On December 11, 2020, the complainant sustained a work-related injury resulting in a bleeding head wound. The complainant left his work area in an attempt to locate a bandage to treat the wound. During this time, his immediate supervisor observed him away from his assigned work station. Upon discovering the complainant, the supervisor began verbally assaulting him, utilizing profane and demeaning language. Specifically, the supervisor shouted the following statement: "Get your ass back on the plane, you do not do shit every day, I want you off my fucking team immediately, and I am tired of your shit." Additionally, the complainant alleged that the supervisor refused to provide first aid assistance for his head injury.

Following this incident, the complainant reported the matter to his second-level supervisor and another Agency official. The complainant did not initially attribute the supervisor's conduct to discriminatory motives based on age or race.

## EEO COMPLAINT AND INVESTIGATION PROCEDURE

On May 25, 2021, the complainant formally filed an EEO complaint with the Agency alleging hostile work environment discrimination. The Agency conducted an investigation and subsequently provided the complainant with a copy of the investigation report along with notification of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ).

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE'S DECISION

The complainant timely requested a hearing. On January 21, 2022, the AJ issued a Notice of Proposed Summary Judgment, outlining the relevant case facts and preliminary findings. The AJ noted that while the supervisor's conduct was unprofessional and unacceptable, it did not constitute harassment under applicable law. The AJ characterized the incident as an isolated occurrence in which the supervisor lost his temper while using facially neutral language. The cursing, though inappropriate, was deemed insufficient to establish the severity required to support a hostile work environment claim.

The AJ offered both parties an opportunity to respond to the proposed summary judgment. In his response, the complainant introduced new allegations for the first time, asserting without supporting evidence that the supervisor harbored a history of hatred toward him and had mistreated other African-American employees. The complainant further alleged that the supervisor had made comments regarding President Obama and displayed Confederate flag imagery within the hangar. These new allegations had not been previously included in the EEO Counselor Report, the formal complaint, or the complainant's affidavit.

The Agency did not timely respond to the proposed summary judgment notice but did submit documentation of the supervisor's disciplinary suspension. On February 25, 2022, the AJ issued a final decision without holding a hearing, adopting the proposed summary judgment. The decision noted that the complainant had initially reported not believing the incident was motivated by race or age. Given the totality of circumstances presented, the AJ concluded that the complainant failed to establish discrimination as alleged. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ's finding.

## DISCIPLINARY ACTION TAKEN

Following investigation of the incident, the Agency imposed disciplinary measures against the supervisor, including a ten-day suspension without pay, reassignment to day shift operations, and a ninety-day restriction from supervisory duties. The supervisor's role as the complainant's supervisor terminated immediately following the incident.

## CURRENT APPEAL CONTENTIONS

The complainant has appealed the AJ's decision, contending that he was subjected to humiliation, intimidation, bullying, and racist treatment. He maintains that he provided investigators with a detailed list of racially motivated incidents and corresponding witnesses. The complainant further argues that discrimination allegations were raised multiple times prior to summary judgment and that the Agency has withheld vital information regarding the supervisor's history that would demonstrate a pattern of racial discrimination against African-American employees. The complainant asserts that the summary judgment decision denied him the opportunity to obtain such information.

The Agency maintains that the AJ's summary judgment decision was procedurally and substantively proper and should be upheld.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as an Administrative Technician, GS-0303-05, at the Agency’s Chicago Regional Office in Oak Brook, Illinois. On August 24, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on disability (diabetes and liver fibrosis) and in reprisal for prior protected EEO activity (requesting a reasonable accommodation) when he was terminated, effective July 28, 2021. Complainant does not challenge the framing of the complaint. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. In accordance with Complainant’s request, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed. In its final decision, the Agency found that Complainant was an individual with a disability and that he was qualified within the meaning of the Rehabilitation Act. Assuming Complainant established a prima facie case of discrimination and retaliation, the Agency concluded that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons that Complainant failed to rebut as pretextual. Complainant began his employment with the Agency on January 17, 2021, with a Competitive- Career Conditional Appointment, which required him to be a probationary employee for one year. He had previously worked for the Agency as an Administrative Manager (Excepted Service Appointment) during the decennial census. In a progress review dated June 15, 2021, the person listed as Complainant’s first-level supervisor stated that Complainant was not performing at the fully successful level 3 or above and listed areas for improvement, including becoming familiarized with the onboarding and payroll processes and timely completion of assignments. In three emails from June 2021, S3 (third level supervisor, Program Coordinator) emailed Complainant regarding some performance issues, including partial or missing pay for two employees in Complainant’s service area, the payroll processing for pay period 11 of that year, and the status of several new hires. S3 also issued Complainant a memorandum on June 17, 2021, titled “Failure to Follow Up on Payroll Issues,” outlining his performance deficiencies. Another of Complainant’s first-level supervisors (S1), Administrative Officer, stated in her affidavit that Complainant had errors and issues with his work that caused several people not to receive their pay on time, which resulted in new hires resigning. S1, who became Complainant’s supervisor in early July 2021, retrained the staff upon learning of these errors. S1 stated that even after retraining, Complainant “continued to have unresolved pay issues for the new hires he was responsible for.” S3 issued Complainant a termination letter on July 28, 2021, citing his unacceptable performance during his probationary period. The letter stated that he had failed to ensure timely onboarding of new hires and tracking them through the hiring process. In addition, the letter stated he failed to successfully process payroll in a timely matter. Another supervisor, Administrative Specialist (AS), said she supervised Complainant until his termination, though her affidavit indicated that she supervised and assigned Complainant tasks related to the Census Investigative Service Missing Documents Project as opposed to payroll/timekeeping. AS claims that she did not observe any unacceptable job performance issues concerning Complainant and that no such issues were brought to her attention regarding his involvement in the Missing Documents Project. AS averred that she believed Complainant was terminated based on his disabilities and for requesting a reasonable accommodation based on her observation of “tension between the Complainant and [S3] regarding his work schedule.” The Agency found that management’s legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for terminating Complainant during his probationary period were based on his performance issues in processing payroll and new hire onboarding, which he often failed to complete without errors or on time. In addressing the question of whether Complainant established pretext, the Agency noted AS’s affidavit, where she stated she did not observe any performance problems by Complainant while under her supervision. The Agency determined that AS only supervised one aspect of Complainant’s work, the Missing Documents Project, not timekeeping and processing of new hires. Because three of Complainant’s supervisors confirmed his deficiencies in those areas, the Agency found that AS’s statements did not cast doubt on the Agency’s explanation. The Agency also reasoned that there was no evidence that S3 voiced opposition to Complainant’s reasonable accommodation or his telework schedule, especially given that all of the Administrative Technicians she supervised teleworked two days per week for at least a portion of the period at issue. The Agency therefore concluded Complainant could not show management’s reasons were pretext for discrimination or reprisal, beyond Complainant’s subjective belief.

# INVESTIGATION RECORD - CASE FILE DOCUMENTATION

## Case Background and Complaint Filing

The complainant, employed as an Administrative Technician at the GS-0303-05 level, worked at the Agency's Chicago Regional Office located in Oak Brook, Illinois. On August 24, 2021, the complainant filed a formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint asserting that the Agency had engaged in discriminatory and retaliatory conduct resulting in his termination, which became effective on July 28, 2021. The complainant alleged that discrimination was based on his disabilities, specifically diabetes and liver fibrosis. Additionally, he claimed the Agency retaliated against him for engaging in protected EEO activity by requesting reasonable accommodations. The complainant did not challenge the framing or characterization of his complaint.

## Investigation and Agency Decision Process

Following completion of the investigation, the Agency provided the complainant with a copy of the investigation report and formal notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge. The complainant exercised his right to request such a hearing. Subsequently, the Agency issued a final decision in accordance with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b), concluding that the complainant failed to establish that the Agency had subjected him to discrimination as alleged in his complaint. This final decision prompted the complainant to file the instant appeal.

## Agency's Findings Regarding Disability Status

The Agency's final decision acknowledged and accepted certain factual findings. Specifically, the Agency determined that the complainant was indeed an individual with a disability under applicable law and that he qualified for protection under the Rehabilitation Act. However, while assuming arguendo that the complainant had established a prima facie case of both discrimination and retaliation, the Agency concluded that it had articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for the complainant's termination that the complainant failed to rebut as pretextual.

## Employment History and Performance Issues

The complainant began employment with the Agency on January 17, 2021, under a Competitive-Career Conditional Appointment, which subjected him to a mandatory one-year probationary period. Prior to this appointment, the complainant had worked for the Agency in an excepted service position as an Administrative Manager during the decennial census operations.

During his tenure, several supervisors documented performance concerns. A progress review dated June 15, 2021, prepared by the complainant's first-level supervisor, indicated that he was not performing at the fully successful level 3 or above. The review identified specific areas requiring improvement, including familiarization with onboarding procedures and payroll processes, as well as timely completion of work assignments.

Additional performance issues emerged in June 2021. The complainant's third-level supervisor (S3), a Program Coordinator, sent three separate emails addressing performance deficiencies related to incomplete or missing compensation for two employees, delayed payroll processing for pay period 11, and the status of newly hired staff members. On June 17, 2021, this supervisor issued a memorandum explicitly titled "Failure to Follow Up on Payroll Issues," further documenting the complainant's performance deficiencies.

## Operational Impact and Supervisory Observations

Another first-level supervisor (S1), an Administrative Officer, provided an affidavit detailing how the complainant's errors resulted in incorrect or delayed compensation for multiple employees, which ultimately led to newly hired staff resigning from their positions. When S1 assumed supervisory responsibility in early July 2021, she initiated retraining of the affected staff members. Despite this retraining intervention, S1 documented that the complainant continued to experience unresolved pay issues affecting the new hires under his responsibility.

## Termination and Stated Reasons
