She was denied her repeated request for reasonable accommodation from April 21, 2020, to her termination on January 22, 2021; 2 and 2. She was charged as Absent Without Leave (AWOL) from August 10, 2020, to her termination on January 22, 2021. At the conclusion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). An investigator noted in the report of investigation that Complainant did not provide an affidavit requested during the investigation of the complaint. 3 The AJ issued a decision without holding a hearing, finding no discrimination. The record indicates that Complainant was appointed as a Primary Care Physician at the Agency on March 3, 2019, subject to a two-year probationary period. As a Primary Care Physician, Complainant’s essential duties included: interviewing and examining patients daily (typically 12), via in-person and virtual; examining patients who were present for face-to-face visits; documenting patient visits in the Agency’s electronic medical record; and ordering consults, labs, and medications using the electronic medical record. Complainant indicated that she sustained a shoulder injury on July 12, 2019. We note that Complainant did not claim that she notified her supervisors or requested a reasonable accommodation at the time of her July 12, 2019 injury. Complainant indicated that in December 2019, she aggravated a prior injury to her right shoulder and notified her supervisors of this December 2019 injury shortly thereafter. Complainant claimed that due to her physical conditions, she was unable to lift her right arm, use a mouse or keyboard, or write, and was therefore unable to perform physical examinations on patients, unable to document notes, or use a computer for more than a few minutes at a time. Regarding claim 1, Complainant’s supervisor (S1) indicated that he became aware of Complainant’s right shoulder condition in December 2019. S1 stated that on February 25, 2020, Complainant made a verbal reasonable accommodation request and submitted Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) requesting no lifting, no prolonged upper extremely fine manipulation with the right arm/hand, part-time, light duties to include 20 hours work week, no grabbing, and assistance with computer tasks as needed. Our records indicate that on August 2, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint, [number removed], regarding her January 22, 2021 termination, recommended by the Professional Standards Board. The Agency issued its final Agency decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision, and that matter is pending before the Commission, in EEOC [number removed]. The investigator noted that when asked on several occasions, Complainant stated that she sent her affidavit to a “higher authority.” Complainant’s affidavit was not included in the Report of Investigation. Complainant indicates that she sent her affidavit to then Secretary of the Agency, instead. The record indicates that Complainant provided the affidavit to the AJ. After being on leave since December 2019, due to her conditions, Complainant returned to work on March 2, 2020, with the work shift restrictions in place as she requested (i.e., work four hours per day and four hours Leave Without Pay (LWOP), five days per week). She was required to complete the Agency’s Talent Management System training modules online and see two or three patients by the end of the week if needed. Complainant failed to see a patient or complete the required training. A Medical Assistant reported that on March 4, 2020, Complainant declined to see a patient in the waiting room who had already waited several months to see her. Complainant told the Medical Assistant that she could not see the patient because her shoulder was bothering her, and she could barely hold a pen to write notes. On March 5, 2020, S1, Complainant’s second level supervisor (S2), and the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator initiated an interactive process regarding Complainant’s accommodation request and held a meeting. During the meeting, Complainant made it clear that she could not perform patient examinations of her patients, was unable to complete patient paperwork, and was unable to use a computer for more than a few minutes at a time. Because there was concern even part-time work would worsen her condition, the Agency decided to grant Complainant’s alternative accommodation of continuing LWOP to rehabilitate her injury for a six-week period. Complainant indicated that she remained in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Two weeks after the meeting, Complainant requested 100% telework. In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested Complainant provide physician documentation regarding her ability to perform essential functions of her position including her limitations with typing notes, placing orders including consults, sending out lab letters, and filling out paperwork and forms as requested by her patients. During this time period, due to COVID-19, non-urgent appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements were made for hospital physicians on ad hoc basis, i.e., 50% telework alternating weeks in-person in the hospital and at-home teleworking. Meanwhile, the Agency prepared dictation software to be installed in Complainant’s computer (to minimize typing); two ergonomic chairs to be delivered to her office for each of her exam rooms; and an ergonomic mouse and keyboard were shipped to her home and a second set was delivered to her office. A laptop was approved on March 3, 2020, but the delivery was delayed due to a shortage of equipment. S1 sent a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation program (CAP), within the Department of Defense, to try to get one sooner but the CAP denied the request because during the “Needs Assessment,” Complainant failed to submit sufficient medical documentation to support the need for a second laptop, as well as a telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency secured a laptop for Complainant, but she never signed a telework agreement, i.e., addressing teleworking for one to three months due to her temporary disability. S1 indicated that the Agency could not offer Complainant’s requested unconditional 100% telework for at least a year because she failed to provide medical documentation to justify the request. Further, S1 stated that the hospital had a shortage of physicians, some providers were sick with COVID-19, and Complainant’s patients were being covered by other physicians. Thus, the Agency decided to offer Complainant a telework agreement for one to three months, dependent upon updates to her medical documentation. Complainant did not accept the Agency’s telework agreement. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator indicated that Complainant made several accommodation requests, including one on April 21, 2020. Complainant requested 100% telework, 20 hours per work week, and modified work assignments for one year to permanent basis. The Coordinator stated, and the record reflects, that she made numerous requests, including several emails in June 2020, to Complainant for medical documentation of her disability in connection with her reasonable accommodation requests. Complainant failed to provide such documentation. Specifically, the Coordinator stated that Complainant was asked to provide medical documentations relating to the effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation with her medical condition and the information relating to the duration of her medical condition, including her consent to contact her physician in order to proceed with her accommodation request. Complainant failed to provide such information. Thus, on August 7, 2020, the Coordinator closed Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation and informed her that the case would be reopened if she provided the requested documentation. The record reflects that Complainant provided the Agency a copy of her doctor’s (DR1) Return to Work statements. In a Return to Work, dated January 13, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on January 13, 2020, and may return to work after follow-up on February 10, 2020. In a Return to Work, dated February 10, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on February 10, 2020, and may return to work on March 2, 2020. The record also reflects that Complainant provided a doctor’s (DR2) statement dated February 25, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant was under DR2’s care for her right shoulder; she should be given light duty and part-time work with no lifting; she should be given assistance with computer tasks; and her return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks. In DR2’s statement, dated April 21, 2020, DR2 indicated that Complainant should be allowed to continue in light duty, work from home via laptop, and telemedicine; and her status to return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020. In two statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 stated that Complainant was evaluated on May 19, 2020, for right shoulder; she had dexterity issues; she was to continue in physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises and working from home via telemedicine; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. The record indicates that on July 15, 2020, Complainant submitted DR2’s statement dated June 22, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant should be allowed to work from home via telemedicine, maximum 20 hours weekly; she was in pain with dexterity issues; she had issues with gripping and right arm/hand manipulation; she reported pain and issues with gripping the wheel when driving; she would continue with physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to resume normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. In a statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2, reiterating the foregoing statement, indicated that he was recommending an evaluation with a back specialist for Complainant’s condition; her status to return would be reevaluated; and her “shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time.” Regarding claim 2, S1 and S2 indicated that after Complainant’s reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant AWOL for her absence. Considering the Coordinator’s suggestion and the fact that Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months without providing medical documentation as requested, management decided to place her in AWOL starting August 10, 2020. The Agency stated that Complainant used all her annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020; she was subsequently granted LWOP on February 7 – 29, 2020 (80 hours), March 2 – 26, 2020 (480 hours), and March 26 – August 7, 2020 (421 hours). Complainant indicated that she was in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Complainant remained in AWOL since August 10, 2020. The AJ found no discrimination as Complainant alleged. Specifically, the AJ stated that Complainant did not establish that the Agency failed to provide her with a reasonable accommodation in that she failed to provide medical documentation the Agency requested showing that she was able to perform her position duty, i.e., examining patients physically. The AJ found: Complainant alleges only that she suffered from her inability to use her right arm. She has provided limited documentation to support having any disability, and all the documentation provided stated the treating physician would reassess in weeks to come. Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to offer any medical documentation of a diagnosis of her condition, or a duration; i.e. whether it was temporary or permanent. She failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information; and she failed to offer a release authorizing medical information to be disclosed even to the investigator in this case. The AJ further found: Complainant has not shown that she would be able to work from home as, by her own admission, she was unable to use a pen or computer on her own. Additionally, the permanent accommodation requested, telework, is one that Complainant is not qualified for as telework would require an increase in use of the computer. Further, as, part of her responsibilities as a [Primary Care Physician], Complainant is required to examine patients physically even as a telework clinician. Complainant stated she was unable to do so on March 4, 2020[,] and after that never provided any documentation that she was able to examine patients. Complainant refused to engage with the Agency on discussions regarding this issue by failing to provide medical documentation, therefore causing the Agency to close her case without a denial or approval. The Agency did not issue a final order and the AJ’s decision effectively became its final action. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final order, contesting its finding of no discrimination. On appeal, Complainant submits numerous documents, including subsequent doctors’ statements.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE REPORT

## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND

This case involves an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by a former employee of the Department of Veterans Affairs, East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center, located in East Orange, New Jersey. At the time of the events that gave rise to this complaint, the Complainant held the position of Primary Care Physician at the Grade Level GS-15. The Complainant's employment relationship with the Agency culminated in her termination on January 22, 2021, following a recommendation from the Agency's Professional Standards Board. The Complainant filed her EEO complaint on August 2, 2021, challenging her termination and seeking relief based on allegations of employment discrimination. Subsequently, the Agency issued its final decision finding no discrimination, which the Complainant then appealed to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. This matter remains pending before the Commission.

## EMPLOYMENT POSITION AND ESSENTIAL DUTIES

The Complainant was appointed to her position as a Primary Care Physician at the East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center on March 3, 2019, subject to completion of a two-year probationary period. In her capacity as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant's position entailed several essential job functions and responsibilities. These duties required her to conduct daily patient interviews and examinations, typically involving approximately twelve patients per day. Her clinical responsibilities encompassed both in-person, face-to-face patient visits and virtual patient consultations. Additionally, the Complainant was responsible for documenting all patient visits within the Agency's electronic medical record system, which required proficiency in computer usage and data entry. As part of her comprehensive patient care responsibilities, the Complainant was also required to order consultations, laboratory tests, and medications using the Agency's electronic medical record system. The performance of these duties was essential to the position and constituted the core responsibilities of a Primary Care Physician at the facility.

## MEDICAL CONDITIONS AND ACCOMMODATION REQUESTS

The Complainant's medical history relevant to this case began on July 12, 2019, when she sustained an initial injury to her shoulder. However, the record indicates that the Complainant did not immediately notify her supervisors of this injury or request reasonable accommodation at that time. Subsequently, in December 2019, the Complainant aggravated a prior injury to her right shoulder and notified her supervisors of this additional injury shortly after its occurrence. The Complainant attributed multiple functional limitations to her physical condition, including an inability to lift her right arm, inability to operate a computer mouse or keyboard, inability to write, and general limitations in fine motor manipulation of her right hand. As a result of these claimed limitations, the Complainant asserted that she was unable to perform necessary physical examinations on patients, unable to document clinical notes in the electronic medical record system, and unable to use a computer for extended periods.

The Complainant's immediate supervisor, hereinafter referred to as S1, became aware of the Complainant's right shoulder condition in December 2019. On February 25, 2020, the Complainant made an initial verbal request for reasonable accommodation and subsequently submitted a formal request under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). This formal accommodation request specified several modifications to her work duties, including no lifting restrictions, prohibition on prolonged upper extremity fine manipulation with the right arm and hand, reduction to part-time status with a maximum of twenty hours per week, restrictions on grabbing or grasping activities, and provision of assistance with computer-related tasks as needed.

## INTERACTIVE PROCESS AND ACCOMMODATION ATTEMPTS

Following her return to work on March 2, 2020, after a period of leave beginning in December 2019, the Complainant was granted work shift restrictions as she had requested. These restrictions permitted her to work four hours per day while taking four hours of Leave Without Pay (LWOP), continuing this schedule for five days per week. Upon her return to work, the Complainant was required to complete mandatory online training modules through the Agency's Talent Management System and to see between two and three patients by the end of that first week if operationally necessary. The Complainant, however, failed to see any patients during this initial return period and did not complete the required training modules.

A Medical Assistant employed at the facility documented that on March 4, 2020, the Complainant declined to see a patient who was already waiting in the clinic and who had been on the scheduling list for several months. When questioned about her refusal, the Complainant indicated that she could not see the patient due to her shoulder condition and stated that her shoulder was bothering her considerably, to the extent that she could barely hold a pen to write clinical notes.

On March 5, 2020, the Complainant's immediate supervisor, her second-level supervisor (hereinafter referred to as S2), and the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator held a formal meeting to initiate the interactive process regarding the Complainant's accommodation request. During this meeting, the Complainant explicitly stated that she could not perform physical patient examinations, was unable to complete necessary patient paperwork, and was unable to utilize a computer for more than a few minutes at any given time. Given the Agency's concern that even part-time in-person work might exacerbate her medical condition, the Agency decided to grant the Complainant an alternative accommodation consisting of continued LWOP status to allow for rehabilitation of her injury over a specified six-week period.

The Complainant remained in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Approximately two weeks following the March 5 meeting, the Complainant submitted a request for one hundred percent telework accommodations. In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested that the Complainant provide physician documentation addressing her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically including documentation of her limitations with typing notes, placing orders and consults, sending laboratory letters, and completing paperwork and forms required for patient care.

During this period, the Agency was simultaneously responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which non-urgent medical appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements for hospital physicians were implemented on an ad hoc basis, typically involving fifty percent telework with alternating weeks of in-person hospital work and remote teleworking from home. Concurrently, the Agency made substantial efforts to accommodate the Complainant's needs through various technological and ergonomic modifications. These accommodations included preparation and installation of dictation software on the Complainant's computer to minimize the necessity for typing; procurement and delivery of two ergonomic chairs, one for each of her examination rooms; shipment of ergonomic mice and keyboards to both her home and office locations; and approval for issuance of a laptop computer on March 3, 2020, though delivery was delayed due to equipment shortages related to the pandemic.

S1 subsequently submitted a second laptop request through the Computer and Electronic Accommodation (CAP) program, which operates within the Department of Defense, in an effort to expedite equipment delivery. However, the CAP program denied this request, citing insufficient medical documentation submitted during the Needs Assessment to support the necessity for a second laptop, as well as the absence of a signed telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency eventually secured a laptop for the Complainant; however, the Complainant never executed the required telework agreement, which would have addressed her teleworking arrangement for a temporary period of one to three months in light of her temporary disability status.

S1 indicated that the Agency could not accommodate the Complainant's request for unconditional one hundred percent telework for an extended period of at least one year because the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation to justify such an extended accommodation. Furthermore, S1 noted that the hospital was experiencing a significant shortage of physicians, that certain providers were absent due to illness from COVID-19, and that the Complainant's patient caseload was being managed by other physicians during her absence. Based on these considerations, the Agency offered the Complainant a telework agreement for a temporary period of one to three months, with the duration to be determined based on updates to her medical documentation and reassessment by her treating physician. The Complainant declined to accept the Agency's offered telework agreement.

## MEDICAL DOCUMENTATION AND ACCOMMODATION COORDINATOR ACTIONS

The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator documented that the Complainant made several separate accommodation requests, including a formal request on April 21, 2020. In that request, the Complainant sought one hundred percent telework, a reduction to twenty hours per work week, and modified work assignments to be implemented either for a one-year period or on a permanent basis. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator stated, and the record confirms, that she made numerous requests of the Complainant, including several written emails in June 2020, requesting provision of medical documentation to support the Complainant's reasonable accommodation requests and to establish the existence and nature of her claimed disability.

The Coordinator specifically requested that the Complainant provide medical documentation demonstrating the effectiveness of telework and telemedicine accommodations in relation to her medical condition, as well as information establishing the expected duration of her medical condition, including whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature. The Coordinator also requested that the Complainant provide authorization and consent for the Agency to contact her treating physician in order to gather necessary information and proceed with processing her accommodation request. Despite these repeated and documented requests, the Complainant failed to provide the requested medical documentation or authorization.

Consequently, on August 7, 2020, the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator closed the Complainant's reasonable accommodation request file and formally notified the Complainant that the case would be reopened if she subsequently provided the requested documentation.

## MEDICAL RECORDS ANALYSIS

The record reflects that the Complainant provided the Agency with copies of Return to Work statements from her treating physicians. In a Return to Work statement dated January 13, 2020, the Complainant's first treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR1, documented that the Complainant had been seen in his office on that date and could return to work after a follow-up examination scheduled for February 10, 2020. In a subsequent Return to Work statement dated February 10, 2020, DR1 documented that the Complainant had been examined on that date and was medically cleared to return to work on March 2, 2020.

Additionally, the record contains a medical statement from a second treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR2, dated February 25, 2020. In that statement, DR2 documented that the Complainant was under his care for her right shoulder condition and recommended that she be assigned light duty and part-time work with restrictions on lifting. DR2 further recommended that the Complainant be provided assistance with computer-related tasks and stated that her status and readiness to return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks.

In a subsequent statement dated April 21, 2020, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to continue on light duty status, work from home utilizing a laptop computer, and provide telemedicine services to patients. DR2 indicated that the Complainant's status for return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020.

In two separate medical statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 documented that the Complainant had been evaluated on that date for her right shoulder condition. The physician noted that the Complainant continued to experience dexterity issues and recommended that she continue physical therapy to address shoulder exercises and functional limitations. DR2 stated that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with appropriate ergonomic support and indicated that her status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.

On July 15, 2020, the Complainant submitted a statement from DR2 dated June 22, 2020. In this statement, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to work from home via telemedicine services, with a maximum of twenty hours per week. The physician documented that the Complainant continued to experience pain with associated dexterity issues, including difficulties with gripping and right arm and hand manipulation, and reported pain and functional difficulties when performing activities such as gripping the steering wheel while driving. DR2 recommended continuation of physical therapy and noted that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support. The physician indicated that the Complainant's status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.

In a final statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2 reiterated the foregoing clinical findings and recommendations. Additionally, DR2 noted that he was recommending evaluation by a spine specialist for the Complainant's condition, stated that her return to work status would be reevaluated, and documented that the Complainant's "shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time" from his direct care.

## AWOL DETERMINATION AND TERMINATION

Following the closure of the Complainant's reasonable accommodation case by the Coordinator, S1 and S2 indicated that the Coordinator suggested it would be appropriate and reasonable to place the Complainant in Absent Without Leave (AWOL) status for her continued absence from work. Management considered the Coordinator's recommendation in conjunction with the fact that the Complainant had not reported for work for nearly eight months and had not provided the medical documentation that the Agency had repeatedly requested. Based on these factors, management determined that it was appropriate to place the Complainant in AWOL status beginning August 10, 2020.

The Agency documented that the Complainant had utilized all available annual leave and sick leave accruals during the period from December 20, 2019, through February 6, 2020. Subsequently, the Complainant was granted LWOP in increments as follows: eighty hours for February 7 through February 29, 2020; four hundred eighty hours for March 2 through March 26, 2020; and four hundred twenty-one hours for March 26 through August 7, 2020. The Complainant remained in AWOL status from August 10, 2020, until her subsequent termination on January 22, 2021.

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

The Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a decision finding no discrimination, concluding that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency had wrongfully denied her request for reasonable accommodation. The AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation demonstrating her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically her ability to perform physical examinations of patients.

The AJ found that although the Complainant alleged she suffered from limitations in using her right arm, she had provided limited documentation to support the existence of a disability as defined under applicable law. The AJ noted that all medical documentation provided indicated that her treating physician would conduct reassessments at future dates. Despite the Agency's repeated requests, the Complainant failed to provide any medical documentation establishing a formal diagnosis of her condition or its duration—specifically, whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature. The AJ further found that the Complainant had failed to execute a release authorization permitting the Agency to obtain medical information from her treating physicians and had declined to provide even the investigator with a release authorizing disclosure of her medical information.

The AJ additionally found that the Complainant had not demonstrated that she would be able to work from home through telework, as the Complainant herself had admitted that she was unable to use a pen or computer without assistance. The AJ noted that the permanent accommodation the Complainant was requesting—telework—was one for which she was not qualified, as telework would require an increase in computer usage, and as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant was required to perform physical examinations of patients even in a telework arrangement. The AJ found that the Complainant had stated she was unable to perform such physical examinations on March 4, 2020, and had never subsequently provided documentation demonstrating that she had regained the ability to perform this essential function. The AJ concluded that the Complainant had refused to engage with the Agency regarding these critical issues by failing to provide the requested medical documentation, thereby causing the Agency to close her accommodation case without issuing either a formal denial or approval of her request.

## APPEAL AND PENDING MATTER

The Agency did not issue a separate final order, and the Administrative Judge's decision effectively became the final action of the Agency. The Complainant has appealed from this final action, contesting the Agency's finding of no discrimination.

During this time period, due to COVID-19, non-urgent appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements were made for hospital physicians on ad hoc basis, i.e., 50% telework alternating weeks in-person in the hospital and at-home teleworking. Meanwhile, the Agency prepared dictation software to be installed in Complainant’s computer (to minimize typing); two ergonomic chairs to be delivered to her office for each of her exam rooms; and an ergonomic mouse and keyboard were shipped to her home and a second set was delivered to her office. A laptop was approved on March 3, 2020, but the delivery was delayed due to a shortage of equipment. S1 sent a second laptop request through the Computer/Electronic Accommodation program (CAP), within the Department of Defense, to try to get one sooner but the CAP denied the request because during the “Needs Assessment,” Complainant failed to submit sufficient medical documentation to support the need for a second laptop, as well as a telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency secured a laptop for Complainant, but she never signed a telework agreement, i.e., addressing teleworking for one to three months due to her temporary disability. S1 indicated that the Agency could not offer Complainant’s requested unconditional 100% telework for at least a year because she failed to provide medical documentation to justify the request. Further, S1 stated that the hospital had a shortage of physicians, some providers were sick with COVID-19, and Complainant’s patients were being covered by other physicians. Thus, the Agency decided to offer Complainant a telework agreement for one to three months, dependent upon updates to her medical documentation. Complainant did not accept the Agency’s telework agreement. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator indicated that Complainant made several accommodation requests, including one on April 21, 2020. Complainant requested 100% telework, 20 hours per work week, and modified work assignments for one year to permanent basis. The Coordinator stated, and the record reflects, that she made numerous requests, including several emails in June 2020, to Complainant for medical documentation of her disability in connection with her reasonable accommodation requests. Complainant failed to provide such documentation. Specifically, the Coordinator stated that Complainant was asked to provide medical documentations relating to the effectiveness of telework/telemedicine accommodation with her medical condition and the information relating to the duration of her medical condition, including her consent to contact her physician in order to proceed with her accommodation request. Complainant failed to provide such information. Thus, on August 7, 2020, the Coordinator closed Complainant’s request for reasonable accommodation and informed her that the case would be reopened if she provided the requested documentation. The record reflects that Complainant provided the Agency a copy of her doctor’s (DR1) Return to Work statements. In a Return to Work, dated January 13, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on January 13, 2020, and may return to work after follow-up on February 10, 2020. In a Return to Work, dated February 10, 2020, DR1 indicated that Complainant was seen in his office on February 10, 2020, and may return to work on March 2, 2020. The record also reflects that Complainant provided a doctor’s (DR2) statement dated February 25, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant was under DR2’s care for her right shoulder; she should be given light duty and part-time work with no lifting; she should be given assistance with computer tasks; and her return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks. In DR2’s statement, dated April 21, 2020, DR2 indicated that Complainant should be allowed to continue in light duty, work from home via laptop, and telemedicine; and her status to return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020. In two statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 stated that Complainant was evaluated on May 19, 2020, for right shoulder; she had dexterity issues; she was to continue in physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises and working from home via telemedicine; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. The record indicates that on July 15, 2020, Complainant submitted DR2’s statement dated June 22, 2020. Therein, DR2 stated that Complainant should be allowed to work from home via telemedicine, maximum 20 hours weekly; she was in pain with dexterity issues; she had issues with gripping and right arm/hand manipulation; she reported pain and issues with gripping the wheel when driving; she would continue with physical therapy to oversee shoulder exercises; she was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support; and her status to resume normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks. In a statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2, reiterating the foregoing statement, indicated that he was recommending an evaluation with a back specialist for Complainant’s condition; her status to return would be reevaluated; and her “shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time.” Regarding claim 2, S1 and S2 indicated that after Complainant’s reasonable accommodation case was closed, the Coordinator suggested it was reasonable to charge Complainant AWOL for her absence. Considering the Coordinator’s suggestion and the fact that Complainant had not worked for nearly eight months without providing medical documentation as requested, management decided to place her in AWOL starting August 10, 2020. The Agency stated that Complainant used all her annual and sick leave from December 20, 2019 through February 6, 2020; she was subsequently granted LWOP on February 7 – 29, 2020 (80 hours), March 2 – 26, 2020 (480 hours), and March 26 – August 7, 2020 (421 hours). Complainant indicated that she was in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Complainant remained in AWOL since August 10, 2020. The AJ found no discrimination as Complainant alleged. Specifically, the AJ stated that Complainant did not establish that the Agency failed to provide her with a reasonable accommodation in that she failed to provide medical documentation the Agency requested showing that she was able to perform her position duty, i.e., examining patients physically. The AJ found: Complainant alleges only that she suffered from her inability to use her right arm. She has provided limited documentation to support having any disability, and all the documentation provided stated the treating physician would reassess in weeks to come. Despite repeated requests, Complainant failed to offer any medical documentation of a diagnosis of her condition, or a duration; i.e. whether it was temporary or permanent. She failed to sign a release authorizing the Agency to obtain medical information; and she failed to offer a release authorizing medical information to be disclosed even to the investigator in this case. The AJ further found: Complainant has not shown that she would be able to work from home as, by her own admission, she was unable to use a pen or computer on her own. Additionally, the permanent accommodation requested, telework, is one that Complainant is not qualified for as telework would require an increase in use of the computer. Further, as, part of her responsibilities as a [Primary Care Physician], Complainant is required to examine patients physically even as a telework clinician. Complainant stated she was unable to do so on March 4, 2020[,] and after that never provided any documentation that she was able to examine patients. Complainant refused to engage with the Agency on discussions regarding this issue by failing to provide medical documentation, therefore causing the Agency to close her case without a denial or approval. The Agency did not issue a final order and the AJ’s decision effectively became its final action. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). Complainant appeals from the Agency’s final order, contesting its finding of no discrimination. On appeal, Complainant submits numerous documents, including subsequent doctors’ statements.

# INVESTIGATION CASE FILE REPORT

## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND

This case involves an Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by a former employee of the Department of Veterans Affairs, East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center, located in East Orange, New Jersey. At the time of the events that gave rise to this complaint, the Complainant held the position of Primary Care Physician at the Grade Level GS-15. The Complainant's employment relationship with the Agency culminated in her termination on January 23, 2021, following a recommendation from the Agency's Professional Standards Board. The Complainant filed her EEO complaint on August 2, 2021, challenging her termination and seeking relief based on allegations of employment discrimination. Subsequently, the Agency issued its final decision finding no discrimination, which the Complainant then appealed to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. This matter remains pending before the Commission.

## EMPLOYMENT POSITION AND ESSENTIAL DUTIES

The Complainant was appointed to her position as a Primary Care Physician at the East Orange Veterans Affairs Medical Center on March 3, 2019, subject to completion of a two-year probationary period. In her capacity as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant's position entailed several essential job functions and responsibilities. These duties required her to conduct daily patient interviews and examinations, typically involving approximately twelve patients per day. Her clinical responsibilities encompassed both in-person, face-to-face patient visits and virtual patient consultations. Additionally, the Complainant was responsible for documenting all patient visits within the Agency's electronic medical record system, which required proficiency in computer usage and data entry. As part of her comprehensive patient care responsibilities, the Complainant was also required to order consultations, laboratory tests, and medications using the Agency's electronic medical record system. The performance of these duties was essential to the position and constituted the core responsibilities of a Primary Care Physician at the facility.

## MEDICAL CONDITIONS AND ACCOMMODATION REQUESTS

The Complainant's medical history relevant to this case began on July 12, 2019, when she sustained an initial injury to her shoulder. However, the record indicates that the Complainant did not immediately notify her supervisors of this injury or request reasonable accommodation at that time. Subsequently, in December 2019, the Complainant aggravated a prior injury to her right shoulder and notified her supervisors of this additional injury shortly after its occurrence. The Complainant attributed multiple functional limitations to her physical condition, including an inability to lift her right arm, inability to operate a computer mouse or keyboard, inability to write, and general limitations in fine motor manipulation of her right hand. As a result of these claimed limitations, the Complainant asserted that she was unable to perform necessary physical examinations on patients, unable to document clinical notes in the electronic medical record system, and unable to use a computer for extended periods.

The Complainant's immediate supervisor, hereinafter referred to as S1, became aware of the Complainant's right shoulder condition in December 2019. On February 25, 2020, the Complainant made an initial verbal request for reasonable accommodation and subsequently submitted a formal request under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). This formal accommodation request specified several modifications to her work duties, including no lifting restrictions, prohibition on prolonged upper extremity fine manipulation with the right arm and hand, reduction to part-time status with a maximum of twenty hours per week, restrictions on grabbing or grasping activities, and provision of assistance with computer-related tasks as needed.

## INTERACTIVE PROCESS AND ACCOMMODATION ATTEMPTS

Following her return to work on March 2, 2020, after a period of leave beginning in December 2019, the Complainant was granted work shift restrictions as she had requested. These restrictions permitted her to work four hours per day while taking four hours of Leave Without Pay (LWOP), continuing this schedule for five days per week. Upon her return to work, the Complainant was required to complete mandatory online training modules through the Agency's Talent Management System and to see between two and three patients by the end of that first week if operationally necessary. The Complainant, however, failed to see any patients during this initial return period and did not complete the required training modules.

A Medical Assistant employed at the facility documented that on March 4, 2020, the Complainant declined to see a patient who was already waiting in the clinic and who had been on the scheduling list for several months. When questioned about her refusal, the Complainant indicated that she could not see the patient due to her shoulder condition and stated that her shoulder was bothering her considerably, to the extent that she could barely hold a pen to write clinical notes.

On March 5, 2020, the Complainant's immediate supervisor, her second-level supervisor (hereinafter referred to as S2), and the Agency's Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator held a formal meeting to initiate the interactive process regarding the Complainant's accommodation request. During this meeting, the Complainant explicitly stated that she could not perform physical patient examinations, was unable to complete necessary patient paperwork, and was unable to utilize a computer for more than a few minutes at any given time. Given the Agency's concern that even part-time in-person work might exacerbate her medical condition, the Agency decided to grant the Complainant an alternative accommodation consisting of continued LWOP status to allow for rehabilitation of her injury over a specified six-week period.

The Complainant remained in an approved LWOP status from March 4, 2020, through August 10, 2020. Approximately two weeks following the March 5 meeting, the Complainant submitted a request for one hundred percent telework accommodations. In response, on March 25, 2020, S1 requested that the Complainant provide physician documentation addressing her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically including documentation of her limitations with typing notes, placing orders and consults, sending laboratory letters, and completing paperwork and forms required for patient care.

During this period, the Agency was simultaneously responding to the COVID-19 pandemic, during which non-urgent medical appointments were cancelled, and telework arrangements for hospital physicians were implemented on an ad hoc basis, typically involving fifty percent telework with alternating weeks of in-person hospital work and remote teleworking from home. Concurrently, the Agency made substantial efforts to accommodate the Complainant's needs through various technological and ergonomic modifications. These accommodations included preparation and installation of dictation software on the Complainant's computer to minimize the necessity for typing; procurement and delivery of two ergonomic chairs, one for each of her examination rooms; shipment of ergonomic mice and keyboards to both her home and office locations; and approval for issuance of a laptop computer on March 3, 2020, though delivery was delayed due to equipment shortages related to the pandemic.

S1 subsequently submitted a second laptop request through the Computer and Electronic Accommodation (CAP) program, which operates within the Department of Defense, in an effort to expedite equipment delivery. However, the CAP program denied this request, citing insufficient medical documentation submitted during the Needs Assessment to support the necessity for a second laptop, as well as the absence of a signed telework agreement. On June 2, 2020, the Agency eventually secured a laptop for the Complainant; however, the Complainant never executed the required telework agreement, which would have addressed her teleworking arrangement for a temporary period of one to three months in light of her temporary disability status.

S1 indicated that the Agency could not accommodate the Complainant's request for unconditional one hundred percent telework for an extended period of at least one year because the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation to justify such an extended accommodation. Furthermore, S1 noted that the hospital was experiencing a significant shortage of physicians, that certain providers were absent due to illness from COVID-19, and that the Complainant's patient caseload was being managed by other physicians during her absence. Based on these considerations, the Agency offered the Complainant a telework agreement for a temporary period of one to three months, with the duration to be determined based on updates to her medical documentation and reassessment by her treating physician. The Complainant declined to accept the Agency's offered telework agreement.

## MEDICAL DOCUMENTATION AND ACCOMMODATION COORDINATOR ACTIONS

The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator documented that the Complainant made several separate accommodation requests, including a formal request on April 21, 2020. In that request, the Complainant sought one hundred percent telework, a reduction to twenty hours per work week, and modified work assignments to be implemented either for a one-year period or on a permanent basis. The Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator stated, and the record confirms, that she made numerous requests of the Complainant, including several written emails in June 2020, requesting provision of medical documentation to support the Complainant's reasonable accommodation requests and to establish the existence and nature of her claimed disability.

The Coordinator specifically requested that the Complainant provide medical documentation demonstrating the effectiveness of telework and telemedicine accommodations in relation to her medical condition, as well as information establishing the expected duration of her medical condition, including whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature. The Coordinator also requested that the Complainant provide authorization and consent for the Agency to contact her treating physician in order to gather necessary information and proceed with processing her accommodation request. Despite these repeated and documented requests, the Complainant failed to provide the requested medical documentation or authorization.

Consequently, on August 7, 2020, the Reasonable Accommodation Coordinator closed the Complainant's reasonable accommodation request file and formally notified the Complainant that the case would be reopened if she subsequently provided the requested documentation.

## MEDICAL RECORDS ANALYSIS

The record reflects that the Complainant provided the Agency with copies of Return to Work statements from her treating physicians. In a Return to Work statement dated January 13, 2020, the Complainant's first treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR1, documented that the Complainant had been seen in his office on that date and could return to work after a follow-up examination scheduled for February 10, 2020. In a subsequent Return to Work statement dated February 10, 2020, DR1 documented that the Complainant had been examined on that date and was medically cleared to return to work on March 2, 2020.

Additionally, the record contains a medical statement from a second treating physician, hereinafter referred to as DR2, dated February 25, 2020. In that statement, DR2 documented that the Complainant was under his care for her right shoulder condition and recommended that she be assigned light duty and part-time work with restrictions on lifting. DR2 further recommended that the Complainant be provided assistance with computer-related tasks and stated that her status and readiness to return to full duty would be reevaluated in six weeks.

In a subsequent statement dated April 21, 2020, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to continue on light duty status, work from home utilizing a laptop computer, and provide telemedicine services to patients. DR2 indicated that the Complainant's status for return to full duty would be reevaluated on May 19, 2020.

In two separate medical statements, both dated May 19, 2020, DR2 documented that the Complainant had been evaluated on that date for her right shoulder condition. The physician noted that the Complainant continued to experience dexterity issues and recommended that she continue physical therapy to address shoulder exercises and functional limitations. DR2 stated that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with appropriate ergonomic support and indicated that her status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.

On July 15, 2020, the Complainant submitted a statement from DR2 dated June 22, 2020. In this statement, DR2 recommended that the Complainant be allowed to work from home via telemedicine services, with a maximum of twenty hours per week. The physician documented that the Complainant continued to experience pain with associated dexterity issues, including difficulties with gripping and right arm and hand manipulation, and reported pain and functional difficulties when performing activities such as gripping the steering wheel while driving. DR2 recommended continuation of physical therapy and noted that the Complainant was able to use a computer and mouse with ergonomic support. The physician indicated that the Complainant's status for return to normal work activities would be reevaluated in six weeks.

In a final statement dated July 30, 2020, DR2 reiterated the foregoing clinical findings and recommendations. Additionally, DR2 noted that he was recommending evaluation by a spine specialist for the Complainant's condition, stated that her return to work status would be reevaluated, and documented that the Complainant's "shoulder symptoms are well controlled and is discharged at this time" from his direct care.

## AWOL DETERMINATION AND TERMINATION

Following the closure of the Complainant's reasonable accommodation case by the Coordinator, S1 and S2 indicated that the Coordinator suggested it would be appropriate and reasonable to place the Complainant in Absent Without Leave (AWOL) status for her continued absence from work. Management considered the Coordinator's recommendation in conjunction with the fact that the Complainant had not reported for work for nearly eight months and had not provided the medical documentation that the Agency had repeatedly requested. Based on these factors, management determined that it was appropriate to place the Complainant in AWOL status beginning August 10, 2020.

The Agency documented that the Complainant had utilized all available annual leave and sick leave accruals during the period from December 20, 2019, through February 6, 2020. Subsequently, the Complainant was granted LWOP in increments as follows: eighty hours for February 7 through February 29, 2020; four hundred eighty hours for March 2 through March 26, 2020; and four hundred twenty-one hours for March 26 through August 7, 2020. The Complainant remained in AWOL status from August 10, 2020, until her subsequent termination on January 22, 2021.

## ADMINISTRATIVE JUDGE DECISION

The Administrative Judge (AJ) issued a decision finding no discrimination, concluding that the Complainant failed to establish that the Agency had wrongfully denied her request for reasonable accommodation. The AJ determined that the Complainant had failed to provide adequate medical documentation demonstrating her ability to perform the essential functions of her position, specifically her ability to perform physical examinations of patients.

The AJ found that although the Complainant alleged she suffered from limitations in using her right arm, she had provided limited documentation to support the existence of a disability as defined under applicable law. The AJ noted that all medical documentation provided indicated that her treating physician would conduct reassessments at future dates. Despite the Agency's repeated requests, the Complainant failed to provide any medical documentation establishing a formal diagnosis of her condition or its duration—specifically, whether her condition was temporary or permanent in nature. The AJ further found that the Complainant had failed to execute a release authorization permitting the Agency to obtain medical information from her treating physicians and had declined to provide even the investigator with a release authorizing disclosure of her medical information.

The AJ additionally found that the Complainant had not demonstrated that she would be able to work from home through telework, as the Complainant herself had admitted that she was unable to use a pen or computer without assistance. The AJ noted that the permanent accommodation the Complainant was requesting—telework—was one for which she was not qualified, as telework would require an increase in computer usage, and as a Primary Care Physician, the Complainant was required to perform physical examinations of patients even in a telework arrangement. The AJ found that the Complainant had stated she was unable to perform such physical examinations on March 4, 2020, and had never subsequently provided documentation demonstrating that she had regained the ability to perform this essential function. The AJ concluded that the Complainant had refused to engage with the Agency regarding these critical issues by failing to provide the requested medical documentation, thereby causing the Agency to close her accommodation case without issuing either a formal denial or approval of her request.

## APPEAL AND PENDING MATTER

The Agency did not issue a separate final order, and the Administrative Judge's decision effectively became the final action of the Agency. The Complainant has appealed from this final action, contesting the Agency's finding of no discrimination.

# CASE FILE MEMORANDUM: INVESTIGATION RECORD

## CASE SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND

This memorandum documents the formal Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) complaint filed by the Complainant, a highly educated research scientist employed by the Agency's National Institute on Aging. During the relevant period, the Complainant worked as a Biologist at the GS-0401-11 level until her promotion to GS-12 in May 2013. She was assigned to the Laboratory of Neurogenetics, specifically within the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section, located in Bethesda, Maryland. On November 8, 2017, the Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint, which was subsequently amended to include additional allegations of discrimination and hostile work environment conditions.

## PROTECTED CLASS CHARACTERISTICS AND BASES FOR COMPLAINT

The Complainant identifies herself as belonging to multiple protected classes under federal employment discrimination law. She alleges discrimination based on the following characteristics: race and color (specifically, African American/Black descent), national origin (Guyanese nationality), and sex (female). Additionally, the Complainant reported several disability conditions that form a basis for her claims, including a diagnosis of bipolar disorder in 2009, which was later re-diagnosed as Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in 2017, generalized anxiety disorder, benign mitral valve prolapse, and fibroid tumors requiring surgical intervention in December 2013. The Complainant also asserts claims of reprisal based on her initiation of EEO counseling proceedings on July 27, 2017, relating to the instant complaint.

## SUPERVISORY RELATIONSHIPS AND KEY PERSONNEL

The Complainant's direct supervisor during the period at issue was the Section Chief, identified as Ireland, a Caucasian male. The Section Chief served as the Complainant's first-line supervisor and maintained responsibility for assigning work, conducting performance-related communications, and overseeing the day-to-day operations of the Section. The Complainant's second-line supervisor was the Lab Chief, identified as British and Caucasian, to whom she was reassigned in February 2018 following the initiation of her EEO complaint.

## SPECIFIC INCIDENTS AND ALLEGATIONS

The Complainant's amended complaint encompasses numerous specific incidents spanning from 2009 through April 2018. In June 2017, the Section Chief failed to conduct a scheduled meeting with the Complainant. Shortly thereafter, on June 15, 2017, the Section Chief notified the Complainant of a reassignment to DNA plate preparation duties, a role typically assigned to summer interns and student employees rather than doctoral-level biologists.

Following the Complainant's initiation of EEO counseling on July 27, 2017, the record reflects several alleged retaliatory actions. Agency management excluded the Complainant from a major project within her laboratory. The Section Chief reportedly ceased communicating with her regarding work assignments, and management failed to assign her additional projects. On February 23, 2018, the Section Chief did not promote the Complainant as allegedly promised.

The allegations of hostile work environment span nearly a decade. According to the Complainant, beginning in 2009, the Section Chief subjected her to inappropriate comments and unfair treatment. In 2009, he directed laboratory employees to engage in a project, made inappropriate comments, then retracted those comments while joking that he should refrain from further remarks lest an EEO complaint be filed against him. In 2010, the Section Chief allegedly stated that the Agency would submit research findings to a top-tier journal without the Complainant's authorship because the work required perfection. During the same year, he purportedly called the Complainant an "idiot" while deliberately distracting her during an experimental procedure and required her to work on Christmas Day. He repeatedly criticized her writing speed and the duration of her doctoral program completion.

In March 2011, after the Complainant was assigned to lead a task force, she experienced difficulties because the Section Chief frequently excluded her from electronic communications concerning task assignments. In April 2011, he made a statement suggesting that no one would tolerate her mental illness outside the current employment relationship. In September 2011, following her meeting with Career Services, the Section Chief questioned her decision to seek career guidance and suggested she remain in her current position. Approximately during the same period, the Complainant alleges the Section Chief placed her name last on a research article. In 2011, he made a comment suggesting she would enjoy the film "The Help." In 2012, he made jokes regarding her African ancestry. By 2013, he had engaged in uncomfortable exchanges concerning her family background and ancestry.

Additional allegations from 2013 include the Section Chief directing post-baccalaureate students to review the Complainant's work, referring to her as a "Diva" in a manner that discouraged colleague interaction, and precluding her from authoring manuscripts for top-tier journals. From 2016 onward, the Section Chief failed to attend their regularly scheduled one-on-one meetings and warned the Complainant not to knock on his closed office door. In May 2017, after initially indicating he would include her, the Section Chief excluded the Complainant from a project. On May 12, 2017, he yelled at her before colleagues, stating "No wonder nothing you do ever works" in response to her answer regarding laboratory protocols.

## MEDICAL PRIVACY VIOLATION AND DISABILITY DISCRIMINATION

In 2013, the Section Chief disclosed to a colleague that the Complainant had a heart condition and expressed dissatisfaction regarding the management of her medical issues. The Complainant denies ever disclosing her heart condition to either the Section Chief or the Lab Chief, asserting the Section Chief made this statement to preemptively protect himself from potential accusations of disclosing confidential medical information. The Complainant underwent surgical removal of fibroid tumors on December 18, 2013, requiring hospitalization and six weeks of recovery. Additionally, in late May or early June 2017, the Section Chief reportedly laughed with a colleague and trainee about an incident requiring the Complainant to work on Christmas Day.

## RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND EQUIPMENT DISCRIMINATION

The Complainant alleges that in June 2015, the Section Chief required her to accept a lower-specification computer compared to other laboratory employees. Additionally, the Section Chief acknowledged the Complainant deserved a promotion in 2015 but deliberately delayed processing the promotion paperwork until 2017, coinciding with an announced hiring freeze. The Complainant was notified of the indefinite hiring freeze in February 2017.

## POST-COMPLAINT RETALIATION AND EXCLUSION

Following the initiation of EEO counseling, the record reflects additional concerning actions. In February 2018, the Agency reassigned the Complainant to report directly to the Lab Chief, ostensibly due to her EEO complaint. In March 2018, the Lab Chief repositioned the Complainant's photograph in the breakroom under a different laboratory group, despite her continued membership in the Neuromuscular Disease Research Section. In March 2018, the Section Chief failed to communicate directly with the Complainant regarding an ongoing collaborative project, preventing her participation. On April 5, 2018, the Section Chief publicly announced to staff that the Complainant no longer reported to him. Subsequently, in April 2018, the Agency removed the Complainant's name from the National Institute on Aging website staff listing—a significant action given that her position required interaction with external agencies and collaborators. Finally, on April 23, 2018, all employees and collaborators began copying the Lab Chief on every email sent to the Complainant, regardless of the message's significance.

## ADMINISTRATIVE PROCESSING AND CURRENT STATUS

The Agency investigated the Complainant's amended EEO complaint. Following an Administrative Judge's remand for final decision, the Agency dismissed claims six through eleven for failure to timely initiate EEO counseling. The Agency found no discrimination on the remaining claims. On appeal, the Complainant documented that more than fifteen months elapsed after the Administrative Judge's prescribed sixty-day period without issuance of a Final Agency Decision. The Complainant submitted evidence that on May 20, 2020, she inquired about the status of the decision. She argues this extraordinary delay warrants a default judgment sanction against the Agency. The Agency did not submit a reply to the appeal.

items.source: At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a probationary Credentials Assistant, GS-0303-07, at the Agency’s Naval Medical Center in Portsmouth, Virginia. On November 8, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated against her based on race (African-American) when she was terminated from her probationary position on August 2, 2018. At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing. The AJ held a hearing and subsequently issued a decision in favor of the Agency. The AJ first determined that Complainant’s theory of discrimination based on direct evidence was unreliable and found that neither Complainant nor her supporting witness were credible. At the hearing, Complainant testified that her second-level supervisor (S2), Department Head, GS- 0301-12, “made the decision to terminate her after learning that her ‘significant other’ was [W]hite.” Complainant testified that S2 became aware of Complainant’s relationship with a White man in May 2018, and that her relationship with S2 changed afterward. She also testified that her first-level supervisor (S1), Professional Affairs Coordinator (Assistant Department Head), GS-0301-11, “had warned [Complainant] not to let [S2] know she was dating a [W]hite man.” To corroborate her theory that S2 discriminated against her based on her race, Complainant presented a key witness, a coworker (CW), Program Analyst, GS-0303-07, who “testified that [S2] openly stated that [S2’s] husband was extremely biased against interracial relationships, and that she was surprised Complainant was dating a [W]hite man. [CW] claims she heard [S2] make other race-related remarks.” Both Complainant and CW testified that S1 had warned them about S2’s prejudice. 2 The AJ found this testimony lacked credibility “due to the glaring omission of any theory about Complainant’s interracial relationship in her complaint, EEO counseling records, or her affidavit [during the investigation].” The AJ reasoned that “[t]his type of evidence, if credible, would not have come up for the first time some three years after her termination.” During EEO counseling and in her affidavit, Complainant explained that she believed her termination stemmed from events that occurred during a work conference in Leesburg, Virginia, where S2 allegedly engaged in inappropriate behavior, and Complainant believed that S2 “did not trust [her] to not share what happened.” Complainant also had indicated that her termination was related to the fact that S2 thought Complainant had filed a grievance against her, though it had been another employee. The AJ noted that these prior theories Complainant posited before the hearing about why S2 terminated her “have no apparent connection to her race.” When cross-examined by Agency counsel during the hearing about the fact that she had not previously raised the theory of S2’s prejudice against interracial couples, Complainant provided no explanation for why she had not included it. Similarly, the AJ found that any reference to S2’s prejudice against interracial relationships was “conspicuously missing from [CW’s] affidavit” submitted during the investigation. CW’s affidavit referenced the events at the training in Leesburg and that she believed “Complainant was discriminated against because she was an African-American with more experience than management.” CW also stated in her affidavit that S1 had made racially inappropriate remarks but nowhere mentioned anything about Complainant’s partner being White or S2’s opposition to it. S1 testified during the hearing and denied making any comments about S2 being racist. The AJ found that the Agency articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for Complainant’s termination. The reason, according to the Notice of Termination letter, was Complainant’s failure to “follow the privileging/credentialing process when [she] misrepresented to [her] leadership that a provider had specifically requested privileges when in fact [Complainant] made the request. According to the provider, [Complainant was] the one who tried to convince him to apply for privileges he did not previously hold.” This incident relates to a credentialing/privileges application submitted by the provider that Complainant helped process. In the application, the provider selected the incorrect privileges, which he had selected based on Complainant’s mistaken belief about the proper protocol for credentialing contract providers. Complainant’s guidance to the provider, which she acknowledged at the time was inaccurate, delayed the provider’s application and prevented him from receiving the proper credentials needed to practice within the Agency until the day his then-current privileges were set to expire. The provider then contacted Complainant’s supervisors “to express frustration with the delay in his application . . . [because Complainant] had provided him with incorrect guidance.” When her supervisors asked about the incident, Complainant explained to S1 that, before the provider’s discussion with Complainant, she had received an application from him within which he had improperly requested the incorrect privileges that he did not previously hold, and that her mistaken guidance was based on this prior application. After S2 obtained a written statement from the provider, S2 concluded that Complainant had misrepresented what happened, which provided part of the basis for Complainant’s termination. 3 The provider was a witness at the hearing, and the AJ found him credible when he testified that “he and Complainant discussed the [privileges] application before he submitted it” and that he submitted his application based on her instructions. The AJ found Complainant “not credible in her testimony that she never spoke to [the provider] prior to him submitting the [first] application.” The AJ therefore concluded that “Complainant has failed to prove pretext because there is no evidence that” the similarly situated employee named by Complainant “was involved in a similar episode, or that she was dishonest with her managers.” The AJ found Complainant’s testimony “simply unreliable” and that her “credibility is doubly important in this case because her lack of candor was part of why she was terminated.” The AJ therefore found that the Agency had not discriminated against Complainant as alleged. Part of Complainant’s Notice of Termination also included that Complainant “failed to initiate the renewal privileging/credentialing process within 90 days as required.” The AJ found, however, that it was untrue Complainant failed to do this, and that a similarly situated employee had several renewals nearing expiration with less than 90 days remaining but was not terminated. The AJ found that “[i]f this were the only reason for Complainant’s termination, she would be able to demonstrate pretext. But it was not.” When the Agency failed to issue a final order within forty days of receipt of the AJ’s decision, the AJ’s decision finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged became the Agency’s final action pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(i). 4 The instant appeal followed.
